01. RAG Foundations and Taxonomy: From REALM and RAG to the Modular Reference Architecture

Overview

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is the family of designs in which a language model's output depends on two things: what is stored in its weights (parametric memory) and text fetched at run time from an external store (non-parametric memory). Lewis et al. gave the idea its name in 2020 [1]. The lineage is older, though. Open-domain QA systems paired a retriever with a reader (ORQA [37]), kNN-LM interpolated a nearest-neighbour datastore into token probabilities [36], and REALM backpropagated through a learned retriever during pre-training a few months before RAG appeared [2].

This chapter covers three things:

  1. The five canonical research systems that set the design space between 2020 and 2022: REALM [2], RAG [1], Fusion-in-Decoder (FiD) [7], RETRO [4] and Atlas [9]. A short section follows on the 2023-2024 "frozen LLM" generation (In-Context RALM [21], REPLUG [22], RA-DIT [23], Retro++/InstructRetro [24][25], Self-RAG [26]), which carried those ideas over to API-served LLMs.

  2. The paradigm taxonomy that the field now uses: Naive, Advanced and Modular RAG, as set out in the Gao et al. survey [12] and the follow-up Modular RAG paper [13], extended by the 2025-2026 agentic-RAG literature [31][32].

  3. An end-to-end reference architecture (ingest, index, retrieve, rerank, generate, cite) with public numbers on cost, latency and quality, and a catalogue of failure modes [14][15][16].

  4. Developments the 2020-2022 canon does not cover (Section 12): graph-structured indexes (GraphRAG [38]), hierarchical summary trees (RAPTOR [39]), retrieval over page images (ColPali [40]) and reinforcement-learned search agents (Search-R1 [41]).

The other chapters of this atlas take the individual stages further. This chapter sets the vocabulary they use.

A useful frame from the start: every RAG design answers four questions.

  • Where does retrieval happen? In pre-training (REALM, RETRO, Atlas), in fine-tuning (RAG, FiD), or only at inference (In-Context RALM, most production systems).
  • What is the unit of retrieval? A 100-word passage (RAG, FiD), a 288-wordpiece block (REALM), a 64-token chunk (RETRO), or a section-aligned passage of up to 200 words (Atlas).
  • Where are retrieved items fused with the query? In the input sequence (RAG, REPLUG), in the decoder's cross-attention (FiD, Atlas), in chunked cross-attention inside the decoder stack (RETRO), or in the output distribution (kNN-LM, continuous cache) [36].
  • Is the retriever trained, and with what signal? It may be frozen (RETRO), trained query-side only (RAG, Atlas few-shot), trained end to end with a refreshed index (REALM, Atlas pre-training), or trained from the LM's own preferences (REPLUG-LSR, RA-DIT).

1. Pre-history: retrieve-then-read and dense retrieval

1.1 Retrieve-then-read open-domain QA

Before 2020, open-domain QA meant two stages. A sparse retriever (TF-IDF/BM25) selected Wikipedia passages, and an extractive reader picked out an answer span. ORQA (Lee et al., 2019) [37] made retrieval a latent variable trained by marginal likelihood. REALM extended this directly [2]. The weakness of an extractive reader is structural: it can only return strings that appear verbatim in a retrieved passage.

1.2 Nearest-neighbour language models (kNN-LM)

kNN-LM (Khandelwal et al., ICLR 2020) is the clearest pre-RAG example of output-level fusion. A trained LM's context vectors are stored as keys in a datastore whose values are the next tokens. At inference the model's next-token distribution is linearly interpolated with a distribution built from the k nearest stored contexts, with no extra training [36]. It showed that a frozen model can gain from a non-parametric memory, and that the datastore can be swapped for domain adaptation, at the cost of one nearest-neighbour search per generated token. RETRO's per-chunk retrieval is in part a response to that per-token cost [4].

1.3 Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR)

DPR [11] is the retriever that RAG and FiD used. It is a bi-encoder: two independent BERT-base encoders, with the [CLS] vector (d = 768) as the representation and dot-product similarity. It was trained with in-batch negatives (batch size 128) plus one hard BM25 negative per question. Its headline numbers made dense retrieval the default:

  • Top-20 retrieval accuracy on Natural Questions was 78.4% against 59.1% for BM25, and top-100 was 85.4% against 73.7% [11].
  • At query time, a FAISS in-memory index served 995 questions/second (top-100 passages) on a Xeon server. BM25/Lucene served 23.7 questions/second per CPU thread [11].
  • Indexing cost ran the other way. Embedding 21M passages took about 8.8 hours on 8 GPUs, and building the FAISS index on a single server took another 8.5 hours, against about 30 minutes for a Lucene inverted index [11].

Lesson. Dense retrieval moves cost from query time to ingest time, and every encoder change re-incurs that cost. Index staleness, covered in REALM and Atlas below, is the training-time version of the same problem.

2. REALM (Google, 2020): retrieval inside pre-training

Problem

Masked language models store world knowledge implicitly in their weights. REALM asked whether a model could learn to look things up during pre-training, with an unsupervised signal deciding which documents help [2].

Architecture

 masked sentence x ──► Embed_input(x) ─┐
                                       │  MIPS over ~13M Wikipedia blocks
 Wikipedia blocks z ─► Embed_doc(z) ───┤  (index rebuilt asynchronously)
                                       ▼
                         top-k docs + null doc ∅
                                       │
                         p(z|x) = softmax(Embed_input(x)·Embed_doc(z))
                                       ▼
            knowledge-augmented encoder p(y|z,x) (BERT over [x ; z])
                                       ▼
            p(y|x) = Σ_z p(y|z,x) p(z|x)   ── gradient flows into retriever
  • Retriever. A BERT-style dual encoder scored by inner product. The knowledge corpus is the 20 December 2018 English Wikipedia, greedily split into chunks of up to 288 BERT wordpieces, giving just over 13 million candidates [2].
  • Objective. Retrieve, then predict. The document is a latent variable and the loss is the marginal likelihood. The retriever gradient raises the score of document z exactly when p(y|z,x) > p(y|x), so documents that help predict the masked tokens are rewarded [2].
  • Asynchronous index refresh. Updating the document embedder makes the MIPS index stale after every step. REALM runs a trainer job and a separate index-builder job in parallel, and the index is refreshed about every 500 training steps. Because the stale index is used only to select the top k, p(z|x) is recomputed with fresh parameters for the selected documents [2].
  • Salient span masking. REALM masks named entities (from a CoNLL-2003 BERT tagger) and dates (from a regex) rather than random tokens, so that masked spans need world knowledge [2].
  • Null document. An empty document is added to the top k as a sink for predictions that need no retrieval [2].

Scale and results

Pre-training ran for 200k steps on 64 Google Cloud TPUs (batch size 512). Document embedding for the index was parallelized over 16 TPUs, and each example marginalized over 8 candidates including the null document [2]. The open-source README says a typical single-machine setup lacks the needed resources, "80 TPUs and numerous CPUs", and notes that the release replaced ScaNN with brute-force matrix multiplication [3]. Fine-tuned for open-domain QA (top-5 candidates), the 330M-parameter REALM reached 40.4 / 40.7 / 42.9 exact match (EM) on NQ / WebQuestions / CuratedTrec with CC-News pre-training. ORQA, with the same fine-tuning setup, scored 33.3 / 36.4 / 30.1 [2].

Failure modes and lessons

The ablations isolate each ingredient [2]:

REALM ablation (NQ dev) EM Gold answer in top-5 at init
Full REALM 38.2 38.5
Random uniform masking 32.3 24.2
Random span masking 35.3 26.1
30x staler MIPS index 28.7 15.1
Baseline (ORQA) 31.3 13.9

Lessons. (a) Index freshness is a first-order concern: a 30x staler index is worse than the baseline. (b) The pretext task must actually require retrieval; salient spans matter. (c) End-to-end retriever training is expensive enough that REALM used asynchronous refresh only in pre-training. During fine-tuning it trained only the query encoder against a fixed index. That compromise reappears in RAG and Atlas.

3. RAG (Facebook AI / UCL / NYU, 2020): the generative template

Problem

Extractive readers cannot synthesize an answer, and parametric seq2seq models cannot cite, update or verify what they know. RAG fine-tunes a pre-trained generator jointly with a pre-trained retriever, so that any seq2seq task can draw on a dense Wikipedia index [1].

Architecture

  x ──► DPR query encoder q(x) (BERT-base, trainable)
           │  MIPS (FAISS, HNSW) over 21M x 100-word passages
           ▼  document encoder d(z) FROZEN; index never rebuilt
   top-K passages z_1..z_K with p_eta(z|x) ∝ exp(d(z)·q(x))
           │
           ├─► BART-large( [z_1 ; x] ) ─┐
           ├─► BART-large( [z_2 ; x] ) ─┼─► marginalize over z
           └─► BART-large( [z_K ; x] ) ─┘   (per sequence or per token)
                                              ▼
                                              y
  • Components. A DPR retriever, made of a BERT-base query encoder and a BERT-base document encoder with 110M parameters each, and a BART-large generator with 406M parameters, for 626M parameters in total [1]. The document encoder and index stay frozen. Only the query encoder and the generator are fine-tuned, which avoids re-embedding the corpus [1].
  • Corpus and index. The December 2018 Wikipedia dump, split into disjoint 100-word chunks for 21M documents, indexed in FAISS with an HNSW approximation. Training used k in {5, 10} [1].
  • Two marginalization schemes. In written-out notation:
    • RAG-Sequence uses one document for the whole output: p(y|x) ≈ Σ_{z∈topK} p(z|x) · Π_i p(y_i | x, z, y_<i).
    • RAG-Token can switch documents at each token: p(y|x) ≈ Π_i Σ_{z∈topK} p(z|x) · p(y_i | x, z, y_<i). For classification the two are equivalent [1].
  • Decoding. RAG-Token uses standard beam search over the marginalized per-token distribution. RAG-Sequence needs a beam search per document plus extra forward passes to score hypotheses that did not appear in every beam ("Thorough Decoding"). A cheaper approximation ("Fast Decoding") skips those extra passes [1]. Test-time QA used 15 documents for RAG-Token and 50 documents with Thorough Decoding for RAG-Sequence [1].

Infrastructure numbers

Training ran on 8 x 32 GB V100 GPUs. The index lived on CPU and needed about 100 GB of CPU memory, which FAISS compression later reduced to 36 GB [1]. The model was ported to Hugging Face Transformers, which ships RagSequenceForGeneration, RagTokenForGeneration and a RagRetriever with a compressed wiki_dpr index [33].

Results

Model (open-domain QA EM) NQ TQA (std / wiki) WQ CT
T5-11B closed-book 34.5 - / 50.1 37.4 -
REALM 40.4 - / - 40.7 46.8
DPR (retrieve+rerank+extract) 41.5 57.9 / - 41.1 50.6
RAG-Token 44.1 55.2 / 66.1 45.5 50.0
RAG-Sequence 44.5 56.8 / 68.0 45.2 52.2

Source: [1], Table 1.

Beyond QA, RAG reached 72.5% / 89.5% label accuracy on FEVER 3-way / 2-way without retrieval supervision. Human raters judged RAG more factual than BART in 42.7% of Jeopardy question-generation comparisons, and BART more factual in only 7.1% [1]. On NQ, RAG answered 11.8% of questions correctly even when no retrieved passage contained the answer string, a case where an extractive reader must score 0 [1].

Index hot-swapping. Built against a December 2016 index, the NQ model answered 70% of "Who is {position}?" questions correctly for 2016 world leaders. The 2018 index gave 68% for 2018 leaders. Mismatched pairs gave 12% and 4% [1]. Knowledge can be updated without gradient steps, which is the property production RAG depends on.

Failure modes and lessons

  • Retrieval collapse. On story generation, the retriever learned to return the same documents for every input, the generator learned to ignore them, and RAG degraded to BART [1]. Weak or long-horizon supervision does not train a retriever reliably.
  • Sparse beats dense on entity-centric claims. Swapping in BM25 gave the best FEVER result (75.1 vs. 72.9 dev accuracy for the frozen-dense variant) [1]. This is an early argument for hybrid retrieval.
  • Neither a reranker nor an extractive reader was necessary for state-of-the-art results in 2020 [1]. Later systems brought reranking back once generators were frozen black boxes and context budgets mattered (Section 10.4).

4. Fusion-in-Decoder (FiD, Facebook AI, 2020-2021): scaling the number of passages

Problem

RAG marginalizes over K separate generator passes, while early-fusion readers concatenate every passage into one quadratic-cost encoder input. Neither handles evidence spread over tens or hundreds of passages efficiently [7].

Architecture

 question + passage_1 ─► T5 encoder ─► H_1 ─┐
 question + passage_2 ─► T5 encoder ─► H_2 ─┤  concatenate [H_1 ... H_N]
        ...                          ...    ├──► T5 decoder cross-attends to all
 question + passage_N ─► T5 encoder ─► H_N ─┘        └─► answer
 (independent, linear in N)            (joint "fusion" happens only in decoder)

Each retrieved passage is concatenated with its title and the question and encoded independently. The decoder attends over the concatenation of all encoded passages. Encoder cost therefore grows linearly with the number of passages, and evidence is fused in the decoder [7].

Numbers

  • T5-base (220M) and T5-large (770M) readers, trained on 64 x V100 32 GB for 10k steps [7].
  • FiD-large reached 51.4 EM on NQ and 67.6 on TriviaQA [7]. The repository reports 54.4 NQ test for a large reader trained with retriever distillation, and a distilled retriever at R@20 = 84.3 on NQ [8].
  • Going from 10 to 100 passages added about 3.5 EM on NQ and 6 EM on TriviaQA, whereas extractive readers typically peaked at 10-20 passages [7].
  • Training on fewer passages and then fine-tuning for 1,000 steps with 100 passages reached 46.0 EM in 147 GPU-hours, against 425 GPU-hours for full 100-passage training [7].

Failure modes and lessons

FiD's inference cost is not dominated by the encoder. FiDO (Google, 2022) showed that the encoder receives most of the FLOPs, while decoder memory bandwidth (cross-attention over thousands of cached encoder states) accounts for most inference time. Two architectural changes yielded about a 7x inference speedup, enough to afford a much larger decoder [20]. Lesson. Benchmark RAG latency on memory traffic, not FLOPs. The same holds for today's long-context prompts, where prefill and KV-cache size dominate.

FiD's cross-attention scores also became a relevance signal: "distilling knowledge from reader to retriever" trains the retriever to imitate where the reader looks [8]. Atlas generalizes this idea.

5. RETRO (DeepMind, 2021): retrieval at trillion-token scale

Problem

Can retrieval substitute for parameters at the scale of pre-training, so that a 7B model matches models 25x larger by consulting a database bigger than its training set [4][5]?

Architecture

 input (2048 tokens) split into 64-token chunks C_1 ... C_32
        │
        │  for chunk C_u: key = mean-pooled FROZEN BERT(C_u)
        ▼  SCaNN approx. kNN over key-value DB (value = neighbour N + continuation F)
  Ret(C_u) = k neighbours x (64 + 64 tokens)
        │
        ▼  small bidirectional encoder over neighbours (conditioned on C_u)
  ┌──────────────────────── decoder stack ─────────────────────────┐
  │ standard blocks: self-attn + FFN                               │
  │ RETRO blocks:   self-attn + CHUNKED CROSS-ATTENTION + FFN      │
  │   tokens of chunk u+1 attend to neighbours retrieved for C_u   │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  • Chunked retrieval. Retrieving per 64-token chunk rather than per token cuts storage and compute "by a large linear factor" [4]. Each database value is a neighbour chunk N plus its continuation F, each up to 64 tokens [4][6].
  • Frozen retriever. Keys are frozen BERT embeddings averaged over time, so the database never needs re-embedding during training. Neighbours were precomputed for all training data because on-the-fly retrieval could not keep up with training [4].
  • Latency. With SCaNN, the 2-trillion-token database can be queried in 10 ms while sampling, a cost amortized over a 64-token chunk [4].
  • Chunked cross-attention (CCA). Cost is linear in the amount of retrieved data. Causality is kept by letting chunk u+1 attend only to neighbours of chunk u, and by filtering neighbours from the same source document during training [4]. RETRO blocks are interleaved with standard blocks at a fixed stride (roughly every third layer, starting later in larger models); see the paper's architecture appendix and Alammar's walkthrough for the exact layer sets [4][6].
  • Data. Multilingual MassiveText (over 5T tokens). The training-time retrieval DB holds 600B tokens and the evaluation DB 1.75T tokens. Training documents with 13-gram Jaccard similarity of 0.8 or more to test documents were removed (MinHash) [4].

Results and scale

  • Gains hold from 150M to 7B parameters and do not shrink with size. Larger databases and more neighbours help even at evaluation time: models trained with 2 neighbours keep improving up to 10 neighbours (172M) or 40 neighbours (7B) [4].
  • The 7.5B RETRO outperforms Jurassic-1 (178B) and Gopher (280B) on a majority of Pile subsets [4]. DeepMind summarized this as performance comparable to GPT-3 with 25x fewer parameters [5].
  • RETROfitting. Freezing a pre-trained transformer and training only the CCA and neighbour-encoder weights (under 10% of the weights for 7B) on 6M sequences (3% of pre-training) nearly matches training from scratch, and leaves performance with retrieval switched off unchanged [4].
  • On NQ, the fine-tuned RETRO 7.5B (with DPR passages) reached 45.5 EM: competitive with RAG (44.5) but below FiD (51.4) and FiD+distillation (54.7). More than 20 neighbours did not help [4].

Failure modes and lessons

  • Leakage. A retriever with access to the training corpus can copy evaluation text. RETRO introduced filtered bits-per-byte as a function of chunk overlap. RETRO exploits leakage more than baselines (steeper slope), yet it still beats baselines at overlap as low as 12.5%, i.e. fewer than 8 shared contiguous tokens [4]. Any RAG evaluation should measure overlap between the corpus and the test set.
  • Reproducibility. There was no official open-source release. NVIDIA later reproduced RETRO up to 9.5B parameters with a 330B-token retrieval corpus [24]. It then continued pre-training a 43B GPT on 100B tokens while retrieving from 1.2T tokens, for about 2.58% extra GPU-hours, producing Retro 48B. After instruction tuning, "InstructRetro" improved over instruction-tuned GPT by on average 7% on short-form QA, 10% on long-form QA and 16% on summarization, zero-shot. The authors also found that the retrieval encoder could be removed with comparable results [25].
  • Industry lesson. Architecturally integrated retrieval works, but the market moved to in-context retrieval with frozen LLMs (Section 8), which needs no custom pre-training.

6. Atlas (Meta AI, 2022): joint pre-training for few-shot RAG

Problem

Large LLMs appeared to need huge parameter counts to store knowledge for few-shot use. Atlas asked whether a much smaller, jointly pre-trained retrieval-augmented model could learn knowledge-intensive tasks from a handful of examples [9].

Architecture

Atlas pairs a Contriever dual-encoder retriever (BERT-base, mean pooling, shared query/document weights) with a FiD reader built on T5 v1.1 (770M, 3B and 11B variants) [9][10]. Retrieval runs in the training loop. Each GPU holds 1/N of the passage embeddings and runs exact inner-product search on its shard; FAISS (for example, IVF-PQ with code size 16) is optional for memory savings [10]. The code was tested up to 11B-parameter readers and 400M-passage (~40B-word) indices [10].

Retriever training objectives compared in the paper [9]:

Objective Training signal for the retriever
Attention Distillation (ADist) reader cross-attention mass on each passage
EMDR2 EM-style, passages as latent variables (token-level)
Perplexity Distillation (PDist) how much each passage alone improves LM likelihood (KL)
Leave-one-out (LOOP) how much worse the LM gets when one passage is removed

Atlas uses PDist with masked-language-model pre-training on a Wikipedia plus Common Crawl mix for its final models [9].

Index staleness is handled three ways [9][10]:

  1. Full refresh. For a 37M-document index, batch 64, 20 retrieved documents, and a refresh every 1,000 steps, the overhead is about 30% [9].
  2. Over-retrieve and rerank. Retrieve L > K with the stale index and re-embed those L with the current retriever. With L = 10K the overhead is about 10% [9].
  3. Query-side fine-tuning. Freeze the document encoder so there is no refresh at all. This was best in few-shot settings (45.0 vs. 44.3 for standard fine-tuning in the 64-shot ablation's NQ column) [9].

Corpus, memory and cost

  • The December 2021 Wikipedia index, with infoboxes and lists linearized and passages under 200 words, holds 37M passages (78 words on average). The CCNet-filtered Common Crawl index holds 350M passages [9].
  • Embeddings stored in fp16 need 49 GB of GPU memory for Wikipedia and 587 GB for the combined index. Product quantization compresses these to 4 GB and 50 GB with negligible loss in retrieval precision and EM [9]. Tokenized passages take 11 GB / 130 GB but can live on disk or be memory-mapped [9].
  • Atlas-11B was trained with about 3.5e22 FLOPs [9].

Results

  • 64-shot NQ: 42.4% EM, ahead of PaLM-540B (39.6%) with about 50x fewer parameters [9]. The repository README reports over 45% with a 2018 index, in line with the paper's +3.6% gain from a temporally matched index [10][9].
  • Full NQ: 60.4% EM, the state of the art at the time. TriviaQA 74.5 [9]. The README quotes 64% for full NQ; the figures differ by setup and version [10].
  • MMLU (11B, with the paper's de-biased inference): 47.9% 5-shot, 56.6% 5-shot multi-task, and 66.0% with full/transfer fine-tuning. Note that Atlas fine-tunes in its "5-shot" setting, unlike in-context baselines, and that appendix tables without de-biasing report lower figures (for example 43.5 multi-task, 54.0 full/transfer) [9].
  • Leakage control. Filtering possibly leaked passages from the index lowered MMLU accuracy by less than one point, indicating that leakage did not drive the result [9].

Lessons

(a) Joint pre-training of retriever and reader pays off most in few-shot regimes. (b) Index compression is close to free: about 10x with negligible loss. (c) Temporal alignment between index and benchmark is worth several EM points, so production indexes need versioning, not just updates.

Cell values come from each system's paper. Where a cell is qualitative, the paper's headline claim is quoted rather than a number.

8. The "frozen LLM" turn (2023-2024)

Once instruction-tuned LLMs became API products, end-to-end training like REALM's and Atlas's no longer fit. The research frontier moved to designs that leave the LLM untouched:

  • In-Context RALM (AI21) prepends retrieved documents to the input of an unmodified LM. It re-retrieves every s tokens (the retrieval stride) and shows that smaller strides perform better at a runtime cost [21]. Secondary summaries put the recommended stride at about 4 tokens, against RETRO's 64; treat that figure as approximate [21].
  • REPLUG treats the LM as a black box: retrieved documents are prepended separately and the output distributions are ensembled. REPLUG-LSR trains the retriever from the LM's own likelihoods. The authors report +6.3% on GPT-3 (175B) language modelling and +5.1% on Codex 5-shot MMLU [22].
  • RA-DIT (Meta, ICLR 2024) retrofits an LLM with two lightweight fine-tuning stages: one teaches the LM to use retrieved text, the other teaches the retriever what the LM prefers. RA-DIT 65B gained up to +8.9% (0-shot) and +1.4% (5-shot) on average over in-context RALM baselines [23].
  • Self-RAG trains one LM to emit reflection tokens: whether to retrieve, whether a passage is relevant (ISREL), whether the generation is supported by the passage (ISSUP), and overall utility. These tokens make retrieval adaptive and decoding controllable [26].
  • CRAG adds a lightweight T5-large retrieval evaluator. It classifies a retrieval as {Correct, Incorrect, Ambiguous}. It then triggers decompose-then-recompose knowledge refinement or a fallback to web search [27].

These designs mark the move from a fixed retrieve-then-read pipeline to control flow, the defining property of Modular RAG.

9. Taxonomy: Naive, Advanced and Modular RAG

The most widely used taxonomy comes from Gao et al.'s survey (Tongji/Fudan, Dec 2023, updated Mar 2024) [12]. It describes three paradigms as nested special cases: "Advanced RAG is a special case of Modular RAG, while Naive RAG is a special case of Advanced RAG" [12].

9.1 Naive RAG ("Retrieve-Read")

 docs ─► parse ─► fixed-size chunks ─► embed ─► vector DB
                                                   │
 query ─► embed ─► top-K similarity ───────────────┘──► prompt(query + K chunks) ─► LLM

Indexing turns PDF, HTML, Word and Markdown into plain text, chunks it, embeds it and stores it. Retrieval embeds the query with the same model and takes the top-K most similar chunks. Generation builds a prompt from the query and chunks [12]. The survey lists the drawbacks [12]:

  • Retrieval: low precision and recall (misaligned or irrelevant chunks, missed facts).
  • Generation: hallucination unsupported by the context; irrelevance, toxicity, bias.
  • Augmentation: disjointed outputs, redundancy across chunks, a single retrieval that is insufficient for complex questions, and over-reliance that merely echoes the retrieved text.

9.2 Advanced RAG (pre- and post-retrieval optimization)

Still a linear chain, but with work added on both sides of retrieval [12]:

  • Pre-retrieval / indexing: sliding windows, finer segmentation, metadata, alignment, mixed (hybrid) retrieval.
  • Pre-retrieval / query: rewriting, transformation, expansion. Examples include Rewrite-Retrieve-Read [35], HyDE, which embeds an LLM-written hypothetical answer document instead of the query [28], and multi-query fusion.
  • Post-retrieval: reranking, including moving the most relevant chunks to the edges of the prompt (a response to "lost in the middle"), and context compression or selection [12][15].

9.3 Modular RAG (reconfigurable modules and flows)

Modular RAG adds new modules: Search (across search engines, databases and knowledge graphs via generated code or query languages), RAG-Fusion multi-query, Memory, Routing, Predict (LLM-generated context) and Task Adapter. It also adds new patterns: Rewrite-Retrieve-Read, Generate-Read, Recite-Read, Demonstrate-Search-Predict [34], ITER-RETGEN's Retrieve-Read-Retrieve-Read loop, and adaptive retrieval (FLARE, Self-RAG) [12].

The follow-up paper "Modular RAG: Transforming RAG Systems into LEGO-like Reconfigurable Frameworks" (Gao et al., July 2024) formalizes this. It decomposes systems into modules, sub-modules and operators, and names four flow patterns: linear, conditional, branching and looping [13].

9.4 Beyond modular: agentic RAG (2025-2026)

Agentic RAG puts an LLM agent in charge of the loop. The agent plans, chooses tools and indexes, reflects on evidence, and decides when to stop. Singh et al. (Jan 2025; v4 April 2026) organize systems around four agentic patterns (reflection, planning, tool use, multi-agent collaboration) and catalogue seven architectures: single-agent (router), multi-agent, hierarchical, corrective, adaptive, graph-based, and agentic document workflows [31]. Mishra et al.'s March 2026 systematization-of-knowledge paper models agentic RAG as a finite-horizon POMDP and classifies systems along four dimensions: planning, memory, tool orchestration and retrieval strategy [32]. Later chapters of this atlas cover these designs. In the taxonomy here, agentic RAG is Modular RAG whose looping and branching operators are chosen at run time by a model rather than fixed by an engineer.

9.5 Paradigm comparison

Dimension Naive RAG Advanced RAG Modular RAG Agentic RAG
Control flow fixed linear fixed linear, extra stages linear / conditional / branching / looping [13] model-decided loops, tools [31]
Query handling raw query rewrite, expand, HyDE [28][35] routing, multi-query, sub-queries planning and decomposition
Index one dense index metadata, hybrid, finer chunks multiple stores (vector, KG, SQL, web) any tool-accessible source
Post-retrieval none rerank, compress fusion, evaluation (CRAG [27]) self-critique, retry
When to retrieve always, once always, once adaptive (FLARE, Self-RAG [26]) agent decides
Training none optional embedder fine-tuning optional joint tuning (RA-DIT [23]) optional RL / tool training
Typical failure misses, noise latency and cost of extra stages orchestration complexity unbounded loops, cost variance

10. The end-to-end reference architecture

Production systems from this period converge on six stages, plus an evaluation loop that runs across all of them. The diagram uses the chapter's vocabulary; the numbers attached to each stage come from the cited sources.

                   OFFLINE (ingest + index)                     ONLINE (query path)
 ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌───────────┐  ┌──────────────┐
 │ 1 INGEST │─►│  chunk   │─►│  enrich / │─►│   2 INDEX    │
 │ parse,   │  │ size,    │  │ contextual│  │ dense (ANN)  │
 │ clean,   │  │ overlap, │  │ -ize, add │  │ + sparse BM25│
 │ ACLs     │  │ structure│  │ metadata  │  │ + metadata   │
 └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └───────────┘  └──────┬───────┘
                                                    │
 user ─► query understanding ─► 3 RETRIEVE ◄────────┘
         (rewrite, HyDE,        hybrid top-N (e.g. N=150), filters
          route, decompose)          │
                                     ▼
                                4 RERANK  cross-encoder / late interaction
                                     │    top-K (e.g. K=20)
                                     ▼
                                5 GENERATE  prompt assembly, ordering,
                                     │      compression, LLM call
                                     ▼
                                6 CITE      span-level attribution,
                                     │      support checking
                                     ▼
                                  answer + sources ──► logs ──► EVALUATE
                                                         (faithfulness, recall)

10.1 Ingest

What it does. Parse heterogeneous formats into clean text, preserve structure (titles, sections, tables), attach metadata (source, page, timestamp, author, permissions), and chunk the result.

Evidence and numbers.

  • The canonical research systems used 100-word disjoint passages (RAG, DPR, FiD) [1][11][7], 288-wordpiece blocks (REALM) [2], or section-aligned passages under 200 words, with linearized infoboxes and lists (Atlas) [9]. Including infoboxes and tables as text was a deliberate choice in Atlas.
  • The survey lists fixed token sizes (100/256/512) as the most common method, notes the trade-off (larger chunks bring more context but more noise and cost), and recommends metadata attachments plus artificial metadata such as summaries or hypothetical questions ("Reverse HyDE") [12].
  • Contextual Retrieval (Anthropic, Sept 2024) shows how much chunking discards. A chunk like "The company's revenue grew by 3%..." loses its company and quarter. An LLM (Claude 3 Haiku in the post) writes 50-100 tokens of chunk-specific context from the whole document, prepended before embedding and before BM25 indexing. With prompt caching, the one-time cost was quoted at $1.02 per million document tokens (assuming 800-token chunks and 8k-token documents) [16]. Generic document summaries added to chunks gave "very limited gains" [16].
  • Barnett et al. found that adding the file name and chunk number to retrieved context helped the reader extract answers [14].

10.2 Index

What it does. Build one or more access paths: an ANN index over embeddings (HNSW, IVF, IVF-PQ), an inverted index for lexical retrieval, and metadata filters.

Evidence and numbers.

  • Memory. RAG's 21M-passage Wikipedia index used about 100 GB of CPU RAM, or 36 GB compressed [1]. Atlas's indexes went from 49 GB to 4 GB and from 587 GB to 50 GB with PQ at negligible quality cost [9].
  • Build cost. DPR needed 8.8 h on 8 GPUs to embed 21M passages plus 8.5 h to build FAISS, against about 30 minutes for Lucene [11]. Changing the embedding model means re-embedding the whole corpus, so plan for it.
  • Freshness. Updating an index changes answers without training (RAG's 2016/2018 swap [1]; Atlas's temporal experiments [9]). Staleness within a learned system is harmful: REALM's 30x-staler-index ablation fell below the baseline [2].
  • Hybrid. Dense and lexical indexes are complementary. DPR+BM25 beat either alone on most datasets [11], BM25 won FEVER inside RAG [1], and Anthropic found that "Embeddings+BM25 is better than embeddings on their own", especially for exact identifiers such as error codes [16].
  • Small corpora. If the knowledge base is under about 200k tokens (about 500 pages), Anthropic suggests skipping retrieval and putting it all in the prompt with prompt caching. Caching was quoted as cutting latency by more than 2x and cost by up to 90% [16].

10.3 Retrieve

What it does. Turn the user request into one or more queries, search each access path, and fuse the candidate lists (for example with reciprocal rank fusion).

Evidence and numbers.

  • Query transformation: Rewrite-Retrieve-Read trains a small rewriter with LM feedback [35]. HyDE embeds a generated hypothetical document for zero-shot dense retrieval [28]. DSP composes multi-hop search and predict programs [34].
  • Recall budgets. Anthropic retrieved the top 150 candidates before reranking. Measured as 1 - recall@20, contextual embeddings cut retrieval failures by 35% (5.7% to 3.7%), and contextual embeddings plus contextual BM25 by 49% (5.7% to 2.9%) [16].
  • Throughput. A dense ANN search over tens of millions of vectors is cheap: DPR served about 1k queries/s on CPU [11], and RETRO queried 2T tokens in about 10 ms [4]. In production, latency is dominated by the query-embedding call, reranking and generation, not by the ANN search.

10.4 Rerank

What it does. Re-score a few hundred candidates with a more expensive model that sees query and document together (a cross-encoder) or uses token-level late interaction (ColBERT), then keep the top K.

Evidence and numbers.

  • ColBERT's late interaction gave over 170x speedup and 14,000x fewer FLOPs than BERT-based cross-encoder reranking on MS MARCO, while beating every non-BERT baseline. The paper also notes that adding as little as 100 ms of latency affects user experience [19].
  • Reranking the contextual-retrieval candidates (Cohere reranker, top 150 down to 20) raised the reduction in retrieval failures to 67% (5.7% to 1.9%) [16].
  • Atlas's "over-retrieve and rerank with the fresh encoder" is the same pattern used during training [9].
  • Trade-off. Reranking adds latency even though candidates are scored in parallel. Cost grows with N [16].

10.5 Generate

What it does. Assemble a prompt (instructions, conversation, ordered evidence with source markers) and call the generator. Optionally compress or filter the context, and decide whether retrieval was needed at all.

Evidence and numbers.

  • Position matters. Liu et al. found a U-shaped accuracy curve: relevant information at the start or end of the context is used best. GPT-3.5-Turbo's multi-document QA accuracy fell by more than 20 points when the answer sat in the middle. In some 20-30 document settings it fell below the closed-book score of 56.1% [15].
  • More is not always better. Anthropic found top-20 chunks better than top-10 or top-5, but warned that extra context can distract [16]. FiD-style readers improved up to 100 passages [7], whereas RETRO stopped improving past 20 neighbours on NQ [4].
  • Long context vs. RAG. Li et al. (EMNLP 2024 industry track) found that long-context LLMs given enough resources outperform RAG on average, while RAG is far cheaper. Their Self-Route sends each query to RAG or to long context based on the model's self-reflection [30]. Per secondary summaries, token savings reached about 65% in some settings; treat this as approximate [30].
  • Adaptive retrieval. Self-RAG and CRAG decide whether and how to use retrieved text instead of always conditioning on it [26][27]. Barnett et al. report that a larger context window (8K vs. 4K) gave more accurate answers in their case studies [14].

10.6 Cite

What it does. Attach verifiable pointers from claims in the answer to source spans, and optionally check that each claim is supported.

Evidence and practice.

  • The original RAG paper already presented provenance and interpretability as a benefit of non-parametric memory [1]. Atlas emphasized inspecting retrieved items [9].
  • API-level citations. Anthropic's Citations feature chunks supplied documents into sentences (or uses caller-defined content blocks). It returns each claim with pointers (character, page or block ranges) into the source. Because cited_text is extracted by the API, citations are "guaranteed to contain valid pointers to the provided documents", and quoted text does not count as output tokens [17]. Search-result content blocks let a custom RAG tool return results that Claude cites with the source and title the caller provides [18].
  • Model-level support checking. Self-RAG's ISSUP token predicts whether a passage supports a generated segment, and the decoder can weight it more heavily [26].
  • Evaluation. RAGAS defines reference-free faithfulness (the share of answer statements inferable from the context), answer relevance and context relevance, each scored by an LLM [29].

10.7 The cross-cutting loop: evaluate, monitor, recalibrate

Barnett et al.'s experience report (three case studies, 15,000 documents, 1,000 questions) reaches two conclusions. RAG validation is only feasible during operation, and robustness "evolves rather than [is] designed in" [14]. Among their lessons: RAG systems need continuous calibration of chunk size, embedding strategy, chunking strategy, retrieval strategy, consolidation strategy, context size and prompts. A semantic cache pre-filled with FAQs cut cost and latency. Jailbreaks can bypass RAG grounding. Open-source embedding models matched closed ones on small texts [14].

10.8 Failure-point map

Barnett et al.'s seven failure points [14] map onto the reference stages:

# Failure point [14] Stage where it originates Typical mitigation (sources)
FP1 Missing content Ingest / corpus scope coverage audits; "I don't know" behaviour; CRAG web fallback [27]
FP2 Missed top-ranked documents Index / retrieve hybrid retrieval, contextual chunks, larger N [16][11]
FP3 Not in context (consolidation limits) Rerank / context assembly rerank to top-K; adjust K [16]
FP4 Not extracted (noise, contradiction) Generate ordering at edges; compression; fewer, better chunks [15][12]
FP5 Wrong format Generate structured output instructions; validation
FP6 Incorrect specificity Query understanding / generate query rewriting; routing [35][12]
FP7 Incomplete Retrieve / generate decompose multi-part questions; iterative retrieval [14][12]

Two failure modes from the research systems complete the map. Retrieval collapse: a jointly trained retriever learns to ignore its input [1]. Leakage: retrieval can copy answers from evaluation data, which inflates scores [4][9].

11. Design lessons drawn across the canon

  1. Decouple the document encoder from training. RAG, REALM fine-tuning, Atlas few-shot and RETRO all freeze the document side to avoid re-indexing [1][2][9][4]. In production the equivalent rule is to treat the embedding model as a versioned dependency, because changing it means re-embedding the corpus.
  2. The fusion point sets cost and quality. Input concatenation (RAG, in-context RALM) is simple and model-agnostic. Decoder fusion (FiD/Atlas) scales to 100 passages but is bound by memory bandwidth [7][20]. Chunked cross-attention (RETRO) scales to trillions of tokens but needs architectural surgery [4].
  3. Retrieval quality is mostly decided before the LLM is called. In Anthropic's experiment, contextual chunking, hybrid search and reranking together cut retrieval failure by about two thirds [16]. DPR's top-20 gain over BM25 (78.4 vs. 59.1) mattered more than reader changes in its era [11].
  4. Index currency is a feature and a risk. Swapping the index updates knowledge without training [1]. Temporal mismatch costs accuracy [9], and stale indexes within training hurt badly [2].
  5. More context is not free. The U-shaped position effect [15], FiDO's bandwidth bottleneck [20] and Self-Route's cost analysis [30] all point the same way: budget context deliberately.

12. Developments beyond the canon (2024-2026)

The five canonical systems all retrieve flat text passages from one corpus and answer local, fact-seeking questions. Four lines of work since 2024 relax those assumptions and now count as standard options in the reference architecture.

12.1 GraphRAG: graph-structured indexes for global questions

Microsoft's GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024) targets query-focused summarization questions such as "what are the main themes of this corpus?", which top-K chunk retrieval answers poorly because no single chunk holds the answer [38]. At ingest an LLM extracts entities and relationships into a knowledge graph, the graph is partitioned into a hierarchy of communities (Leiden clustering), and the LLM writes a summary for every community. At query time "global search" maps the question over community summaries and reduces the partial answers. "Local search" starts from entities matched to the query. The paper reports gains in comprehensiveness and diversity over vector RAG on global sensemaking questions, judged by an LLM [38]. Cost. Indexing calls the LLM over the whole corpus, and the project's own README warns that indexing "can be an expensive operation" and advises starting small [38]. In this chapter's terms GraphRAG moves work into the ingest and index stages and adds a second, non-vector access path.

12.2 RAPTOR: hierarchical summary trees

RAPTOR (Sarthi et al., ICLR 2024) recursively embeds, clusters and summarizes chunks, building a tree whose upper levels hold progressively more abstract summaries [39]. Retrieval can search the collapsed tree, so a query can match a leaf chunk or a high-level summary, whichever fits its granularity. The authors report that pairing RAPTOR with GPT-4 improved the best published QuALITY accuracy by 20 points absolute [39]. Like GraphRAG it trades a one-time LLM cost at ingest for better recall on questions that span many passages.

12.3 Visual document retrieval: ColPali

ColPali (Faysse et al., 2024; ICLR 2025) skips the parse-OCR-chunk pipeline of Section 10.1 for visually rich documents [40]. It embeds each page image with a vision-language model (PaliGemma-3B), projecting the ViT patch outputs into a multi-vector representation, and scores queries with ColBERT-style late interaction [19][40]. The authors released the ViDoRe benchmark with it; the reference repository lists vidore/colpali at 81.3 and colpali-v1.3 at 84.8 on the ViDoRe leaderboard [40]. The design matters for tables, charts and slides, where text extraction is a major source of FP1/FP2 failures. The cost is a multi-vector index that is larger than a single-vector one.

12.4 Reinforcement-learned search agents

Following DeepSeek-R1-style reinforcement learning for reasoning, Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025) trains an LLM with outcome rewards to interleave reasoning tokens with search-engine calls, masking retrieved tokens out of the loss so the policy is optimized only on its own outputs [41]. Base models such as Qwen2.5 and Llama-3.2 learn when and what to search without supervised trajectories. This is the training-based counterpart of the agentic paradigm in Section 9.4: where Self-RAG [26] learned retrieval decisions from critic-labelled data, Search-R1 learns them from task reward. It also echoes the canon: like REALM and RAG it trains the use of retrieval end to end, now against a fixed external search engine instead of a differentiable retriever.

Development Stage it changes What it adds Main cost
GraphRAG [38] Ingest, index, retrieve entity graph + community summaries; global search LLM calls over whole corpus at ingest
RAPTOR [39] Ingest, index recursive summary tree; multi-granularity retrieval clustering and summarization at ingest
ColPali [40] Ingest, index, retrieve page-image embeddings; no OCR or parsing larger multi-vector index
Search-R1 [41] Retrieve, generate (control) RL-learned when/what to search RL training; variable query-time cost

Key takeaways for system designers

  • Start from the six-stage reference pipeline (ingest, index, retrieve, rerank, generate, cite) and instrument each stage separately. Most production failures (FP1-FP3) happen before generation [14].
  • Default to hybrid retrieval (dense plus BM25, fused) and add a reranker over a wide candidate set (about 100-150 candidates down to about 20). This is the best-documented quality gain for the cost: 49% and 67% reductions in retrieval failure in Anthropic's tests [16].
  • Fix chunk context at ingest. Contextualized chunks, section-aware passages, linearized tables and infoboxes, and file and chunk metadata are cheap one-time costs with measurable recall gains [16][9][14].
  • Treat the embedding model and the corpus snapshot as versioned artifacts. Re-embedding is hours of GPU time even at Wikipedia scale [11]. Temporal alignment moves accuracy by several points [9]. PQ compression is close to free (about 10x) [9].
  • Order and trim context deliberately. Put the strongest evidence at the edges, cap K by evaluation rather than habit, and consider routing between RAG and long context per query [15][30].
  • Make citations structural, not stylistic. Prefer API- or model-level attribution with verifiable spans [17][18][26] over asking the model to "cite sources", and measure faithfulness continuously [29].
  • Pick the paradigm by need, not fashion. Naive RAG suits small, homogeneous corpora. Advanced RAG is the production baseline. Modular or agentic flows earn their complexity only when queries need routing, multiple hops or multiple tools [12][13][31].
  • Fine-tuning and RAG are complements. RA-DIT [23], RETROfitting [4] and InstructRetro [25] all show that lightweight training to use retrieved evidence adds gains on top of retrieval itself.
  • Match the index structure to the question type. Flat chunk retrieval suits local, fact-seeking questions. Corpus-wide "sensemaking" questions favour graph or summary-tree indexes [38][39], and visually rich documents favour page-image retrieval [40], each at a higher ingest cost.
  • Guard evaluations against leakage. Measure n-gram overlap between corpus and test set, as RETRO and Atlas did [4][9]. Otherwise retrieval quietly memorizes the benchmark.

02. Document Parsing and Chunking: From Pixels to Retrievable Units

Overview

Every RAG system rests on its ingestion layer. Whether a retriever can find the right evidence depends on decisions made long before any query arrives: how a PDF page becomes text, whether a table keeps its header row, where one chunk ends and the next begins, and what metadata travels with each chunk into the index. Retrieval errors that look like embedding or ranking problems are often parsing and chunking problems that started upstream.

This chapter covers three layers of ingestion design.

  1. Layout-aware parsing. This layer turns heterogeneous documents (born-digital PDFs, scans, Office files, HTML) into a structured, ordered representation. The systems covered are open-source toolkits (Docling, Unstructured, Marker, MinerU, olmOCR, PaddleOCR-VL, DeepSeek-OCR), commercial APIs (LlamaParse, Reducto, Azure AI Document Intelligence, Mistral OCR) and "parse-free" visual retrieval (ColPali).
  2. Chunking. This layer segments the parsed representation into retrieval units. Strategies covered are fixed-size, recursive, structure- or element-aware, semantic (embedding-breakpoint and clustering), LLM-driven ("agentic") and perplexity-based, hierarchical/multi-granularity, proposition-level, late chunking, trained contextualized chunk embeddings, and Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval.
  3. Metadata enrichment. This layer attaches headings, provenance, bounding boxes, LLM-generated summaries, questions and situating context, so that chunks can be found, filtered, cited and expanded.

The canonical ingestion pipeline that most of the designs in this chapter instantiate looks like this:

 raw files                 parse                      structure                 index
+-----------+   +---------------------------+   +-------------------+   +----------------+
| PDF/scan  |-->| text layer / OCR / VLM    |-->| typed elements    |-->| chunker        |
| DOCX/PPTX |   | layout detection (boxes)  |   | (title, para,     |   | (size, struct, |
| HTML/XLSX |   | table structure recog.    |   |  table, figure,   |   |  semantic,     |
| images    |   | reading-order recovery    |   |  list, caption)   |   |  late, ctx)    |
+-----------+   +---------------------------+   | + hierarchy tree  |   +-------+--------+
                                                | + bbox/provenance |           |
                                                +-------------------+           v
                                       +-----------------------------------------------+
                                       | enrichment: heading path, page, bbox, doc     |
                                       | title, LLM context/summary/questions, entities|
                                       +-------------------------+---------------------+
                                                                 v
                                              dense index + BM25 index + doc store

The rest of the chapter goes through each stage, system by system, then compares them and ends with design guidance.

Part I: Layout-aware parsing

The problem

A PDF is a set of drawing instructions, not a semantic document. Characters are placed at coordinates. Columns, tables, headers, footers and reading order are implicit, and scanned pages have no text layer at all. Naive text extraction therefore interleaves columns, merges page furniture (running headers, page numbers) into body text, flattens tables into token soup and silently drops image-only content. The benchmark literature summarized below shows that the gap between a plain text dump and a layout-aware parser is very large. On olmOCR-Bench, a CPU text-layer extractor with no layout model scores about 20-22 points overall, while layout-aware pipelines and VLMs score 66-86 [37].

Two architectural families have emerged, plus a hybrid of the two.

  • Modular pipelines use a layout detector (object detection over page images), then specialized models per region type (OCR, table structure, formula recognition), then rule-based or learned reading-order assembly. Examples are Docling, Unstructured hi_res, Marker, the MinerU pipeline backend and Azure Layout.
  • End-to-end VLM parsers use one vision-language model that reads a page image and emits Markdown, HTML or a custom markup. Examples are olmOCR, Granite-Docling and SmolDocling, MinerU's VLM backend, Mistral OCR, and general-purpose models such as Gemini.
  • Hybrids route regions or pages to different engines by difficulty and often add an LLM or VLM correction pass. Examples are Reducto, LlamaParse's agentic tiers and Marker's --use_llm mode.

Docling (IBM Research)

Problem and positioning. Docling is an MIT-licensed, self-contained package for PDF and document conversion that runs on commodity hardware. Its specialized models are DocLayNet-trained layout analysis and TableFormer table-structure recognition [12]. Docling v2 shipped on 16 October 2024 and introduced a unified document model [12][15]. Today it accepts PDF, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX, HTML, EPUB, images, audio and several XML schemas, exports Markdown, HTML, DocTags and lossless JSON, and integrates with LangChain, LlamaIndex, CrewAI and Haystack and with agents through an MCP server [13].

Architecture. Docling's default PDF pipeline runs in stages, with a pluggable model at each stage [16]:

PDF page --> text-layer parse ----------------------------+
         \-> page image --> Layout (RT-DETR family) ------+--> assemble -> DoclingDocument
                        \-> OCR (auto/Tesseract/EasyOCR/  |    (reading     (body tree,
                             RapidOCR/macOS Vision/Surya)-+     order,       furniture,
                        \-> TableFormer (accurate/fast) --+     captions)    groups, prov)
                        \-> optional enrichers: picture classification,
                            chart extraction, formula/code
  • Layout. The current default layout model is docling-layout-heron. Larger variants are heron-101 and the egret medium, large and xlarge models, all object detectors from the RT-DETR family [16]. The September 2025 report on these models says heron-101 (RT-DETRv2 with a ResNet-101 backbone) reaches about 78% mAP on DocLayNet. Across the five new models the report gives relative mAP improvements of 20.6-23.9% over Docling's previous layout baseline (relative gains, not percentage points). heron-101 runs at about 0.028 s per image on one A100, on par with the old model, and egret-m is the fastest at about 0.024 s per image [17]. The authors also argue that mAP may be an imperfect proxy for layout quality [17].
  • Tables. TableFormer (TableModel04rs, which uses the OTSL representation) predicts table structure and cell bounding boxes. It was trained on datasets including PubTabNet (516k+ tables), FinTabNet (112k+) and TableBank (417k) [19].
  • Representation. DoclingDocument is a Pydantic model. It has content lists (texts, tables, pictures, key_value_items) and structure trees: body for main content, furniture for headers and footers, and groups for lists and chapters. All nodes are linked by JSON pointers, and each item carries bounding boxes and provenance. Reading order is encoded as the order of children in the body tree [15]. Because furniture is kept separate from body, page headers and footers can be excluded from chunks without writing heuristics.
  • VLM path. VlmPipeline converts pages end-to-end with a VLM that emits DocTags (preferred), Markdown or HTML [16]. IBM's Granite-Docling-258M was released on 17 September 2025 under Apache 2.0. It succeeds the experimental SmolDocling-256M-preview, swaps the SmolLM-2 backbone for a Granite 3-based one and moves the vision encoder from SigLIP to SigLIP2. IBM says it addressed SmolDocling's repetition-loop instability through dataset filtering, and it positions Granite-Docling as complementary to the Docling pipeline rather than a replacement for it [18].

Chunking integration. Docling's chunkers operate on DoclingDocument directly, not on flattened text [14]:

  • HierarchicalChunker emits one chunk per document element. It merges list items by default and attaches headings and captions as metadata.
  • HybridChunker takes the hierarchical output and makes it tokenizer-aware. It splits only chunks that exceed the token limit, then merges successive undersized chunks, but only when they share the same headings and captions (merge_peers=True). For tables that span several chunks it repeats the header row in each (repeat_table_header=True).
  • LineBasedTokenChunker keeps lines intact for tables, code and logs.
  • contextualize(chunk) returns the chunk text enriched with metadata such as headings. This string is the one meant to be embedded [14].

Failure modes and lessons. In Datalab's olmOCR-Bench comparison, Docling's default pipeline scores 50.3 overall (64.0 on born-digital pages) at about 2.1 pages/s on a B200 host. That is well below Marker's balanced mode and MinerU's pipeline on the same bench [37]. The comparison is vendor-run, but it is consistent with the general pattern that text-layer pipelines lose most on math and scans. The design lesson from Docling is that the representation matters as much as the models. A typed tree with furniture separated out and provenance attached makes structure-aware chunking and citation almost free.

Unstructured

Problem. Unstructured partitions dozens of file types into a flat list of typed elements (Title, NarrativeText, ListItem, Table, Image and others), each with metadata. It then chunks those elements.

Architecture.

  • Partition strategies. The open-source library defines auto, fast, ocr_only and hi_res [20]. fast reads the PDF text layer. hi_res runs a document layout model, and the default model in unstructured-inference is YOLOX, with a Detectron2-ONNX alternative [23]. ocr_only OCRs the page image. Reading order for detected regions can be sorted with an XY-cut mode [20].
  • Chunking. Chunking happens after partitioning, on elements. In the hosted API, basic, by_title, by_page and by_similarity are available, and if no strategy is specified no chunking occurs [22]. The by_title docstring describes the core rule: a new chunk starts when a Title element is detected or when metadata such as page or section changes, and sections are cut once they exceed max_characters (or max_tokens) [21]. The default hard maximum is 500 characters, as set in the options validator [21]. A soft maximum (new_after_n_chars) and small-section combining (combine_text_under_n_chars) let short sections merge. Overlap applies by default only when an oversized element has to be text-split. overlap_all=True extends it to normal chunks, but the docstring warns of a certain level of "pollution" of otherwise clean semantic chunk boundaries [21]. Tables are isolated in their own chunks by default (isolate_table=True), and oversized tables become TableChunks with repeated headers (repeat_table_headers=True). orig_elements keeps the original element metadata inside each chunk [21].

Evidence. Unstructured's own researchers studied element-type-based chunking on financial reports (FinanceBench). The paper's abstract reports that element-type chunking "largely improves" RAG results and yields the best chunk size without tuning [10]. The README of the open-source project compares its own OSS output against the hosted Transform v2 API on vendor benchmarks: table cell content 0.426 vs 0.866, adjusted text accuracy 0.715 vs 0.878, and so on. The OSS figures come from more than 1,000 pages and the hosted figures from a 224-page set [20]. That gap illustrates a recurring pattern: hosted parsers ship newer models than the open-source releases they grew from.

Lesson. An element-first design ("partition, then chunk elements") makes section-boundary-respecting chunking the default, and keeping orig_elements preserves provenance through the merge step.

LlamaParse (LlamaIndex)

Problem. LlamaParse is a hosted parser that produces LLM-ready Markdown or JSON from complex documents. Its distinguishing feature is tiered LLM/VLM-assisted ("agentic") parsing.

Architecture and cost. LlamaParse v2 was announced in December 2025 with four tiers priced in credits per page: Fast at 1 credit, Cost-effective at 3, Agentic at 10 and Agentic Plus at 45. Layout extraction is a +3-credit add-on, and re-parsing the same file within 48 hours is free [24][25]. Secondary coverage says Agentic Plus became roughly 50% cheaper than its v1 equivalent; we could not confirm this in the official pricing pages, so treat it as unverified. The docs list $1.25 per 1,000 credits in North America and Europe. Older pages show $1.00, so the rate appears to have changed and should be checked at the source [24]. At $1.25 per 1,000 credits, Agentic Plus works out to roughly $56 per 1,000 pages and Fast to about $1.25 per 1,000 pages (approximate, derived arithmetic). LlamaIndex's tier guide also describes a "Cost Optimizer" that routes each page to an appropriate tier, reserving premium processing for complex pages [24]. The older llama_parse / llama-cloud-services client repository is deprecated in favor of llama-cloud 1.0+, with maintenance until 1 May 2026 [26].

Lesson. Price discrimination per page, routing cheap pages to fast parsers and hard pages to VLM-backed modes, is now a standard design pattern. Ingestion cost can vary by more than an order of magnitude depending on routing policy.

Reducto

Problem. Reducto targets enterprise documents where table fidelity and citations matter, such as finance, insurance and healthcare.

Architecture. According to a 2025 write-up of Reducto's architecture, Reducto combines traditional OCR, layout detection and specialized VLMs in one pipeline, routing different models to different regions by complexity. The motivation it gives is that end-to-end LLMs fail systematically on document parsing, for example by hallucinating values in dense financial tables. The same write-up reports more than 1 billion documents processed [29]. Reducto's own blog says OCR provides character-level text accuracy while VLMs supply visual context for tables and multi-column layouts. Outputs include bounding boxes for citations, per-block layout labels and LLM-ready chunks. The blog also describes "Agentic OCR", a multi-pass self-correction step [28].

page --> layout detect --> region router --+--> classic OCR (dense text)
                                           +--> VLM (tables, charts, complex)
                                           +--> ...
                         merge + verify <--+
                               |
                     agentic multi-pass correction --> blocks{type,bbox,text} --> chunks

RD-TableBench. Reducto released RD-TableBench, 1,000 hand-labeled table images with grading code and a results viewer. In Reducto's original evaluation Reducto scored an average similarity of 0.902, against 0.646 for Google Document AI [27]. A rerun by Pulse, a competitor, using Reducto's ground truth and scorer, reports Reducto Agentic (2026) at 0.9308 and also notes that a Reducto audit found 43 ground-truth files (4.3%) with verifiable errors [30]. Third-party coverage of a February 2025 practitioner post, as reported by Gigazine, cites rd-tablebench scores of Gemini 2.0 Flash 0.84 ± 0.16, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.81 and GPT-4o 0.67, against Reducto's 0.90 [31].

Failure modes and lessons. The benchmark is vendor-owned and the vendor scores at the top, so results should be read as directional. The architectural lesson is still general. Pure generative parsing has a hallucination failure mode that is unacceptable for numeric tables, and hybrid systems use deterministic OCR as an anchor for character accuracy.

Azure AI Document Intelligence (Layout)

Problem. Azure Document Intelligence is a managed OCR and layout service integrated with Azure AI Search and Azure OpenAI ingestion.

Architecture. prebuilt-layout (v4.0, API version 2024-11-30 GA) extracts pages, paragraphs, lines, words, selection marks, tables (with row and column spans and header detection), figures (with captions and optional cropped images) and hierarchical sections [32]. Paragraphs carry logical roles, which are useful signals for chunking: title, sectionHeading, pageHeader, pageFooter, pageNumber and footnote, with role support varying by file type [32]. Setting outputContentFormat=markdown emits Markdown in which tables are rendered as HTML tables and selection marks as ☒/☐ [32]. Limits include up to 2,000 pages per PDF or TIFF, 500 MB per file on the paid tier, and only the first two pages on the free tier [32].

Chunking pattern. Microsoft's RAG guidance is to emit Markdown from Layout and split on headings, for example with LangChain's MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter mapping #, ## and ### to header metadata [33]. For Azure AI Search, the chunking guide recommends starting fixed-size chunking at 512 tokens (about 2,000 characters) with 25% (128-token) overlap. It also illustrates that chunk count for the same long document varies sharply with the Text Split skill's mode (pages vs sentences), size and overlap parameters. It suggests "custom combinations" such as appending the document title to mid-document chunks to prevent context loss [34].

Lesson. A parser that emits semantic roles (headings vs page headers vs footnotes) lets downstream chunkers drop furniture and use heading paths as metadata. Microsoft's own docs effectively endorse "Markdown headings as chunk boundaries" as the default enterprise pattern.

Marker (Datalab)

Architecture. Marker reads the PDF text layer and OCRs selectively. Layout, OCR and table recognition run through a single "surya" VLM served by a local inference server (vLLM or llama.cpp). Many thin CPU workers share that server [37]. An optional --use_llm mode adds an external LLM (a Gemini Flash model by default, gemini-3.5-flash at the time of writing, with Claude, OpenAI-compatible, OpenRouter and Ollama also supported) to merge tables across pages, fix inline math and extract form values [37].

Numbers (vendor-published, olmOCR-Bench, one B200 host). Balanced mode scores 76.0 overall and 83.5 on born-digital pages at 2.9 pages/s sustained, about 341 ms effective per page. Fast mode scores 66.6 at 7.4 pages/s. CPU-only no-OCR mode scores 43.6 at 23.7 pages/s. In the same table the MinerU pipeline scores 72.7 at 0.54 pages/s and Docling 50.3 at 2.1 pages/s; for reference, Datalab's hosted Chandra 2 scores 85.8, the Gemini Flash 3.5 API 76.4 and the CPU-only LiteParse 22.4 [37]. Marker states that balanced mode saturates only about 30% of the GPU because the ceiling is VLM decode throughput, and that concurrency rather than single-stream latency (about 0.3 pages/s) drives production throughput [37].

Lesson. At scale, parsers become inference-serving problems. The relevant design metric is sustained pages per second per GPU under concurrency, not single-document latency.

MinerU (OpenDataLab / Shanghai AI Lab)

MinerU began as a pipeline system. In the description used by the OmniDocBench authors, it uses a layout model to segment regions and then applies task-specific models per region [39]. It has since added a VLM backend (MinerU 2.5, plus the 2026 MinerU 2.5 Pro report). MinerU 4.0 offers four parsing tiers: Flash for fast previews and indexing, Basic for OCR and model-based parsing, and Standard and Advanced for demanding layouts. It parses Office, EPUB, HTML and CSV formats natively and keeps "stable citation locators" for agent reading [38]. Datalab notes that MinerU's VLM backend scores higher than its pipeline backend but is "a different, full-page-VLM approach" [37].

End-to-end VLM parsers: olmOCR, Mistral OCR, Gemini

  • olmOCR (Ai2). olmOCR fine-tunes a 7B VLM (initially from Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct). Its "document anchoring" technique injects coordinates of salient elements and raw text from the PDF's text layer into the prompt alongside the page image [36]. Ai2 quotes about $190 per million pages, roughly 1/32 the cost of GPT-4o batch processing [36]. The README says "less than $200 USD per million pages", requires a GPU with at least 12 GB, and lists v0.4.0 (October 2025) as adding synthetic data and RL training for about +4 points on olmOCR-Bench, a suite of more than 7,000 test cases across 1,400 documents [35]. On that bench olmOCR v0.4.0 scores 82.4. In the same README table, Mistral OCR API scores 72.0, Marker 1.10.1 76.1, MinerU 2.5.4 75.2, DeepSeek-OCR 75.7, PaddleOCR-VL 80.0 and Chandra OCR 0.1.0 83.1. The weakest category for nearly every system is "old scans", at 29-51 [35].
  • Mistral OCR. Coverage of the March 2025 launch reported about 1,000 pages per dollar (2,000 with batch) and 2,000 pages per minute per node. Mistral OCR 3 (mistral-ocr-2512, December 2025) is reported at $2 per 1,000 pages, or $1 with the Batch API, with a vendor-claimed 74% win rate over its predecessor, OCR 2, on Mistral's internal evaluation (forms, scans, complex tables, handwriting) [40]. The launch-era throughput figures come from secondary coverage; the OCR 3 prices are from Mistral's announcement.
  • General multimodal LLMs. A widely discussed February 2025 practitioner post argued that Gemini 2.0 Flash made PDF-to-text for RAG dramatically cheaper. It contrasted this with NVIDIA's nv-ingest, which in that account required Kubernetes, eight services and two GPUs [31]. Google staff have clarified that the often-quoted 258 tokens per page is an approximate average, not a fixed cost [31].

Compact and compression-oriented VLM parsers (late 2025)

In late 2025 a group of small, open document VLMs closed much of the gap to large general-purpose models. Several of them bring back a layout stage in front of the VLM.

  • PaddleOCR-VL (Baidu). It is a two-stage design. A layout detector finds regions first, and then a 0.9B VLM recognizes each cropped element. The VLM pairs a NaViT-style dynamic-resolution vision encoder with ERNIE-4.5-0.3B through a 2-layer MLP projector. It covers 109 languages and handles text, tables, formulas and charts [51]. The paper reports 92.86 overall on OmniDocBench v1.5, and a later PaddleOCR-VL-1.5 report claims 94.5. These are author-reported numbers, and they were taken here from secondary summaries [51]. On olmOCR-Bench it scores 80.0 [35]. Its authors argue that layout-then-crop inference is faster and cheaper to train than the full-page grounding approaches of MinerU 2.5 and Dolphin [51].
  • DeepSeek-OCR (DeepSeek-AI, October 2025). It treats OCR as a test of "optical context compression". A DeepEncoder chains a window-attention SAM encoder, a 16x token compressor and a global-attention CLIP encoder, and feeds the result to an MoE decoder. When there are fewer than 10 text tokens per vision token it decodes with about 97% precision, and at 20x compression it still reaches about 60% [52]. On olmOCR-Bench it scores 75.7 [35]. For RAG ingestion the useful knob is the explicit trade between vision tokens per page and fidelity. The authors themselves caution that OCR results alone do not validate long-context compression [52].
  • Chandra (Datalab). Chandra OCR 0.1.0 scores 83.1 in olmOCR's README table [35], and the hosted Chandra 2 scores 85.8 in Datalab's own table [37]. Both are vendor-reported.

The design lesson is that "pipeline vs end-to-end" is no longer a clean split. The strongest small models keep a cheap layout detector, which supplies reading order, bounding boxes and region crops, and spend VLM capacity only on recognition.

Failure modes of VLM parsers. The known failure modes are repetition loops (which IBM explicitly addressed for Granite-Docling [18]), hallucinated output on blank pages (fixed in olmOCR v0.3.0 [35]), auto-rotation errors [35], and numeric hallucination in dense tables (Reducto's stated motivation for hybrid routing [29]). OmniDocBench's supplementary analysis finds that colored backgrounds hurt pipeline tools much more than VLMs, while pipeline tools hold up better on merged-cell tables. MinerU and Marker also lose accuracy on mixed Chinese and English content [39].

Benchmarks for parsing

  • OmniDocBench (CVPR 2025). 1,651 PDF pages across 10 document types, 5 layout types and 5 languages in the current version, with component-level evaluation of text, tables, formulas and reading order. The v1.5 Overall metric is ((1 - text edit distance) x 100 + table TEDS + formula CDM) / 3 [39]. Its leaderboard has been updated continuously through 2026 with dozens of pipeline and VLM systems [39].
  • olmOCR-Bench. More than 7,000 unit-test-style checks over about 1,400 PDFs in categories such as arXiv math, old scans, tables, headers and footers, multi-column and long tiny text [35][37].
  • RD-TableBench. 1,000 table images, vendor-owned (see above) [27].
  • OHRBench ("OCR Hinders RAG", ICCV 2025). Unlike the parser benchmarks above, OHRBench measures what OCR errors do to downstream RAG. It separates semantic noise (recognition errors) from formatting noise (inconsistent representation of elements, for example a table emitted as HTML, Markdown or LaTeX). It finds that even the best OCR solutions trail ground-truth structured text by at least 14% on end-to-end RAG. Semantic noise hurts every retriever and LLM, while more capable models are more robust to formatting noise [53]. The later version covers 8,561 document images from seven domains with 8,498 QA pairs [53]. The practical lesson is to evaluate parsers by downstream retrieval and answer quality, not only by edit distance.

Parse-free retrieval: ColPali

ColPali feeds PaliGemma-3B ViT patch outputs through a linear projection to produce ColBERT-style multi-vector page embeddings, and is trained so queries match page images directly. The authors argue this "removes the need for potentially complex and brittle layout recognition and OCR pipelines" [41]. The repository now marks the colpali-engine package as deprecated and recommends Sentence Transformers for new projects and production use [41]. In this design the page itself is the chunk. It suits visually rich corpora such as slides, charts and infographics, but answer generation still needs a VLM that can read the retrieved page, and per-page multi-vector storage is much larger than one vector per chunk.

NVIDIA NeMo Retriever extraction (nv-ingest)

NVIDIA's open framework splits documents into pages, classifies artifacts (text, tables, charts, infographics), extracts them with NIM microservices or Hugging Face models, and then embeds and uploads the results. For production it is deployed on Kubernetes via Helm, with a lighter library mode for workloads under about 100 PDFs [42]. Its design treats charts and infographics as first-class extraction targets, a direction other parsers have followed with chart-to-table enrichers; Docling's optional chart extraction (do_chart_extraction=True) defaults to Granite Vision 4.1 4B [16].
