07. GraphRAG and Knowledge Graphs: Community Summaries, Graph Memory, and When Graphs Beat Vectors

Overview

Vector RAG treats a corpus as a bag of independent chunks. Each chunk is embedded, and at query time the top-k nearest neighbours go into the prompt. That model fails in two ways, and the GraphRAG family of designs was built to fix them. Microsoft Research named both failures in its first public GraphRAG post [3]:

  1. Connecting the dots. An answer may need facts spread across documents that share an entity, but no single chunk is close to the query in embedding space. In Microsoft's example, asked "What has Novorossiya done?", a LangChain vector-RAG baseline said the text did not say, because none of the retrieved chunks mentioned the term. GraphRAG found the entity in its graph and answered in detail [3].
  2. Holistic understanding. Some questions are about the whole corpus, such as "What are the top 5 themes in the data?". No top-k set of chunks can answer them. On this query the baseline matched chunks that contained the word "theme". GraphRAG returned themes that described the dataset [3].

The GraphRAG paper reframes the second failure. A global question is a query-focused summarization (QFS) task, not a retrieval task, and earlier QFS methods do not scale to RAG-sized corpora [1][2]. Everything in this chapter is some answer to the same question: which structure should be built over the corpus at index time, so that multi-hop and corpus-level questions become cheap at query time?

The designs differ mainly in where they spend LLM tokens:

  index-time LLM cost  ------------------------------------------------>  high
  |                                                                         |
  vector RAG     LazyGraphRAG   FastGraphRAG    HippoRAG/LightRAG    GraphRAG (standard)
  (embed only)   (NLP concept   (NLP graph +    (LLM triples or      (LLM entities +
                  graph, no     LLM community    entity/relation      relationships +
                  summaries)    reports)         profiles)            summaries + claims
                                                                      + community reports)
  query-time cost, global questions: high <-------------------------> low (pre-summarized)

The chapter covers, in order:

  • Microsoft GraphRAG: indexing, global/local/DRIFT search, dynamic community selection, auto-tuning, FastGraphRAG, and LazyGraphRAG.
  • LightRAG: dual-level keyword retrieval over an entity/relation graph.
  • HippoRAG and HippoRAG 2: OpenIE knowledge graphs with Personalized PageRank (PPR) as associative memory. Also fast-graphrag, GFM-RAG, and the relation-free LinearRAG, which build on the same idea.
  • The Neo4j GraphRAG stack: property-graph retrievers, Text2Cypher, the KG builder, and LLM Graph Builder.
  • Other industrial designs: AWS GraphRAG Toolkit, Zep/Graphiti temporal knowledge graphs, Ant Group's KAG, Think-on-Graph, LinkedIn's customer-service KG, NodeRAG's heterogeneous graph, and RL-trained agentic traversal (Graph-R1).
  • KG construction with LLMs: schemas, extraction, entity resolution, and pruning.
  • The evidence on when graphs beat vectors, and when they do not.

1. Microsoft GraphRAG

1.1 Problem and origins

GraphRAG came out of Microsoft Research. The first blog post (February 2024) used the VIINA dataset: thousands of Russian- and Ukrainian-language news articles from June 2023, translated into English. The data was too large for a context window and recent enough to be absent from the base model's training data [3]. The paper "From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization" followed in April 2024 [1][2]. Code was released on GitHub in July 2024, with an Azure "GraphRAG Accelerator" for code-free deployment [4][48]. The paper evaluates on "global sensemaking questions over datasets in the 1 million token range" [2].

1.2 Indexing pipeline

The default dataflow in the documentation has six phases [13]:

 documents
    |
    v
 [1] Compose TextUnits ---- chunk (default 1,200 tokens); unit of extraction + provenance
    |
    v
 [2] Document processing -- link documents <-> TextUnits; export Documents table
    |
    v
 [3] Graph extraction ----- LLM per TextUnit -> entities (title,type,description)
    |                       + relationships (source,target,description)
    |                       merge by (title,type) / (source,target)
    |                       LLM summarizes merged description lists
    |                       optional: claim extraction -> Covariates (off by default)
    v
 [4] Graph augmentation --- hierarchical Leiden community detection, recursive until
    |                       communities reach a size threshold -> multi-level hierarchy
    v
 [5] Community summarization -- LLM report per community (overview, key entities,
    |                            relationships, claims), then a shorter summary
    v
 [6] Text embeddings ------ TextUnit text, entity descriptions, report content
                            -> vector store (LanceDB default; Azure AI Search)
 outputs: Documents, TextUnits, Entities, Relationships, Communities,
          Community Reports, (Covariates)

Key techniques:

  • Chunk size is a fidelity knob. The docs warn that "larger chunks result in lower-fidelity output and less meaningful reference texts" [13].
  • Merge, then summarize. Each chunk yields a subgraph. Entities with the same title and type are merged across chunks, and their descriptions are collected into a list. A second LLM pass reduces each list to one description [13]. This is a simple form of entity resolution. Because it matches on exact title and type, spelling variants stay separate unless the prompt normalizes them.
  • Claims as covariates. Optional claim extraction produces time-bounded factual statements with a status. It is off by default because it "usually requires prompt tuning" [13].
  • Hierarchical Leiden. Clustering produces levels (C0 root, C1, C2, ...). Each level partitions the graph at a different granularity. A report is written for every community at every level [13].

Cost profile. The repository's main warning is that "GraphRAG indexing can be an expensive operation": read the cost docs and start small [12]. The indexing-methods page estimates that graph extraction is about 75% of indexing cost [14]. The project is now in maintenance mode: bug fixes and CVE-driven dependency updates continue, but no new features are accepted [12].

1.3 Query modes

GraphRAG ships several query engines over the same index.

Global search (map-reduce over community reports). This engine is for whole-corpus questions [15]. Reports from one chosen hierarchy level are split into chunks of fixed size. Map: each chunk produces an intermediate answer made of points, and each point carries a numeric importance rating. Reduce: the highest-rated points are filtered, aggregated, and used to write the final answer. Lower levels give more detailed reports and usually more thorough answers, but they cost more time and LLM calls because there are more reports [15]. Configuration includes max_data_tokens, separate map/reduce LLM parameters, concurrent_coroutines for map-stage parallelism, and allow_general_knowledge. That last flag lets the reduce step use outside knowledge, and the docs warn it may increase hallucination [15].

          query
            |
   +--------+---------+---------+          level-k community reports
   v        v         v         v          (batched into context-size chunks)
 [map]    [map]     [map]     [map]   --> rated points {text, score}
   \        |         |        /
    +-------+----+----+-------+
                 v
        filter/sort by score, pack to token budget
                 v
             [reduce] --> final answer (+ report/source references)

Local search (entity-anchored). This engine answers questions about specific entities [16]:

  1. Embed the query, plus optional conversation history, and match it against entity description embeddings to find entry points.
  2. Fan out from those entities to linked TextUnits, community reports, neighbouring entities, relationships, and covariates.
  3. Rank and filter each candidate set.
  4. Pack everything into one context window of fixed size and generate the answer [16].

DRIFT search (Dynamic Reasoning and Inference with Flexible Traversal). DRIFT mixes global and local search [6][17]:

  • Primer. The query is expanded with HyDE and compared with the top-K most relevant community reports. This yields an initial broad answer and follow-up questions.
  • Follow-up. Each follow-up runs as a local-search variant and produces more intermediate answers and follow-ups. The loop stops at a termination criterion, set to two iterations at the time of the post.
  • Output. A hierarchy of question/answer pairs ranked by relevance. Unlike naive map-reduce, intermediate answers are not weighted equally.

On 50 "local" questions over more than 5,000 AP News articles, an LLM judge preferred DRIFT to local search 78% of the time on comprehensiveness and 81% on diversity [6]. The post gives no cost numbers. It lists a "lite-global" variant and a query router as future work [6].

There is also a basic search mode, which is plain vector RAG over the same TextUnits. It is useful as a baseline.

1.4 Published results

From the July 2024 release post, which summarizes the paper [4]:

  • Datasets: podcast transcripts and news articles (linked to the MultiHop-RAG dataset). GPT-4 generated "activity-centered sense-making questions" from short dataset descriptions. An LLM judge compared answers on comprehensiveness, diversity, and empowerment.
  • GraphRAG at any community level beat naive RAG on comprehensiveness and diversity, with roughly 70-80% win rates.
  • Intermediate- and low-level community summaries beat hierarchical source-text summarization while using about 20-70% of its tokens per query.
  • Root-level summaries were competitive with source-text summarization at about 2-3% of its tokens per query. That is roughly 97-98% fewer tokens.

The February 2024 post also reported that SelfCheckGPT faithfulness was similar to baseline RAG [3]. That result matters: the gains come from coverage, not from fewer hallucinations.

1.5 Prompt auto-tuning

Default prompts are tuned for news: organization, geography, and person entities, with 15 hand-written entity examples and 12 relationship examples [5]. Auto-tuning works in four steps:

  1. Sample the corpus. The example given is 1% of 10,000 chemistry papers.
  2. Have the LLM identify the domain.
  3. Generate a persona.
  4. Generate the extraction, summarization, and community-report prompts in parallel, with few-shot examples taken from the corpus itself [5].

On the Behind the Tech podcast with GPT-4 Turbo, auto-tuned prompts increased extracted entities from 1,796 to 4,896, relationships from 2,851 to 8,210, and communities from 352 to 1,027 [5]. The CLI can select sample chunks randomly (the default), take the first n, use all of them, or use auto. The auto method embeds up to n_subset_max = 300 chunks and picks the k = 15 nearest to the centroid. The tuning chunk size defaults to 200 tokens [18]. The README "strongly recommends" prompt tuning, because out-of-the-box results may be poor [12].

1.6 Making global search cheaper: dynamic community selection

Static global search runs map-reduce over every report at the chosen level. Dynamic community selection (November 2024) instead walks the hierarchy from the root [7]:

  1. An LLM rates each community report for relevance to the query.
  2. Irrelevant reports are pruned, along with their whole subtree.
  3. The children of relevant reports are rated in turn.
  4. Only the surviving reports go into map-reduce.

A GPT-4o-mini rater was used for pruning and GPT-4o for map-reduce. The authors say the small rater reached "a very similar retrieval rate" to a GPT-4o rater [7]. Results on AP News with 50 global questions [7]:

Configuration Reports into map-reduce Token cost vs static L1 Quality vs static L1
Static global search, level 1 ~1,500 baseline baseline
Dynamic selection, up to level 1 ~470 (average) -77% (average) no significant difference
Dynamic selection, up to level 3 more than L1 dynamic about +34% win rates: comprehensiveness 58.8%, diversity 48.0%, empowerment 60.0%

The level-3 comparison covers only the 29 of 50 questions for which dynamic selection pulled in more reports than the static baseline [7], so it is not a like-for-like comparison with the level-1 row.

The lesson is that a cheap relevance classifier, placed in front of an expensive summarizer, recovers most of the efficiency of retrieval without giving up corpus-level coverage.

1.7 FastGraphRAG: an NLP-built graph

The --method fast indexer replaces LLM extraction with NLP [14]:

  • Entities are noun phrases, found with NLTK plus regexes by default, or with spaCy. They have no descriptions; the source TextUnit serves as context.
  • Relationships are co-occurrences within a TextUnit, again without descriptions.
  • Entity/relationship summarization and claim extraction are skipped.
  • The LLM still writes community reports.

The docs recommend much smaller chunks (50-100 tokens) so the co-occurrence graph is less noisy. They describe the result as much cheaper but noisier, and say the extracted graph is "less directly relevant for use outside of GraphRAG". Use Standard when you need high-fidelity entities and graph exploration. Use Fast when the main need is global summarization at low cost [14].

1.8 GraphRAG 1.0 engineering changes

The 1.0 release (December 2024) changed the engineering more than the algorithm [9]:

  • Embeddings moved out of parquet into a default vector store (LanceDB, or Azure AI Search). Parquet disk usage fell by 80%, and total disk usage by 43%.
  • 88 DataShaper workflows were collapsed into 11 functional workflows.
  • CLI start-up time fell from 148 s to 2 s on average.
  • A new update command computes deltas against an existing index and merges them. Reruns use LLM caching, so incremental updates are often cheaper than the first run.

Because 1.0 broke backward compatibility, it needs a migration [9]. Incremental update matters because the Leiden hierarchy and its reports depend on the whole graph. Appending documents can change community membership, and changed communities need new reports.

1.9 LazyGraphRAG: deferring all LLM work to query time

LazyGraphRAG (November 2024) removes the main barrier to adoption, which is indexing cost [8]:

INDEX (no LLM)                         QUERY (budgeted LLM work)
--------------                         --------------------------------------------
docs -> chunks                         query -> LLM: 3-5 subqueries, expanded query,
   -> noun-phrase concepts                      refine with matching graph concepts
   -> co-occurrence concept graph      per subquery:
   -> graph-statistics optimization       best-first: rank chunks by embedding sim,
   -> hierarchical communities                       rank communities by top-k chunks
   -> chunk embeddings                    breadth-first: LLM sentence-level relevance
                                                  test on top-k untested chunks of
                                                  communities in rank order
                                          iterative deepening: recurse into
                                                  sub-communities after z empty
                                                  communities in a row
                                          stop: no relevant communities left or
                                                relevance-test budget / q reached
                                       map: concept subgraph -> group chunks by
                                            community -> LLM extracts claims
                                            -> rank, filter to context window
                                       reduce: LLM answers expanded query from claims

The cost-quality trade-off is controlled by one parameter, the relevance-test budget [8]. Reported numbers, from 5,590 AP news articles and 100 synthetic queries (50 local, 50 global) judged on comprehensiveness, diversity, and empowerment [8]:

  • Indexing cost is the same as vector RAG and 0.1% of full GraphRAG.
  • At query cost comparable to vector RAG, it outperformed all competing methods on local queries.
  • On global queries it matched GraphRAG global search quality at more than 700x lower query cost.
  • At 4% of GraphRAG global search (C2) query cost, it significantly beat all competitors on both local and global queries.

Three configurations were reported [8]:

  • Z100_Lite: budget 100, low-cost LLM at every step. Its cost matched an 8K-context vector baseline.
  • Z500: budget 500. Low-cost LLM for relevance tests, a stronger LLM for refinement and map/reduce.
  • Z1500: budget 1,500, with the same split as Z500.

At budget 100, LazyGraphRAG beat everything except GraphRAG global search on global queries. At 500 it beat everything, and win rates kept rising at 1,500. The competitors included GraphRAG C1/C2/C3-dynamic, local search, DRIFT, vector RAG with 8K and 64K contexts, and RAPTOR [8].

BenchmarkQED (June 2025) added a stronger baseline [10]. It compared LazyGraphRAG with vector RAG using a 1M-token context window, on 200 queries: 50 in each of the four AutoQ classes (data-local, activity-local, data-global, activity-global). Each query had six trials, and GPT-4.1 was the judge. LazyGraphRAG won every comparison. The one non-significant result was relevance on data-local queries, which the authors attribute to vector RAG's strength at ranking directly relevant chunks [10]. A June 2025 editor's note says LazyGraphRAG was integrated into Microsoft Discovery and Azure Local (public preview) [8][11].

Lesson. LazyGraphRAG shows that the costly part of GraphRAG (LLM summaries precomputed for every community) is not needed for the gains. The structural part, a community hierarchy over a concept graph that guides breadth-first exploration, can be built with cheap NLP. The LLM is then spent only on the parts of the corpus a query touches.

1.10 Failure modes observed in GraphRAG-style systems

  • Index cost and staleness. Full LLM indexing is expensive [12]. Updates can change community structure, so reports must be regenerated [9].
  • Domain mismatch. News-tuned prompts under-extract in other domains: about 2.7x fewer entities on the podcast corpus [5].
  • Entity fragmentation. Exact-match merging on (title, type) [13] leaves aliases as separate nodes, which splits communities.
  • Detail loss in global search. Community summaries are lossy. Questions that need exact figures fall back to local or basic search. The BenchmarkQED data-local relevance result is consistent with this [10].
  • Judge-based evaluation. Most published GraphRAG results are pairwise LLM-judge win rates on comprehensiveness, diversity, and empowerment [4][7][8][10]. These metrics reward long, multi-perspective answers. They do not measure exact-answer accuracy.

2. LightRAG

2.1 Problem

LightRAG (HKU Data Intelligence Lab, October 2024; listed as EMNLP 2025) presents itself as a lighter alternative to GraphRAG [20][21]. It keeps an entity/relation graph but drops the community hierarchy and its reports, and it supports incremental insertion.

2.2 Architecture

INDEX                                          QUERY
-----                                          -----
chunks --LLM--> entities + relations           query --LLM (keyword role)-->
          (name, type, description;               low-level keywords  (entities)
           relation keywords/description)         high-level keywords (themes)
   |                                                 |                 |
   v                                                 v                 v
dedupe/merge into graph  <------------------  match entity       match relation
   |                                          vectors (local)    vectors (global)
   +--> KV store: entity/relation profiles           \               /
   +--> vector store: entity, relation, chunk         +--> 1-hop neighbourhood +
   +--> graph store: nodes/edges                      |    source chunks
   +--> doc-status store                              v
                                              (mix mode: + naive chunk vectors)
                                                      v
                                              [optional reranker] -> LLM answer

Key techniques:

  • Dual-level retrieval. An LLM pulls low-level keywords (specific entities) and high-level keywords (broad themes) from the query. Low-level keywords are matched against entity vectors and high-level keywords against relation vectors. The results are expanded to their graph neighbourhood and source text [20][21].
  • Query modes [21]: local (entity-focused), global (relationship-focused), hybrid, naive (plain chunk vectors), and mix (all of these combined; now the default; it merges local, global, and naive results). Reranker support was added in August 2025. The README says reranking typically adds about 1-2 s of latency and recommends BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3 locally [21].
  • Incremental update. New documents are extracted and merged into the existing graph without rebuilding any community structure. Deleting a document rebuilds the affected entities and relations from the LLM cache [21].
  • Model roles. The README separates four model roles [21]. Extraction should use a fast non-thinking model; Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct is called "a reasonable minimum" locally. The query model should be stronger and may be a thinking model. The keyword model should be fast. A VLM handles multimodal input. The embedding model must not change after indexing starts; bge-m3 is suggested locally.

Production storage. The defaults (JSON KV, NanoVectorDB, NetworkX) are for testing only. The README recommends PostgreSQL for all four storage roles, and lists MongoDB and OpenSearch as single-backend options. Milvus or Qdrant can serve vectors, and Neo4j or Memgraph the graph [21]. 2025-2026 changes include citations, a WebUI, RAGAS evaluation, Langfuse tracing, selectable chunking strategies, and in May 2026 the RAG-Anything multimodal pipeline (MinerU/Docling parsing) merged into the core [21].

2.3 Results and cost claims

The evaluation uses the UltraDomain datasets (Agriculture, CS, Legal, Mix). Questions are generated GraphRAG-style: an LLM imagines 5 users with 5 tasks each and writes 5 whole-dataset questions per user-task pair. Answers are compared pairwise by an LLM judge [22]. (Microsoft's BenchmarkQED toolkit [10][19] packages this kind of synthetic query generation and pairwise judging for reuse.) Overall win rates for LightRAG [21]:

Baseline Agriculture CS Legal Mix
NaiveRAG 67.6% 61.2% 84.8% 60.0%
RQ-RAG 67.6% 62.0% 85.6% 60.0%
HyDE 75.2% 58.4% 73.6% 57.6%
GraphRAG 54.8% 52.0% 52.8% 49.6%

Against GraphRAG the margins are small. Most of the gap is on diversity (for example 77.2% in Agriculture), while comprehensiveness is close to parity (51.6-54.4%). On Mix, GraphRAG is slightly ahead overall [21][22].

On cost, the paper argues that GraphRAG global retrieval sends hundreds of community reports through the LLM per query, while LightRAG needs a single short keyword-extraction call plus retrieval [20]. The paper's worked example puts GraphRAG at roughly 610,000 tokens for its level-2 communities, against under 100 tokens for LightRAG keyword generation. These figures are approximate, taken from the paper's cost-analysis section.

2.4 Failure modes and lessons

  • Extraction quality depends on the model. The README says LightRAG needs stronger LLMs than plain RAG because of entity-relation extraction, and a query LLM that can handle long, noisy context [21].
  • Fixed embedding model. Changing the embedding model forces a full re-index [21].
  • No corpus-level summaries. "Global" in LightRAG means relation-centric retrieval, not map-reduce over the whole corpus. Truly corpus-wide questions are answered from whatever relations the high-level keywords match.
  • Lesson. Much of what GraphRAG gains on sensemaking benchmarks can be had without community reports, if retrieval units are graph elements (entities and relations with LLM-written descriptions) and not raw chunks.

3. HippoRAG, HippoRAG 2, and PPR-based graph memory

3.1 HippoRAG (NeurIPS 2024)

HippoRAG (Ohio State NLP group) takes its design from the hippocampal indexing theory of human long-term memory [23][25]. The LLM plays the neocortex, which processes text. A schemaless knowledge graph plays the hippocampal index, which stores associations. Retrieval is pattern completion by Personalized PageRank [23][26].

OFFLINE INDEXING                              ONLINE RETRIEVAL
passages --LLM OpenIE--> (s, p, o) triples    query --LLM NER--> query entities
                     |                                         |
                     v                          retrieval encoder: nearest KG nodes
          schemaless KG (noun-phrase nodes)                    |
                     +                                         v
   retrieval encoder (ColBERTv2/Contriever):    seed PPR at those nodes (node
   synonymy edges between similar nodes         specificity weighting)
   (example scripts: cosine >= 0.8)                            |
                     |                                         v
          node -> passage incidence matrix      PPR mass over nodes -> aggregate to
                                                passages -> rank -> LLM reader

Key techniques [23][26]:

  • OpenIE with an LLM. The original release used GPT-3.5 Turbo for NER and triple extraction, and also supported Llama-3 and REBEL.
  • Synonymy edges. An embedding encoder links near-duplicate nodes, using a 0.8 similarity threshold in the example scripts. This makes up for not having strict entity resolution.
  • PPR from query entities. One graph walk spreads relevance across multi-hop paths, so multi-hop retrieval happens in a single step. The example commands use a damping value of 0.5.
  • Node specificity. Seed nodes are weighted by how rare they are across passages, an IDF-like signal.

Results (from the paper abstract [23]): on multi-hop QA (MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA), HippoRAG beat state-of-the-art retrievers by up to about 20%. Single-step HippoRAG matched or beat iterative retrieval with IRCoT while being about 10-30x cheaper and 6-13x faster. It can also be combined with IRCoT for further gains [23][26].

PathRAG (BUPT) is a related idea. It retrieves relational paths rather than neighbourhoods, and prunes them with a propagation decay rate (alpha) and a pruning threshold before prompting [42].

3.2 HippoRAG 2 (ICML 2025)

"From RAG to Memory: Non-Parametric Continual Learning for Large Language Models" recasts the system as long-term memory for LLMs [24][25]. It is evaluated on three axes:

  • Factual memory: NaturalQuestions, PopQA.
  • Sense-making: NarrativeQA.
  • Associativity: MuSiQue, 2Wiki, HotpotQA, LV-Eval.

The motivation is that structure-augmented RAG systems, GraphRAG and LightRAG among them, often fall below a strong dense retriever on simple factual QA even when they help on multi-hop questions. HippoRAG 2 aims to improve associativity and sense-making without that regression [25]. As described in the paper [24]:

  • Passages are added as nodes next to phrase nodes, which ties dense and sparse (entity-level) signals together in one graph.
  • Query-to-triple matching is followed by an LLM "recognition memory" filter that drops irrelevant triples before seeding PPR.

The repository claims HippoRAG 2 beats other methods in all three categories. It describes online retrieval as cost- and latency-efficient and offline indexing as using "significantly fewer resources" than GraphRAG, RAPTOR, or LightRAG [25]. The paper's abstract reports a 7% improvement on associative memory tasks over the state-of-the-art embedding model it compares against [24]. Supported back ends include OpenAI/Azure, Bedrock, vLLM (for example Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct), NV-Embed-v2, and GritLM embeddings, with Parquet, Qdrant, Chroma, or Milvus as stores [25].

3.3 Descendants: fast-graphrag and GFM-RAG

  • fast-graphrag (Circlemind) uses Personalized PageRank to explore the graph and credits HippoRAG for the method. It reports $0.08 against $0.48 for GraphRAG on The Wizard of Oz, about 6x cheaper, and says the savings grow with data size and the number of insertions. No methodology is published for this comparison [27].
  • GFM-RAG (NeurIPS 2025) replaces hand-tuned PPR with a pre-trained graph foundation model, a query-conditioned GNN based on ULTRA. It runs over a "universal graph index" with entity, document, and summary nodes [40]. The 8M-parameter checkpoint was pre-trained on 286 KGs (June 2025 release). It claims single-step multi-hop retrieval and transfer to unseen datasets without fine-tuning. The follow-up G-reasoner (34M parameters) was accepted at ICLR 2026 [40].

Lesson. PPR, or a GNN that learns to imitate it, is a cheap and deterministic way to do multi-hop retrieval. It moves the "hop" from repeated LLM calls (IRCoT) into a graph walk that costs milliseconds.

3.4 LinearRAG: dropping relation extraction altogether (ICLR 2026)

LinearRAG (Hong Kong Polytechnic University, October 2025; ICLR 2026) pushes the PPR idea toward lower indexing cost [50]. Its argument is that LLM relation extraction is the unreliable, expensive part of graph RAG: it yields noisy or inconsistent edges, and those edges then mislead the graph walk. LinearRAG therefore builds a relation-free Tri-Graph from lightweight entity extraction plus semantic links between entities, sentences, and passages. The authors state that construction scales linearly with corpus size and needs no extra LLM tokens [50]. Retrieval has two stages:

  1. Local semantic bridging activates the entities relevant to the query.
  2. Global importance aggregation runs Personalized PageRank over the activated subgraph to rank passages.

The paper reports gains over graph and dense baselines on four multi-hop datasets; these are the authors' own results [50]. The design point is that much of the multi-hop benefit in HippoRAG-style systems comes from entity co-occurrence and the walk, not from typed predicates. LazyGraphRAG (section 1.9) made the same bet for global questions.

4. The Neo4j GraphRAG stack

Neo4j approaches GraphRAG from the database side. The graph is a typed property graph that the application owns, and retrieval is a Cypher query composed with vector or full-text search.

4.1 Retrievers (neo4j-graphrag-python)

The official package [28] provides a GraphRAG orchestrator: retriever, then prompt template, then LLM. It has a return_context option and a response_fallback that skips the LLM call when nothing is retrieved [29]. The retrievers are [29]:

Retriever First stage Graph use Notes
VectorRetriever Neo4j vector index (ANN) none return_properties
VectorCypherRetriever vector index retrieval_query Cypher from node, score the core GraphRAG pattern
HybridRetriever vector + full-text index none no filters
HybridCypherRetriever vector + full-text retrieval_query traversal
Text2CypherRetriever LLM writes Cypher from question (+ schema, examples) the whole query is graph no embedder; queries may be invalid (Text2CypherRetrievalError)
ToolsRetriever LLM selects 0..n retriever tools any attributes results to tools
Weaviate/Pinecone/QdrantNeo4jRetriever external vector DB map ids to Neo4j nodes provider filter syntax

The central pattern is vector entry plus Cypher expansion:

question --embed--> vector index on :Chunk(embedding) --top-k (node, score)-->
   retrieval_query:
     MATCH (node)<-[:PART_OF_CHUNK]-(e:__Entity__)-[r]-(nbr:__Entity__)
     RETURN node.text, collect(e.name + ' ' + type(r) + ' ' + nbr.name)
   --> context strings --> RagTemplate(context, question, examples) --> LLM

This is close to GraphRAG local search (section 1.3), but the developer writes the expansion as an explicit, testable Cypher query instead of a fixed library heuristic. (The Cypher above is an illustration, not code from the docs.)

4.2 KG construction pipeline

The SimpleKGPipeline wrapper takes an LLM, a Neo4j driver, an embedder, and a schema of node types, relationship types, and allowed patterns. It accepts text or PDF [28]. Its components run in this order [30]:

  1. Loader: PDF or Markdown.
  2. Splitter: FixedSizeSplitter, or LangChain/LlamaIndex adapters.
  3. TextChunkEmbedder (optional).
  4. Schema: written by hand with SchemaBuilder, or derived by an LLM with SchemaFromTextExtractor. It can be saved as JSON or YAML.
  5. LexicalGraphBuilder: Document and Chunk nodes, with NEXT_CHUNK and PART_OF_DOCUMENT relationships.
  6. LLMEntityRelationExtractor: schema-guided extraction with structured output and an on_error policy. Entities are linked to their chunk with PART_OF_CHUNK.
  7. GraphPruning: removes elements that break schema patterns or EXISTENCE constraints, drops empty nodes, and fixes relationship direction.
  8. Neo4jWriter: batched writes, 1,000 by default.
  9. Entity resolution: exact match on label and name; fuzzy match with RapidFuzz Levenshtein distance (faster, less precise); or semantic match with spaCy embeddings (better, but limited by static vectors).

The KG-builder components live in an experimental namespace and may change [28].

            LEXICAL LAYER                         DOMAIN LAYER
(:Document)<-[:PART_OF_DOCUMENT]-(:Chunk)-[:NEXT_CHUNK]->(:Chunk)
                                    ^
                                    | [:PART_OF_CHUNK]
                              (:__Entity__:Person)-[:WORKS_AT]->(:__Entity__:Org)

Keeping a lexical graph (documents and chunks) next to the domain graph (entities) recurs across vendors. It preserves provenance and lets every retriever fall back to chunk text.

4.3 LLM Graph Builder

Neo4j Labs' LLM Graph Builder is an application built on these ideas [31]:

  • Ingestion from local files, GCS, S3, YouTube, Wikipedia, and web pages, using LangChain-based extraction with OpenAI, Gemini, Diffbot, and (in dev deployments) Bedrock, Anthropic, Ollama, and others.
  • Optional schema constraints.
  • Post-processing that cleans the graph and merges duplicates by similarity score.
  • Chat modes: vector, graph_vector, graph, fulltext, graph_vector_fulltext, entity_vector, and global_vector.

It is a practical reference for multi-strategy retrieval over one graph.

5. Other industrial and research designs

5.1 AWS GraphRAG Toolkit: hierarchical lexical graph

The AWS graphrag-toolkit has two parts [34][35]:

  • lexical-graph builds a "hierarchical lexical graph" (HLG) from unstructured text and answers questions with traversal-based search. The accompanying paper (Ghassel et al., KDD 2025) describes three tiers [49]: a lineage tier that traces every atomic proposition (statement) back to its source chunk, a summarization tier that clusters propositions into latent topics, and an entity-relationship tier that links entities across documents. Two retrievers sit on top: StatementGraphRAG, an entity-aware beam search over statements for precise factoid questions, and TopicGraphRAG, which selects topics first and then expands along entity links for exploratory questions [49].
  • BYOKG-RAG answers questions over a knowledge graph the user already has.

Supported stores are Neptune Analytics, Neptune Database, and Neo4j for the graph, and Neptune Analytics, OpenSearch Serverless, S3 Vectors, and Postgres with pgvector for vectors. Models run on Bedrock. Batch extraction uses Bedrock batch inference, and "versioned updates" support documents that change over time [35]. The design choice to note: the graph is built around statements (sentence-level propositions), so retrieval returns compact facts with their provenance, not whole chunks.

5.2 Zep and Graphiti: temporal knowledge graphs for agent memory

Graphiti is the open-source core of Zep. It targets dynamic data such as conversations and business events, not static corpora [32][33]:

  • Episodes are ingested incrementally, without recomputing the graph in batch.
  • Facts are entity-relationship-entity triplets with validity windows. When a fact changes, the old one is invalidated, not deleted, so past states can still be queried. The README calls this bi-temporal tracking.
  • Retrieval combines embeddings, BM25, and graph traversal, without LLM summarization at query time.
  • Custom entity types are defined as Pydantic models.
  • Back ends: Neo4j, FalkorDB, Neptune (with OpenSearch Serverless), and Kuzu, which is now deprecated.

The README contrasts Graphiti's "typically sub-second" query latency with GraphRAG's "seconds to tens of seconds". It also says Zep's managed platform gets sub-200 ms at scale, but publishes no benchmark for that [32]. The Zep paper reports better results than MemGPT on the Deep Memory Retrieval benchmark, and accuracy and latency gains on LongMemEval. Treat these as vendor-reported [33].

5.3 KAG (Ant Group / OpenSPG)

KAG ("Knowledge Augmented Generation") targets professional domains where vector similarity is ambiguous and OpenIE adds noise [36][37]:

  • It has a kg-builder and a kg-solver. The kag-model component is not yet open-sourced.
  • Its knowledge representation follows the DIKW hierarchy and supports both schema-free and schema-constrained extraction.
  • Mutual indexing links graph elements and text chunks in both directions.
  • Logical-form-guided hybrid reasoning breaks a question into planning, retrieval, and reasoning operators. Each step can use exact match, text retrieval, numerical computation, or semantic reasoning [36].

Release 0.7 (April 2025) added a "Lightweight Build" mode that the README says cuts construction token cost by 89%. Release 0.8 (June 2025) added MCP support and KAG-Thinker [36].

5.4 Think-on-Graph (ICLR 2024): the LLM as graph explorer

Think-on-Graph has the LLM explore an existing KG (Freebase or Wikidata) iteratively. It expands and prunes candidate relation and entity paths, then reasons over the paths it kept [41]. This is the "agentic traversal" end of the design space: no precomputed summaries, with an LLM call at every hop. It is suited to curated KGs rather than graphs extracted from a private corpus.

5.5 LinkedIn: a KG over support tickets

LinkedIn's customer-service QA system (SIGIR 2024) builds a graph from historical support tickets [45]:

  • Each ticket is parsed into a tree of sections, which keeps the ticket's internal structure.
  • Tickets are linked to each other by explicit references and by similarity.
  • At query time, the system extracts entities and intents, and retrieves sub-graphs either by translating the question into a graph query or by embedding search.

The abstract reports that the method beats a chunk-based RAG baseline by 77.6% (relative) in MRR and by 0.32 in BLEU, and that after about six months of deployment with LinkedIn's customer-service team it cut median per-issue resolution time by 28.6% [45]. The design point is that the graph encodes document structure (intra-ticket trees) as well as entities.

5.6 NodeRAG: heterogeneous node types

NodeRAG (Columbia, Penn, and Lehigh; April 2025) argues that most graph RAG work neglects the design of the graph itself [51]. Instead of a single entity/relation layer, it builds a heterogeneous graph with functionally distinct node types. Decomposed document content (text units, entities, relationships) sits next to LLM-derived insight and summary nodes, and the graph is built in decomposition, augmentation, and enrichment stages. Graph algorithms such as PPR can then find the key multi-hop nodes directly, and each retrieved node has a clear role, which makes retrieval easier to explain. Against GraphRAG and LightRAG the authors report lower indexing time, query time, and storage, and better multi-hop and open-ended QA with fewer retrieval tokens [51]. NodeRAG reads as a synthesis of GraphRAG (summary nodes), LightRAG (entity/relation units), and HippoRAG 2 (passage nodes plus PPR) in one typed graph.

5.7 Agentic GraphRAG trained with reinforcement learning: Graph-R1

Think-on-Graph (section 5.4) prompts a frozen LLM to traverse a graph. Graph-R1 (July 2025; ICML 2026) instead trains the traversal policy [52]. It targets three weaknesses of standard GraphRAG: high construction cost, fixed one-shot retrieval, and heavy dependence on long-context reasoning. Graph-R1:

  • builds a lightweight knowledge hypergraph, in which an n-ary hyperedge can join several entities into one fact;
  • treats retrieval as a multi-turn agent-environment loop, in which the model decides what to query next and when to stop; and
  • optimizes the whole loop end to end with RL, using one reward that combines answer quality, retrieval relevance, and the structural reliability of the graph paths it took.

The authors report that it beats prompt-based GraphRAG and RL-trained text-retrieval baselines on accuracy, retrieval efficiency, and generation quality [52]. It is one of a growing set of 2025-2026 systems that bring the "search agent trained with RL" pattern (covered in the agentic RAG chapter) to graph indexes.

5.8 Survey context

The Graph RAG survey by Peng et al. [46] splits the field into three stages: graph-based indexing, graph-guided retrieval, and graph-enhanced generation. The systems in this chapter map onto those stages. G-Retriever [47] is an example of the "retrieve a subgraph, then encode it for the LLM" family; it is mainly aimed at textual-graph question answering.

6. KG construction with LLMs: the shared engineering problem

Every design above, except LazyGraphRAG and FastGraphRAG, depends on LLM extraction. The same issues come up in each.

Schema: open or closed.

  • Open extraction (GraphRAG, HippoRAG, LightRAG) maximizes recall but gives heterogeneous types and predicates.
  • Closed schemas (the Neo4j SchemaBuilder with allowed patterns [30], KAG's schema-constrained mode [36], Graphiti's Pydantic entity types [32]) produce queryable graphs, but they miss anything outside the schema.
  • A common hybrid has the LLM propose a schema from samples, then constrains extraction to it. Examples are GraphRAG auto-tuning [5] and SchemaFromTextExtractor [30].

Extraction granularity.

Unit extracted Example systems Strength Weakness
Entities + relations with descriptions GraphRAG, LightRAG [13][21] rich, summarizable nodes costly; descriptions drift
OpenIE triples HippoRAG [23] cheap, precise links for PPR noisy predicates; loses context
Statements/facts AWS lexical graph [35], Graphiti [32] compact, citable, time-aware needs a proposition model
Noun-phrase co-occurrence LazyGraphRAG, FastGraphRAG [8][14] no LLM cost no relation semantics
Schema-typed property graph Neo4j KG builder [30], KAG [36] Cypher-queryable, constrained brittle to schema gaps

Entity resolution is the step most often underestimated. The options, from cheapest to most expensive:

  1. Exact match on name and type: GraphRAG [13], Neo4j's exact resolver [30].
  2. Embedding-similarity synonymy edges, which leave nodes separate: HippoRAG [26].
  3. Fuzzy or semantic merging: Neo4j's RapidFuzz and spaCy resolvers [30], LLM Graph Builder's similarity merge [31].
  4. LLM-assisted clustering of entities and edges: KGGen [38][39].

KGGen (Stanford, NeurIPS 2025) generates triples with LiteLLM and DSPy, then clusters similar entities and edges, so the graph is less sparse and less redundant. It is evaluated on the MINE benchmark [38][39].

Prompt tuning has a large effect. GraphRAG's own numbers show that domain-adapted prompts can nearly triple the number of extracted entities and communities [5]. KAG's lightweight build and LazyGraphRAG show how much token cost can be saved by moving extraction to cheaper models or to NLP [8][36].

Pruning and validation. Schema-based pruning drops invalid patterns and fixes relationship direction [30]. on_error policies decide whether a malformed LLM output breaks the pipeline [30]. Structured-output support is "important for reliable ingestion" according to Graphiti [32].

A reference construction pipeline, assembled from the components above:

docs -> parse -> chunk (+lexical graph: Document/Chunk/NEXT_CHUNK)
     -> [sample] -> LLM schema proposal / prompt auto-tune
     -> per-chunk LLM extraction (structured output, schema-constrained)
     -> validate + prune (schema patterns, direction, empties)
     -> entity resolution (exact -> fuzzy/semantic -> LLM adjudication)
     -> write graph (batched) + embed nodes/relations/chunks
     -> optional: community detection (Leiden) + LLM reports
     -> optional: temporal validity on edges (valid_from / invalidated_at)

7. When graphs beat vectors, and when they do not

7.1 The evidence

  • Corpus-level sensemaking. On global questions judged for comprehensiveness and diversity, every GraphRAG variant beat naive RAG with roughly 70-80% win rates [4]. LazyGraphRAG beat vector RAG even when vector RAG had a 1M-token context [10].
  • Multi-hop association. PPR over an OpenIE graph improved multi-hop retrieval by up to about 20%, and single-step graph retrieval rivalled iterative LLM retrieval at a fraction of the cost [23].
  • Entity-anchored questions that need many mentions combined. The Novorossiya example [3] and DRIFT's results over local search [6].
  • Structured, relational domains. These include ticket graphs [45], professional knowledge bases with logical constraints [36], and agent memory where facts change over time [32][33].

On the other side:

  • Single-hop factual lookup. HippoRAG 2 was motivated by structure-augmented RAG falling below strong dense retrievers on simple factual QA [25]. BenchmarkQED's one non-significant result was relevance on data-local queries, where vector RAG ranks directly relevant chunks well [10]. GraphRAG-Bench (ICLR 2026) starts from the observation that "GraphRAG frequently underperforms vanilla RAG on many real-world tasks" [43]. It sorts tasks into four levels: fact retrieval, complex reasoning, contextual summarization, and creative generation. The paper's analysis finds graph structure helps mainly on the harder reasoning and summarization levels [43]. A separate systematic comparison, "RAG vs. GraphRAG", reports the same split: vector RAG is better on detailed single-hop questions, and graph methods help on multi-hop and summarization queries [44].
  • The judge can favour graph methods. Comprehensiveness and diversity favour long answers built from many reports. LightRAG's lead over GraphRAG comes mostly from diversity, with comprehensiveness close to parity [21]. Systems built for exact answers should also be evaluated on correctness, which BenchmarkQED's AutoE supports when ground truth exists [10].
  • Cost and freshness. If the corpus changes often and global questions are rare, full GraphRAG indexing is hard to justify. LazyGraphRAG [8], LightRAG's incremental merge [21], or Graphiti's episodic updates [32] fit better.

7.2 Comparison table

7.3 Decision heuristics

Is the question about the WHOLE corpus (themes, trends, "what are the main...")?
   yes -> community-hierarchy method: LazyGraphRAG (cheap index) or GraphRAG global /
          dynamic selection (precomputed reports, repeated queries on a stable corpus)
   no  -> Does the answer need >= 2 hops through shared entities?
            yes -> PPR graph (HippoRAG 2 / fast-graphrag) or vector entry + Cypher
                   expansion (Neo4j); DRIFT if a GraphRAG index already exists
            no  -> Is the domain inherently relational/typed with exact constraints
                   (org charts, tickets, products, regulations)?
                     yes -> property graph + Text2Cypher / curated KG (KAG, Neo4j)
                     no  -> hybrid vector + BM25 + reranker (chapter 05); add a graph
                            only when evaluations show multi-hop failures
Do facts change over time and must history be queryable? -> temporal KG (Graphiti)

8. Cross-cutting failure modes

  1. Extraction noise propagates. A wrong edge in the KG becomes a confident multi-hop path. KAG cites OpenIE noise as a motivation [36]. HippoRAG 2 filters triples with an LLM recognition step before PPR [24].
  2. Entity fragmentation or over-merging. Too little resolution splits communities and breaks PPR paths. Too much merges distinct entities, for example two people with the same name. Resolution needs its own evaluation set.
  3. Summary drift. Merged entity descriptions and community reports are LLM summaries of summaries. Their claims should be traced back to TextUnits. GraphRAG reports cite source records for this reason [3]. Microsoft's later VeriTrail work on tracing provenance in multi-step pipelines targets the same risk [11].
  4. Text2Cypher brittleness. Generated queries may be syntactically or semantically wrong [29]. Production systems pair Text2Cypher with templated retrievers or route through a ToolsRetriever [29].
  5. Hidden cost cliffs. Lower community levels, larger relevance-test budgets, and DRIFT iterations all multiply LLM calls [8][15][6]. Budgets must be explicit configuration, not defaults nobody looked at.
  6. Benchmark mismatch. Most published wins are LLM-judge win rates on synthetic sensemaking queries [4][8][21]. Check them against domain queries that have ground truth before committing to a costly index.

Key takeaways for system designers

  1. Name the query class first. Graphs pay off for corpus-level sensemaking and for multi-hop association. They often do not for single-hop fact lookup, where a tuned hybrid vector stack is as good or better [10][25][43][44].
  2. Precompute only what repeated queries will reuse. Full GraphRAG community reports make sense for a stable corpus that gets many global questions. Otherwise LazyGraphRAG gets similar global quality with an index at 0.1% of the cost [8].
  3. Put a cheap model in front of an expensive one. A GPT-4o-mini relevance rater cut global-search tokens by 77% [7]. LazyGraphRAG uses a low-cost LLM for its relevance tests [8]. LightRAG uses a fast model for extraction and keywords [21].
  4. Use graph walks for multi-hop, not repeated LLM calls. PPR (HippoRAG, fast-graphrag) or a learned GNN (GFM-RAG) replaces iterative retrieval at a fraction of the cost [23][27][40].
  5. Keep a lexical graph under the knowledge graph. Document, chunk, and statement nodes linked to entities keep provenance and give a fallback to raw text [30][35].
  6. Treat entity resolution and prompt tuning as first-class work. Domain-tuned prompts nearly tripled extracted structure in Microsoft's test [5]. Resolution quality decides whether communities and paths mean anything.
  7. Make incrementality a requirement. Choose designs whose update cost scales with the delta: GraphRAG update, LightRAG merge and delete, Graphiti episodes, AWS versioned updates [9][21][32][35].
  8. Build a router, not a single engine. GraphRAG's own design ships global, local, DRIFT, and basic modes. LightRAG defaults to mix. Neo4j offers ToolsRetriever [6][21][29]. Route by query class.
  9. Evaluate on two axes. Use LLM-judge win rates for sensemaking, and correctness against ground truth for factual queries (BenchmarkQED AutoQ/AutoE, GraphRAG-Bench) [10][43].
