10. Multimodal RAG: Visual Document Retrieval, Cross-Modal Embeddings, and Video and Audio Retrieval

Overview

Most of this atlas treats the corpus as text. Real corpora are not text. An investor deck carries its key numbers in bar charts. A 10-K puts its comparisons in tables. A maintenance manual explains with exploded diagrams. A lecture archive is hours of video, and its spoken explanation exists only in the audio. A text-only RAG pipeline first converts these artefacts into text by parsing, OCR, captioning or transcription. Whatever the conversion drops (the shape of a trend line, the row a number sits in, the slide a speaker points at) is gone before retrieval starts. Weaviate's 2026 write-up on chart-heavy PDFs puts it directly: charts and tables "are primary information that gets destroyed in extraction" [29].

Multimodal RAG covers the designs that keep non-text signal available to retrieval and to generation. Since 2023 the field has split into four architectural families:

  1. Convert-to-text (parse, caption, transcribe). Every modality is turned into text or structured text, which is then indexed with the text machinery of Chapters 2-7. Chapter 2 covers the parsers. This chapter covers the multimodal extensions: element-level captioning, table interpretation, ASR, and multimodal knowledge graphs (RAG-Anything, VideoRAG, Video-RAG) [33][47][49].
  2. Single-vector screenshot embedding. A page, slide or screenshot is rendered as an image and encoded by a vision-language model (VLM) into one dense vector. Examples are DSE, vdr-2b, VisRAG-Ret, VDocRetriever and UniSE, and API models such as Gemini Embedding 2 [8][10][11][14][17][46].
  3. Multi-vector late interaction over image patches. This is the ColPali family. Each patch of a page image becomes a 128-dimensional vector, and query tokens are scored against patches with ColBERT's MaxSim. It is the current state of the art on visual-document benchmarks, and it is also the most expensive to serve [1][2][27].
  4. Universal or omni-modal embedding spaces. CLIP, ImageBind, CLAP, UniIR, VLM2Vec, Qwen3-VL-Embedding and ColQwen-Omni map text, images, audio and video into one space, so that any modality can retrieve any other [28][37][38][39][40][43].

In practice the generator side has converged. Retrieved pages, frames or clips go to a VLM as images, together with any extracted text. This chapter is organised by retrieval design. It covers the ColPali lineage in depth, then single-vector screenshot retrievers, benchmarks, serving at scale, end-to-end visual RAG systems, convert-to-text multimodal pipelines, universal embedding spaces, video RAG and audio RAG. It ends with a comparison table and takeaways.

                       MULTIMODAL RAG: FOUR RETRIEVAL FAMILIES
 source artefact                index representation                     generator
+----------------+   (1) parse/OCR/caption/ASR -> text chunks (+KG)   +--------------+
| PDF page       |---------------------------------------------------->|              |
| slide, chart   |   (2) render -> VLM -> 1 dense vector per page      |   VLM / LLM  |
| table, figure  |---------------------------------------------------->|  (page img,  |
| screenshot     |   (3) render -> VLM -> ~700-1,030 patch vectors     |   frames,    |
| video, audio   |---------------------------------------------------->|  transcript, |
|                |   (4) any modality -> shared omni-modal space       |   captions)  |
+----------------+---------------------------------------------------->+--------------+

10.1 ColPali: Late Interaction over Page Images

Problem

Before 2024, PDF RAG meant a brittle chain of PDF parsing, OCR, layout detection, table recognition, figure captioning, chunking and text embedding. The ColPali authors measured the cost of that chain. In their latency table (1,000 ViDoRe pages, one NVIDIA L4 GPU), an Unstructured pipeline with layout detection (0.81 s), OCR (2.67 s) and figure captioning (3.71 s) took 7.22 seconds of offline processing per page, against 0.39 seconds per page for ColPali to embed the page image directly, roughly an 18x gap [1][35]. Even after all that work, the parsed pipelines still lost to direct visual retrieval on visually rich pages [1].

Architecture

ColPali (Faysse, Sibille, Wu et al., ILLUIN Technology / CentraleSupélec; arXiv 2024, ICLR 2025) takes the PaliGemma-3B VLM and turns it into a ColBERT-style retriever [1][2]:

  • Vision encoder. SigLIP-So400m resizes each page to 448x448 pixels and cuts it into 14x14-pixel patches. That gives a 32x32 grid of 1,024 patches [5].
  • Language model. Gemma-2B contextualises the patch features together with a short instruction prompt.
  • Projection. A linear layer maps every output token to a 128-dimensional, L2-normalised vector. The page embedding is 1,030 vectors x 128 dims: 1,024 patch vectors plus 6 vectors from the instruction and special tokens [5][18].
  • Query side. The same model encodes the text query into one 128-dim vector per token.
  • Scoring. MaxSim, from ColBERT [31]. For each query token, take the maximum dot product over all document vectors, then sum those maxima over the query tokens.
 OFFLINE (per page)                               ONLINE (per query)
 PDF -> rasterise -> 448x448 image                "which year has highest outlay?"
            |                                                 |
   SigLIP-So400m (32x32 = 1,024 patches)            Gemma tokenizer + LM
            |                                                 |
   Gemma-2B contextualisation (+ prompt)            linear proj -> n_q x 128
            |                                                 |
   linear proj -> 1,030 x 128 (bf16/fp32)                     |
            |                                                 v
   multi-vector store ---------------------->  MaxSim(Q,D) = sum_i max_j <q_i, d_j>
                                                              |
                                               top-k page IDs -> page images -> VLM

Training follows ColBERT's in-batch contrastive objective on query-page pairs. The pairs come from academic DocVQA-style sets plus synthetic queries that a VLM generated over web-crawled PDFs [1]. The model lineage shows how much the recipe matters. ColPali v1.3 keeps the same backbone as v1.1 but trains with an effective batch size of 256 for 3 epochs, and its ViDoRe score rises from 81.5 to 84.8 [2].

Interpretability

MaxSim is a sum of per-query-token maxima, so every point of a page's score can be attributed to one query token and one patch. ColPali's "similarity maps" overlay this on the page as a heatmap. In the Sentence Transformers example, the query token "water" lights up the "Water Resources & Power" bar of a 1971 budget chart [2][27]. This is the main explainability advantage that late interaction has over single-vector retrievers, and production demos (Vespa's ColPali app, Weaviate's Query Agent) surface it to users [23][29].

Failure modes and lessons

  • Storage blow-up. 1,030 x 128 float32 values is 512 KB per page, so 1M pages need about 512 GB before compression. A single 768-dim vector needs 3 KB per page, which makes ColPali roughly 170x larger [20].
  • Index-construction blow-up. HNSW assumes a symmetric, query-independent distance. MaxSim is neither, so vector databases index the individual patch vectors. Inserting one ~700-vector page with ef_construct = 100 takes on the order of 49M vector comparisons [19][21].
  • Fixed resolution. At 448x448, dense small print is downsampled. Later models moved to dynamic resolution (Section 10.2).
  • Special-token contribution. Non-content tokens contribute to MaxSim. In one text example, three special tokens made up 22.7% of the score [27]. Qdrant kept the 6 special vectors in its pooled representation for this reason [18].
  • Lesson. Page-as-chunk removes chunking decisions, but the page becomes the unit of retrieval and of generator context. Weaviate notes that when the answer is one paragraph of a dense contract, a whole page "may be more context than you want" [29].

10.2 The ColVision Family: 2024-2026 Evolution

After ColPali, a family of "Col*" retrievers swapped the backbone, the resolution policy, the attention direction or the training data. The colpali-engine repository and the Qdrant multi-vector course document the main variants [2][6]:

Model Backbone Params Notable design choice ViDoRe score* License
ColPali v1.0 / v1.3 PaliGemma-3B ~3B fixed 448 px, 1,030 vecs/page 81.3 / 84.8 Gemma
ColQwen2 v1.0 Qwen2-VL-2B ~2B dynamic resolution, up to 768 patches 89.3 Apache 2.0
ColQwen2.5 v0.2 Qwen2.5-VL-3B ~3B dynamic res, 768 patches in training 89.4 Apache 2.0
tomoro-colqwen3-embed-4b Qwen3-VL ~4B 320-dim vectors; 8B sibling handles short video 90.6 Apache 2.0
colqwen3.5-4.5B-v3 Qwen3.5-4B (hybrid GatedDeltaNet) 4.5B LoRA-trained, 320-dim 90.9 Apache 2.0
ColSmol-256M / 500M SmolVLM 256M / 500M edge/browser deployments 80.1 / 82.3 Apache 2.0
ColFlor Florence-2 174M 17x smaller, up to 9.8x faster than ColPali n/a n/a
ColModernVBERT ModernVBERT (bidirectional) ~250M bidirectional attention encoder n/a n/a
ColNetraEmbed Gemma-3-4B ~4B 22 languages 86.4 Gemma
ColNomic-Embed-Multimodal (Nomic) 3B / 7B open, commercial-use multilingual n/a open
Llama-NeMoRetriever-ColEmbed-3B SigLIP-2 + Llama 3.2-3B ~3B multilingual; non-commercial license n/a NVIDIA NC

*Scores are as listed in the colpali-engine README's ViDoRe column [2]. Other sources do not report comparable numbers, so those rows show n/a. ColFlor, ColNomic and NVIDIA details are from the Qdrant course [6].

Four design lessons stand out in this lineage:

  1. Dynamic resolution beats a fixed grid. ColQwen2 caps a page at 768 patches but keeps its aspect ratio, and it gained about 5 points over ColPali v1.2 on the same benchmark. In Qdrant's measurements it typically produces about 700 vectors per page instead of 1,030 [2][19].
  2. Bidirectional encoders are more parameter-efficient retrievers. ModernVBERT (Teiletche, Macé, Conti, Loison, Viaud, Colombo, Faysse, 2025) argues that causal decoders are a poor fit for embeddings. ColModernVBERT has about 250M parameters, more than 10x fewer than ColPali, and scores only slightly lower on ViDoRe [6][7].
  3. Batch size and compute matter as much as architecture. ColQwen2 v1.0 differs from v0.1 mainly in "more powerful GPUs" and an effective batch of 256 instead of 32. The result was +2.0 points [2]. Fused MaxSim kernels (late-interaction-kernels) avoid materialising the [B, B, Lq, Ld] score tensor, and they doubled the largest trainable batch on an 80 GB H100 from 64 to 128 [2].
  4. Ecosystem consolidation. In 2026, ILLUIN deprecated colpali-engine in favour of Sentence Transformers v6, whose MultiVectorEncoder loads ColPali-family, PyLate and Stanford ColBERT checkpoints behind one encode_query / encode_document / similarity API [2][27]. Byaldi offered the earlier RAGatouille-style wrapper, with uncompressed indexes [51].

10.3 Single-Vector Screenshot Retrievers

Document Screenshot Embedding (DSE)

DSE (Ma, Lin, Li, Chen, Lin, University of Waterloo, 2024) proposed the simplest possible unification: treat every document, whether a Wikipedia page, a slide or a PDF page, as a screenshot, and encode it with a VLM into one vector by end-of-sequence pooling [8]. The Tevatron recipe fine-tunes Phi-3-vision with LoRA, and later Qwen2-VL-2B, on wiki-ss-nq screenshot/question pairs. It uses temperature 0.02, train_group_size 2 (one positive and one hard negative), query_max_len 128 and passage_max_len 4096 tokens for the image side [9]. DSE avoids every multi-vector cost: one vector per page fits any ANN index. The price is that a chart, a table and three paragraphs must share a single vector [27][35].

vdr-2b-multi (LlamaIndex, 2025)

vdr-2b-multi-v1 starts from dse-qwen2-2b-mrl-v1 and is a useful case study in data engineering for visual retrievers [10]:

  • Corpus construction. Topic-driven search queries per language found about 50k PDFs. A layout-analysis model labelled each page as text-only, visual-only or mixed, and about 100k pages were sampled evenly across those three types.
  • Query synthesis. Gemini-1.5-Pro and Qwen2-VL-72B each wrote a "specific" and a "general" question per page. Only the specific question was kept, but forcing the contrast produced sharper questions.
  • Filtering. A specific query was kept only if its paired general query appeared in the top 100 results of a voyage-3 index. This removed about 40% of queries per language. Hard negatives were mined with voyage-3 at a 0.75 similarity threshold.
  • Result. The dataset holds 496,167 pages, 280,679 of them with queries. The model averages +2.3% nDCG@5 over its base across languages, and +6.33% on German visual-only pages. At 768 image tokens the English model beats the base model run at 2,560 patches, which the authors report as about 3x faster inference. Matryoshka truncation to one third of the dimensions keeps about 98% of quality [10].

VisRAG-Ret, VDocRetriever and UniSE

  • VisRAG-Ret (OpenBMB/Tsinghua, 2024) builds on MiniCPM-V 2.0 (SigLIP plus MiniCPM-2B). It is trained on 362,110 query-document pairs: 34% from academic datasets and 66% synthetic GPT-4o queries over web-crawled PDFs [11][12].
  • VDocRetriever (NTT, CVPR 2025) adds two self-supervised pre-training tasks, RCR and RCG, that "compress visual information into dense token representations while aligning them with textual content". It is released with OpenDocVQA, a unified open-domain DocVQA collection [14].
  • UniSE / VisIR (BAAI, 2025) generalises the screenshot idea to "Visualized Information Retrieval". Text, images, tables and charts are all represented as screenshots. The work releases the VIRA training data and the MVRB benchmark, and its queries can themselves be screenshot-plus-text [17].

Dual-mode and bidirectional VLM retrievers: jina-embeddings-v4 and Nemotron ColEmbed

Two 2025 releases blurred the line between families 2 and 3:

  • jina-embeddings-v4 (Jina AI, June 2025) is a 3.8B-parameter model built on Qwen2.5-VL-3B that embeds text and page images in one space and can emit either a single 2,048-dim vector (Matryoshka-truncatable to 128) or ColBERT-style multi-vector output from the same forward pass. Task-specific LoRA adapters (retrieval, text matching, code) are selected at inference time. The release also introduced the Jina-VDR benchmark for visually rich documents [55]. One model can therefore serve a cheap single-vector first stage and a multi-vector rerank, which is the pattern behind the jina rows in Section 10.4.
  • Llama Nemoretriever ColEmbed (NVIDIA, July 2025) starts from the Eagle2 VLM, switches its LLM attention from causal to bidirectional, and adds late interaction. The 3B model reported nDCG@5 of 91.0 on ViDoRe V1 and 63.5 on ViDoRe V2, first on both leaderboards as of June 2025. The technical report quantifies the storage and latency cost of multi-vector output and motivates the smaller single-vector embed-vl siblings [56]. The later nemotron-colembed-vl checkpoints appear in the ViDoRe V3 pipeline results (Section 10.4). Like ModernVBERT, it supports the lesson that bidirectional attention suits retrieval better than causal decoding.

API-hosted multimodal embedders

Google's Gemini Embedding 2 (public preview, March 2026) maps text, images, video, audio and PDFs into one space. Its input limits, as reported at launch, are: up to 6 PNG/JPEG images per request, one PDF of up to 6 pages, MP3/WAV audio up to about 80 s, MP4/MOV video up to about 128 s (secondary sources disagree on the exact video cap, and Google's Vertex AI documentation expresses the limits as per-frame and per-second token costs), and an 8,192-token context shared by all modalities in a request. Output dimensions run from 128 to 3,072 via Matryoshka learning. Qdrant recommends a two-pass design: retrieve on a truncated vector, then rescore with the full 3,072 dims [46].

10.4 Benchmarks: From ViDoRe V1 to Pipeline-Level Evaluation

ViDoRe V1 (2024) combined academic sets (DocVQA, InfoVQA, TAT-DQA, ArxivQA, TabFQuAD) with synthetic "practical" sets (energy, government, healthcare, AI, Shift Project). These quickly saturated: vdr-2b scores 95-98 nDCG@5 on several of them [10]. ViDoRe V2 (Macé, Loison, Faysse, 2025) "raised the bar" with harder, more realistic queries [3]. ViDoRe V3 (Loison, Macé, Edy et al., ACL 2026) has about 26,000 pages and 3,099 human-verified queries, each available in 6 languages, across 10 datasets (8 public and 2 private). The source documents are English and French, covering HR, finance (English and French), industrial, pharmaceutical, computer-science, energy and physics. Roughly 12,000 hours of annotation produced relevance labels, bounding-box evidence localisation and reference answers. The paper finds that visual retrievers and late interaction help, but that current models still struggle with non-text elements, open-ended queries and fine-grained visual grounding [6][54]. Single-model evaluation has moved into MTEB. The vidore-benchmark repository now evaluates whole pipelines (OCR, retriever, reranker, agent) and records indexing and search times [4].

The public V3 pipeline submissions are the best evidence available on the trade-offs between OCR, visual and agentic designs. The table below summarises them. nDCG@10 is the mean of the "overall" scores across the 8 public English splits. Per-query search time is total search time on the HR split divided by its 318 queries. All runs used a single A100-80GB GPU, but CPU and RAM differed between submitters. The figures were computed by this chapter from the submitted JSON files [4].

Pipeline (submitter) Modality indexed nDCG@10 (mean of 8) Index time, HR Search time/query
mxbai-edge-colbert-v0-32m (Mixedbread) OCR text, late interaction 0.440 5 s ~4 ms
llama-nemotron-embed-vl-1b-v2 (NVIDIA) page image, 1 vector 0.524 382 s ~3 ms
qwen3-embedding-8B OCR text, 1 vector 0.535 177 s ~40 ms
llama-nemotron-embed-vl-1b-v2 (NVIDIA) image + OCR text 0.558 261 s ~4 ms
nemotron-embed-vl-1b + rerank-vl-1b (NVIDIA) page image 0.578 201 s ~5.2 s
jina-embeddings-v4 + jina-reranker-m0 page image 0.601 549 s ~17 s
llama-nemotron-colembed-vl-3b-v2 (NVIDIA) image, late interaction 0.609 671 s ~0.46 s
nemotron-embed-vl-1b + rerank-vl-1b (NVIDIA) image + OCR text 0.620 274 s ~6.2 s
nemotron-colembed-vl-8b-v2 (NVIDIA) image, late interaction 0.644 492 s ~1.1 s
jina-embeddings-v4 (text) + zerank-2 OCR text 0.656 161 s ~9.8 s
NeMo Retriever Agentic: colembed-8b + Claude Opus 4.5 image, agentic loop 0.692 68 s** ~102 s

**The agentic run's indexing time is reported as submitted. Its configuration preloads the corpus to the GPU [4].

Five observations follow from these numbers:

  1. Late interaction beats single-vector at equal modality. The 3B ColEmbed (0.609) beats the 1B single-vector image embedder (0.524) by about 8.5 points. Its search cost is two orders of magnitude higher, though still sub-second.
  2. Adding OCR text to image embeddings helps. Image plus text beats image alone both without a reranker (0.558 vs 0.524) and with one (0.620 vs 0.578). The modalities are complementary, not substitutes.
  3. A strong text pipeline is still competitive. jina-v4 on transcribed text with the zerank-2 reranker (0.656) beats the same embedder on page images with a visual reranker (0.601), and edges out the 8B visual ColEmbed (0.644). On V3's text-heavy enterprise documents, "OCR is dead" is not supported.
  4. Rerankers are expensive. The 1B VL reranker adds about 5-6 s per query on the HR set for 5-6 points.
  5. Agentic retrieval wins on quality at about 100x the latency. The NVIDIA agent rewrites queries, calls the ColEmbed-8B retriever (top-500) repeatedly, and has the LLM (Claude Opus 4.5 in this submission) submit the final ranked 10 pages. It reaches the best score, 0.692, at roughly 100 s per query, against 1.1 s for the same retriever alone [4][53]. This is the visual counterpart of the agentic-RAG trade-offs in Chapter 8.

10.5 Serving Late-Interaction Visual Retrieval at Scale

The central engineering problem of ColPali-style RAG is cost. Its storage and compute are proportional to the number of vectors per page. Every production design attacks one of three terms: vectors per page, bytes per vector, or pages scored per query.

 cost ~ (#pages scored) x (#vectors/page) x (bytes/vector) x (#query tokens)
          |                    |                  |
          |                    |                  +-- scalar int8 (4x), binary (32x),
          |                    |                      PLAID residuals [20][27][32]
          |                    +-- token pooling: hierarchical (3x), row/col mean (32x),
          |                        k-means [2][18][26]
          +-- multi-stage: MUVERA / pooled / dense prefetch -> full MaxSim rerank
              on 100-1,000 candidates [19][22][24]

Reducing vectors per page: token pooling

  • Hierarchical token pooling (Clavié, Chaffin, Adams, 2024) clusters a document's vectors with Ward linkage on cosine distance and replaces each cluster with its mean [26][27]. It is "CRUDE-compliant": each document is pooled independently, so additions and deletions need no global retraining. For ColPali, the ILLUIN team found that a pool factor of 3 removed 66.7% of the vectors while keeping 97.8% of retrieval quality [2]. LightOn later trained models with a hierarchical-pooling regulariser and reports 99.4% retention at 5x compression on text [27].
  • Grid pooling uses the spatial layout of patches. Mean-pooling each row of ColPali's 32x32 grid gives 32 vectors per page (plus the 6 special vectors, 38 in total). That is 8 KB per page instead of 256 KB in float16. Column pooling captures vertical structure such as table borders. Using both gives 64 vectors [18][20].
  • Lesson. Mean pooling preserves ranking and max pooling does not. In Qdrant's experiment, mean-pooled first-stage retrieval followed by full-resolution reranking reached NDCG@20 = 0.952 and Recall@20 = 0.917 relative to unpooled ColPali. With max pooling the figures were 0.759 and 0.656 [18].

Reducing bytes per vector: quantisation

Qdrant's course works through the arithmetic for 1M pages of ~1,024 x 128 vectors. Float32 needs 512 GB. Scalar int8 cuts that by 4x to 128 GB with less than 1% accuracy loss. Binary quantisation cuts it by 32x, to 16 KB per page [20]. Vespa's ColPali sample app goes all the way to binary. Each patch vector is stored as tensor<int8>(patch{}, v[16]), which is 128 sign bits packed into 16 bytes, with Hamming distance and an HNSW index. The query is sent twice: as binarised tokens for a cheap Hamming MaxSim in the first phase (1/(1+hamming) summed over the per-token maxima), and as float tokens for an exact MaxSim against unpack_bits(embedding) in a second phase limited to a small rerank window (the demo's Python client requests ranking.rerankCount of 100) [23]. PLAID (ColBERTv2) stores a centroid ID plus a quantised residual per vector. A 608,414-vector text index shrinks from 311.5 MB (float32) to 92 MB as a fast-plaid index [27][32]. The same residual compression took ColBERT's MS MARCO index from 154 GB to 16-25 GB (1- and 2-bit residuals) [30].

Reducing pages scored: multi-stage retrieval and MUVERA

  • Pooled or dense prefetch, then MaxSim rerank. Qdrant's recommended design builds HNSW only over the pooled vectors, prefetches about 200 candidates, and reranks them with the original multi-vectors. On a 20,000-page corpus (ViDoRe, UFO and DocVQA) it reports 13x faster retrieval and an order-of-magnitude faster indexing [18][19]. Oversample in the prefetch: if both stages fetch 10, the reranker can never recover the 11th document [22].
  • MUVERA (Google Research) turns a multi-vector set into one fixed-dimensional encoding (FDE). It SimHash-partitions the token vectors into buckets using k_sim random hyperplanes, aggregates each bucket, applies random +/-1 projections to d_proj dims, and concatenates the results [24][25]. A standard single-vector HNSW then retrieves on the FDE, and exact MaxSim reranks. For 1M documents of 100 vectors each, the HNSW graph is 1% of the multi-vector graph's size. Weaviate 1.31 reports about 70% lower memory and import times falling from over 20 minutes to 3-6 minutes, with "some loss in recall" that can be recovered by raising HNSW ef [24]. Qdrant's FastEmbed (0.7.2+) ships MUVERA as a post-processor for any late-interaction model, including ColModernVBERT [22].

Database support (2024-2026)

Vespa (tensor ranking expressions), Qdrant (multivector with MAX_SIM comparator), Weaviate (multi-vector plus MUVERA, and the hosted multi2multivec-weaviate vectoriser), Milvus, Elasticsearch, LanceDB and AstraDB all have documented ColPali integrations [2][19][23][29]. Weaviate's 2026 drag-and-drop pipeline renders each PDF page to a 2,000-pixel PNG, stores it as a BLOB and vectorises it server-side. Its 92-page NVIDIA earnings demo imported in about 90 seconds. The team found no strong case for rendering below 1,500 px or above 2,500 px [29].

10.6 End-to-End Visual RAG Systems

M3DocRAG (UNC Chapel Hill and Bloomberg, 2024)

M3DocRAG targets open-domain, multi-page, multi-document question answering, where the evidence may sit only in a figure [15][16]. It has three stages: (1) ColPali v1.2 embeds every page, (2) MaxSim retrieves the top-K pages, with approximate page indices for open-domain speed, and (3) Qwen2-VL-7B answers over the retrieved page images. The authors built M3DocVQA, which covers more than 3,000 PDFs and 40,000 pages, and report state-of-the-art results on MP-DocVQA [15][16]. The design lesson: a multimodal retriever lets a VLM with limited context "handle single or many documents while preserving visual information", instead of stuffing whole documents into context.

VisRAG and EVisRAG (OpenBMB, 2024-2026)

VisRAG pairs VisRAG-Ret (Section 10.3) with a VLM generator. The paper used MiniCPM-V 2.0, MiniCPM-V 2.6 and GPT-4o, and studied how to feed several retrieved page images to the generator [11][12]. EVisRAG (VisRAG 2.0), accepted at ACM MM 2026, attacks the next bottleneck: multi-image reasoning. The VLM first "linguistically observes" each retrieved image to collect per-image evidence, then reasons over that evidence. It is trained with Reward-Scoped GRPO, which binds token-level rewards to perception tokens and to reasoning tokens separately. 3B and 7B checkpoints on Qwen2.5-VL are released [12][13].

VDocRAG (NTT, CVPR 2025)

VDocRAG pairs VDocRetriever with VDocGenerator, both Phi-3-vision with LoRA, so that a single pipeline runs "purely from visual features". Pages are resized to 1,344x1,344. Queries carry an instruction prefix ("I'm looking for an image that answers the question") [14].

ViDoRAG (Alibaba Tongyi Lab, EMNLP 2025): multi-agent visual RAG

ViDoRAG (Wang et al., 2025) addresses two weaknesses of single-pass visual RAG: purely visual retrieval integrates text and visual cues poorly, and the generator gets too few reasoning tokens for multi-page questions [57]. Retrieval fuses a text and a visual retriever, and a Gaussian Mixture Model fitted to the similarity scores picks a query-specific number of pages instead of a fixed top-k. Generation is a loop of three agents. A seeker explores retrieved images, an inspector examines selected pages in detail and returns feedback or a draft, and an answer agent checks consistency and produces the final answer. The authors frame the loop as test-time scaling for RAG. They also release ViDoSeek, a benchmark of questions that need retrieval and reasoning over a large visually rich corpus rather than a single given page [57]. ViDoRAG is an early academic version of the agentic pattern that NVIDIA's ViDoRe V3 submission scaled up (Section 10.4).

Production patterns: Vespa, Weaviate and NVIDIA

 PDF/slide decks -> rasterise (1,500-2,500 px) -> page store (BLOB/object storage)
                         |
                         v
              Col* / DSE embedder (GPU)  -> [pooled|FDE|binary] ANN index
                                         -> full-precision multivectors (rerank store)
 query -> query encoder -> stage 1: ANN prefetch (100-1,000) -> stage 2: MaxSim rerank
       -> optional VL reranker / LLM-agent selection (top 5-10)
       -> VLM generator(page images + query) -> answer + page-image citations + heatmaps
  • Vespa's ColPali demo app combines BM25 over extracted title and text with binary MaxSim and full-precision reranking in "hybrid" rank profiles. It returns per-token similarity scores for heatmaps, and generates Gemini answers grounded in the retrieved page images [23].
  • Weaviate's Query Agent wraps multi-vector page retrieval in multi-step reasoning. It returns a synthesised answer whose numerical claims are "anchored to a specific page in a specific PDF, with the page image right there for verification" [29].
  • NVIDIA's NeMo Retriever agentic pipeline gives an LLM agent think, retrieve and final_results tools over a dense or ColEmbed backend (top-500 candidates per call), falls back to RRF over its retrieval calls if the agent fails, and returns 10 pages. The LLM is a configuration parameter; the ViDoRe V3 submission used Claude Opus 4.5 (Section 10.4) [4][53].

Failure modes

  • Generator context cost. Each page image consumes hundreds to thousands of VLM input tokens, so top-k must stay small (5-10). Selection quality, whether from a reranker or an agent, then dominates answer quality.
  • Multi-image reasoning. Generators confuse evidence across several pages. This is the motivation for EVisRAG [12].
  • Domain-specific visual conventions. Weaviate warns that highly stylised internal templates should be validated before rollout [29].
  • Text-dominated corpora. For contracts, transcripts or logs, "a text embedding model will still be cheaper and just as accurate" [29].

10.7 Convert-to-Text Multimodal RAG: Parsing, Captioning and Multimodal Graphs

Visual retrieval does not make parsing obsolete. Section 10.4 showed OCR-text pipelines matching visual ones on ViDoRe V3. Many systems also need text for keyword search, filtering, citations at sub-page granularity, or downstream LLMs that cannot read images. The convert-to-text family has moved from "drop the images" to element-aware interpretation.

RAG-Anything (HKUDS, 2025)

RAG-Anything extends LightRAG (Chapter 7) into an "all-in-one" multimodal document RAG system [33][34]. Its pipeline:

  1. Parsing. MinerU decomposes PDFs and Office files into text blocks, images, tables and equations, and keeps the document hierarchy.
  2. Modality routing. Each element type goes to a dedicated analyser. A visual content analyser (a VLM) writes context-aware captions and spatial relations. A structured data interpreter reads tables for trends and cross-table relations. A math parser handles LaTeX. Text and multimodal pipelines run concurrently.
  3. Multimodal knowledge graph. Significant multimodal elements become entities. Cross-modal edges link text entities to figures and tables, belongs_to chains preserve section hierarchy, and relation types carry weights.
  4. Retrieval. Vector-graph fusion combines embedding search with graph traversal and adds modality-aware ranking.
 PDF/DOCX/PPTX --MinerU--> {text | image | table | equation} + hierarchy
      text  ---------------------------------> chunks + entities --+
      image --VLM caption + spatial relations-> entity nodes ------+--> multimodal KG
      table --structured interpretation-------> entity nodes ------+    + vector index
      eqn   --LaTeX parse + concept mapping---> entity nodes ------+
 query -> vector search + graph traversal -> modality-aware rerank -> LLM/VLM answer

The trade-off is the reverse of ColPali's. Indexing is LLM- and VLM-heavy and error-prone, because each caption is a lossy, possibly hallucinated summary. In exchange, retrieval runs on cheap text and graph structures, and answers can cite individual elements.

Tables and charts as text

Modern VLM-based OCR models (olmOCR, PaddleOCR-VL and others) either keep charts as images with coordinates, caption them inline, or convert a bar chart into a Markdown table or JSON [36]. Converting charts to data makes the numbers searchable and quotable, but it discards visual salience such as trends, outliers and annotations. Weaviate's hybrid recommendation is pragmatic: "identify pages with charts to implement as multi-vectors and the remaining corpus as text, and then use an RRF-style approach to merge results at query time" [29]. Chapter 2 covers parser choice in depth.

10.8 Universal Cross-Modal Embedding Spaces

Contrastive dual encoders: CLIP, ImageBind, CLAP

  • CLIP (OpenAI, 2021) aligned image and text encoders contrastively. It is the default for natural-image retrieval and the ancestor of every model in this section [37].
  • ImageBind (Meta FAIR, CVPR 2023) learns one embedding space over six modalities: images, text, audio, depth, thermal and IMU. It binds each modality to frozen image representations, so audio-to-text retrieval emerges without paired audio-text data [38][50]. VideoRAG uses ImageBind for video-segment features [48].
  • CLAP (LAION, ICASSP 2023) applies the CLIP recipe to audio and text, with feature fusion and keyword-to-caption augmentation. It is the standard audio-text retriever [39].

Instruction-following universal retrievers

  • UniIR / M-BEIR (TIGER-Lab, ECCV 2024) trains one retriever with instructions to handle heterogeneous queries (text, image, or both) against a pool of millions of mixed-modality candidates. It tests CLIP and BLIP backbones with score fusion and feature fusion [40].
  • VISTA / Visualized-BGE (BAAI, 2024) injects image-token embeddings into the BGE text embedder for hybrid queries such as composed image retrieval and image-plus-text knowledge retrieval [41]. BGE-VL (BAAI) is trained on MegaPairs, more than 26M synthetic heterogeneous-KNN triplets, and reports an 8.1% mAP@5 gain on CIRCO [42].
  • VLM2Vec (2024), VLM2Vec-V2 (2025) and MMEB turn VLMs into embedders for images, video and visual documents. MMEB-V3 (2026) adds 111 tasks, for 190 in total. The new tasks cover audio, text retrieval and agent scenarios (tool, GUI and memory retrieval). It also adds OmniSET, a set of semantically equivalent tuples across text, image, video and audio, to diagnose whether embedders follow modality-specific instructions [43][44][45].
  • Qwen3-VL-Embedding and Qwen3-VL-Reranker. Sentence Transformers v5.4 (April 2026) supports these directly. The 2B models need about 8 GB of VRAM and the 8B about 20 GB. Multimodal cross-encoders score mixed text+image pairs [28].

The modality gap

Cross-modal similarities are systematically lower than within-modality ones. In the Sentence Transformers examples, the best text-image matches score only 0.51-0.67. This is the "modality gap" [28][52]. The relative ordering within one modality pair is preserved, so retrieval works. But a single absolute threshold or a naive score merge across modalities is wrong. Text-to-text hits will crowd out text-to-image hits. Fuse by rank (RRF), normalise per modality, or rerank with a multimodal cross-encoder (Chapter 5).

10.9 Video RAG

Video multiplies every visual cost by the frame count and adds an audio track. Published designs differ mainly in what they index per time segment.

VideoRAG (HKUDS, 2025; KDD 2026): graph plus segment embeddings

VideoRAG targets "extremely long-context" video, hundreds of hours, on a single RTX 3090 (24 GB) [47][48]. Its default configuration, from the code:

  • Segmentation. 30-second segments [48].
  • Dual-channel indexing. (a) A textual knowledge channel: faster-distil-whisper- large-v3 ASR plus MiniCPM-V-2.6 (int4) captions from 5 sampled frames per segment feed a LightRAG-style entity/relation graph and text-chunk index, embedded with nomic-embed-text (768-d). (b) A visual channel: ImageBind-huge segment embeddings (1,024-d) for direct query-to-visual retrieval [48].
  • Retrieval and generation. Retrieval combines chunk search, entity-graph search and visual segment search. For retrieved segments the system re-samples 15 frames for fine-grained captioning, keyed to timestamps, before a VLM or LLM answers [48].
  • Results. The authors built the LongerVideos benchmark (164 videos, about 134.6 h, 602 queries across lectures, documentaries and entertainment) and report that VideoRAG outperforms existing long-video methods on it. On Video-MME's long-video track, VideoRAG reaches 60.2% accuracy, against 56.3% for its MiniCPM-o and MiniCPM-V backbones with subtitles [48].
 video --split 30 s--> segment_i
    |-- audio  -> Whisper ASR ------------------+
    |-- 5 frames -> VLM caption ----------------+--> text chunks -> entity/relation KG
    |-- frames  -> ImageBind 1,024-d -> visual vector index           + text vectors
 query --> {KG/entity search, chunk search, visual search} -> top segments
       --> re-sample 15 frames -> fine captions w/ timestamps -> LLM/VLM answer

Video-RAG (2024): training-free auxiliary text

Video-RAG takes the opposite stance. It does not build a new index structure. Instead it augments any open large video-language model with three kinds of "visually aligned auxiliary text", extracted by open tools: OCR (EasyOCR), ASR (Whisper) and open-vocabulary object detection (APE). The query retrieves the relevant auxiliary text, which is then added to the frames in the prompt. It is plug-and-play and needs no training. Applied to a 72B open model, the authors report state-of-the-art open-model results on Video-MME, surpassing Gemini-1.5-Pro. The work appeared at NeurIPS 2025 [49].

VideoRAG over a video corpus (KAIST, Findings of ACL 2025)

A second, unrelated system also called VideoRAG (Jeong, Kim, Baek, Hwang, 2025) tackles a different problem: retrieving which videos in a large corpus are relevant to a query, instead of assuming the relevant video is given [58]. A large video-language model represents each video jointly from its frames and its subtitles or ASR text. The retrieved videos are then passed, with the query, to the same class of model for generation. The authors show that it beats text-only and static-image RAG baselines on knowledge-seeking QA. The two VideoRAG papers are complementary. KAIST's work is corpus-level video retrieval. HKUDS's work is about indexing and navigating within very long videos. Check which one a citation means.

Embedding video directly

  • ColQwen-Omni (ILLUIN) encodes short clips with late interaction. Frame sampling is the key control. At 1 fps and full resolution, two cooking videos produced 8,426 and 5,137 vectors with a 20.8 GB VRAM peak. At 0.5 fps and low resolution they produced 4,240 and 2,446 vectors at 12.5 GB, with an identical ranking [27].
  • tomoro-colqwen3-embed extends image-trained late interaction to short video. It encodes sampled frames and pools the frame embeddings with a per-dimension max before MaxSim, without large-scale video training [6].
  • Gemini Embedding 2 embeds MP4/MOV clips of up to 128 s into the same space as text and PDFs. Longer videos must be segmented by the application [46].

Lessons. For long video, segment at 10-60 s granularity, index both a text view (ASR plus captions) and a visual view, and return timestamps so the generator can re-look at a fine frame rate. Sample frames aggressively at index time, because the published VRAM-per-vector numbers make full-rate encoding unaffordable [27][48].

10.10 Audio RAG

Four designs are documented:

  1. ASR-first. Transcribe with Whisper-class models and index the text. This is the default inside VideoRAG and Video-RAG [48][49]. It is cheap and keeps everything in text, but it loses tone, speaker identity, music and non-speech sounds, and transcription errors on names and jargon carry into retrieval.
  2. Audio-text contrastive embeddings. CLAP and ImageBind embed sound directly, which suits sound effects, music and environmental audio [38][39].
  3. Omni-modal late interaction. ColQwen-Omni (Qwen2.5-Omni backbone) supports text, image, audio and video. Although it was trained only on image-text pairs, it retrieves audio zero-shot. Over 20 recorded conversations (about 28 s each), the query "medicine for car nausea" ranked the "carsickness" pharmacy dialogue first by a clear margin, with no transcription step. The release guidance is to chunk long audio into 30-second pieces of about 800 tokens [27]. Gemini Embedding 2 embeds MP3/WAV clips of up to 80 s [46].
  4. Audio-native retrieval for spoken dialogue. WavRAG (Chen, Ji et al., ACL 2025) drops the ASR step. Its WavRetriever embeds raw speech queries and a mixed audio-and-text knowledge base into one space. Chain-of-thought prompting then helps the spoken dialogue model use the retrieved material. The authors report retrieval quality comparable to ASR-plus-text pipelines at roughly 10x faster processing, while keeping non-speech audio retrievable [59].

A practical pattern combines (1) with (3) or (4). Keep the transcript for BM25, dense retrieval and citation, keep a native audio embedding for paralinguistic or non-speech queries, and fuse the two by rank.

10.11 Comparison of Multimodal RAG Designs

Design Index unit Vectors/unit Strengths Weaknesses Representative

Parse + caption + KG element/entity 1 + graph element-level citation; cross-modal relations LLM-heavy indexing; caption hallucination RAG-Anything [33]

10.12 Cross-Cutting Failure Modes

  • Benchmark saturation and leakage. ViDoRe V1 subsets are near ceiling (95-99 nDCG@5), and V1 training splits feed many models [10][35]. Prefer V3, private splits, or your own documents [4][6].
  • Resolution mismatch. A fixed 448 px input loses small print. Dynamic-resolution models cap tokens (768 patches for ColQwen2), so very dense pages are still downsampled. Render at about 1,500-2,500 px and let the processor resize [2][29].
  • Multilingual drift. Early Col* models were English/French. vdr-2b shows that targeted multilingual synthetic data adds up to 6 points on non-English visual pages [10].
  • Licensing. Gemma-licensed ColPali, NVIDIA non-commercial ColEmbed checkpoints, and Apache-2.0 ColQwen/ColSmol checkpoints impose different deployment constraints [2][6].
  • Cross-modal score fusion. The modality gap breaks absolute thresholds [28][52].
  • Truncation. document_length caps silently drop content. A 662-token passage passed through LateOn's 300-token cap keeps only 273 vectors [27]. Check the equivalent image-token caps for VLM retrievers.

Key takeaways for system designers

  1. Decide per corpus, not per company. For chart-, slide- and figure-heavy documents, page-image late interaction (ColQwen/ColEmbed class) is the strongest retriever. For text-dominated documents, an OCR-text pipeline with a strong reranker can match or beat it at lower cost, as the ViDoRe V3 pipeline results show [4][29].
  2. Index both views when you can. Image plus OCR-text representations beat image-only both with and without a reranker on ViDoRe V3 [4]. Route chart pages to multi-vector and plain pages to text, then fuse by rank [29].
  3. Budget for multi-vector cost from day one. Expect ~700-1,030 vectors x 128 dims per page (~512 KB float32). Plan pooled or MUVERA first-stage retrieval, binary or int8 storage, and an exact MaxSim rerank over 100-1,000 candidates. Published results show 13x speedups and ~70% memory savings for small recall losses [18][20][24].
  4. Use mean pooling, not max pooling. Hierarchical pooling at factor 2-3 or grid mean pooling keeps 95-98% of quality. Max pooling did not [2][18][26].
  5. Keep the page image for generation. Send the top 5-10 page images to a VLM. Return page-image citations and similarity heatmaps so that users can verify numbers [23][29].
  6. Spend reranking or agent compute deliberately. A VL reranker buys about 5-6 nDCG points for seconds per query. An LLM agent buys about 5 more for about 100 s per query. Reserve both for high-value queries [4].
  7. Smaller can be enough. Bidirectional ~250M-parameter retrievers (ColModernVBERT) and ColSmol/ColFlor run where 3B VLMs cannot, at a modest quality cost [6][7].
  8. For video, segment and dual-index. Use 30-second segments, ASR plus captions for a text/graph view, a segment embedding for a visual view, and timestamped fine-grained re-inspection at answer time. Sample frames sparsely at index time [27][48].
  9. For audio, keep the transcript and add native embeddings. ASR gives cheap, citable text. CLAP or omni-modal embedders cover tone, music and sound [27][39].
  10. Never merge cross-modal scores raw. The modality gap makes absolute similarities incomparable across modality pairs. Use RRF, per-modality normalisation, or a multimodal cross-encoder [28].
  11. Evaluate pipelines, not models. Use pipeline-level benchmarks (ViDoRe V3 pipeline track, MMEB-V3) that record indexing and query latency next to nDCG, and validate on your own document templates before rollout [4][29][45].
