21. RAG System Design Interview Playbook: Enterprise Q&A, Support Bots, Code Assistants, and Web Answer Engines

Overview

"Design a retrieval-augmented assistant" has become a standard prompt in ML, AI-engineer, and forward-deployed-engineer interviews. Typical versions include "design a system that answers employee questions from our internal wiki", "design a customer-support bot", "design context retrieval for a coding assistant", and "design a Perplexity-style answer engine" [1][2][3]. Prep platforms and candidate reports agree on what separates strong answers. Strong candidates treat retrieval as the hard part and generation as the easy part. They scope the corpus (size, change rate, formats such as scanned PDFs and tables) before naming any technology. They spend the closing minutes on evaluation and failure diagnosis. The recurring theme is that a wrong RAG answer is either a retrieval failure or a generation failure, and a strong candidate can show how to tell which [2][4][5].

This chapter is a playbook built on publicly documented production systems. It covers:

  1. A reusable interview framework: the 45-60 minute arc, the requirement questions, and a canonical component diagram.
  2. Back-of-envelope sizing formulas with worked numbers. These are illustrative arithmetic based on published prices and index-memory formulas.
  3. Four reference designs, each anchored to real systems:
    • Enterprise Q&A: Glean, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Uber Genie, Dropbox Dash.
    • Customer support: LinkedIn's knowledge-graph RAG, DoorDash, Klarna, Intercom Fin.
    • Code assistants: GitHub Copilot, Sourcegraph Cody, Cursor, Augment.
    • Web answer engines: Perplexity on Vespa, plus the FreshLLMs line of research.
  4. The 2024-2026 developments interviewers now probe: agentic just-in-time retrieval, multi-agent deep research, MCP connectors, built-in citations, GraphRAG, and vision-based document retrieval.
  5. A comparison table, a bank of common follow-up questions with model answers, and takeaways.

The other chapters of this atlas go deep on components: chunking (Ch. 2), embeddings (Ch. 3), vector databases (Ch. 4), hybrid search (Ch. 5), evaluation (Ch. 11), and security (Ch. 16). This chapter covers how to assemble them under interview time pressure and defend the tradeoffs.

1. The interview framework

1.1 The 45-60 minute arc

One published mock-interview transcript for a corporate RAG platform uses checkpoints at roughly minutes 10, 30, 45, and 60 [3]. Its main advice is to connect each design decision back to a stated requirement or scale number rather than listing technologies. A workable arc:

Minutes Phase What to produce
0-8 Requirements and scoping Users, corpus, freshness, ACLs, latency SLO, quality bar
8-15 Back-of-envelope sizing Chunks, index RAM, QPS, tokens per query, cost per query
15-30 High-level design Offline ingestion path and online answer path, drawn separately
30-45 Deep dives (interviewer picks) Retrieval quality, permissions, freshness, hallucination control
45-55 Evaluation and operations Offline eval set, online metrics, LLM-as-judge, feedback loop
55-60 Follow-ups and evolution Scale x10, multilingual, agentic multi-hop, long context vs RAG

1.2 Requirement questions that change the design

Ask questions whose answers change the architecture. Generic questions do not earn credit.

  • Corpus: How many documents, and how many tokens on average? What formats (HTML, PDF with tables, scans, slides, code, tickets)? What is the change rate? A static manual set and a constantly edited wiki need different ingestion pipelines [2].
  • Permissions: Is the data public to all users or ACL-scoped per user or group? In enterprise settings this is the defining constraint. Educative's framing of enterprise RAG puts access control, citation traceability, and answer accuracy at the center [1].
  • Freshness: Is minutes-stale acceptable (wiki), or must answers reflect seconds-old changes (code edits, stock prices, news)?
  • Latency SLO: Time to first token versus full answer. Interactive chat typically tolerates 1-3 s to first token. IDE autocomplete tolerates far less.
  • Quality bar and risk: Is a wrong answer an annoyance (internal wiki) or a compliance incident (payments support)? This determines whether you need a pre-delivery guardrail and human fallback.
  • Answer form: Free text with citations, structured action (refund, ticket), or code edit?
  • Traffic: Daily active users, queries per user per day, and peak-to-mean ratio.

1.3 The canonical component diagram

Almost every RAG design question reduces to two paths. Draw them separately; interviewers check that you know ingestion is a separate, asynchronous system [3].

OFFLINE / ASYNC INGESTION PATH
 sources --> connectors/crawlers --> parse & clean --> chunk --> enrich
 (wiki, tickets,  (incremental,       (OCR, tables,    (struct-   (title, path,
  code, web)       webhooks, ACLs)     dedupe)          aware)     context blurb)
                                                                  |
          +-------------------+------------------+----------------+
          v                   v                  v
     lexical index       vector index       metadata / ACL store
     (BM25 / inverted)   (HNSW / IVF / BQ)  (doc->groups, freshness)

ONLINE ANSWER PATH
 user --> auth --> query understanding --> hybrid retrieve --> fuse (RRF)
          |        (rewrite, condense,     (BM25 + dense,     |
          |         route, decompose)       ACL pre-filter)   v
          |                                              rerank (cross-enc.)
          |                                                   |
          +--> conversation memory          context assembly (top-k, order,
                                            dedupe, token budget)
                                                   |
                                                   v
                         LLM generation with citations --> guardrails --> user
                                                   |
                        logs, feedback, LLM-judge <-+--> eval sets, dashboards

Each box maps to a documented technique:

  • Contextual enrichment of chunks: Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval prepends an LLM-generated context blurb to each chunk before embedding and BM25 indexing [6].
  • Rank fusion: reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) combines lexical and dense result lists using ranks only, with k typically 60 [7].
  • Reranking: a cross-encoder rescoring stage [6].
  • Retrieval-quality gating: Corrective RAG (CRAG) uses a lightweight evaluator that decides whether to use, refine, discard, or supplement retrieved evidence with web search [8].

1.4 Numbers worth memorizing

Interviewers reward candidates who anchor choices in published data:

  • Contextual Retrieval [6]: contextual embeddings cut the top-20 retrieval failure rate about 35% (5.7% to 3.7%). Adding contextual BM25 brings the reduction to about 49% (2.9%). Adding a reranker brings it to about 67% (1.9%). Gains vary by domain. A critique notes the reduction falls to about 41% on a vague-codebase category [9].
  • Long context vs RAG [10]: the Google DeepMind / Michigan EMNLP 2024 study found long-context models outperform RAG on average when resourced sufficiently, but RAG is far cheaper because it shrinks input tokens. Their Self-Route method routes each query to RAG or long context based on the model's self-reflection, keeping comparable accuracy at much lower cost.
  • Lost in the middle [11]: accuracy follows a U-shape over the position of relevant evidence in the prompt. It is best at the start or end and degrades as context grows. This argues for small, well-ordered contexts rather than stuffing.
  • Binary quantization [12]: 1-bit embeddings cut memory 32x. Rescoring a larger binary candidate set with float32 query vectors preserves about 96% of retrieval quality.
  • RRF [7]: score(d) = sum over lists of 1/(k + rank). k = 60 is the default in many engines.
  • The seven failure points [13]: missing content, missed top-ranked documents, not in context (consolidation), not extracted, wrong format, incorrect specificity, incomplete answer. Barnett et al. also conclude that RAG robustness "evolves rather than is designed in", and that validation is only feasible during operation.

2. Back-of-envelope sizing toolkit

All numbers in this section are illustrative arithmetic. They combine published unit prices and index-memory formulas with assumed workloads. State your assumptions aloud in the interview.

2.1 Corpus to chunks

chunks = documents x avg_tokens_per_doc / (chunk_size - overlap)

OpenAI's hosted file search defaults to 800-token chunks with 400-token overlap. Overlap may be at most half the chunk size, and chunk size ranges from 100 to 4,096 tokens [14]. With a 50% overlap the effective stride is 400 tokens, so chunk count doubles compared with non-overlapping chunks. Say this when you justify a smaller overlap at scale.

2.2 Embedding cost

Third-party price trackers list text-embedding-3-small at about $0.02 per million input tokens, about $0.01 via batch, with 1,536 default dimensions [15]. Embedding cost is therefore usually negligible compared with LLM generation. The real ingestion costs are parsing (OCR, table extraction) and optional LLM enrichment. Anthropic estimated contextual chunk generation at roughly $1.02 per million document tokens with prompt caching [6][9].

2.3 Vector index memory

OpenSearch-style HNSW sizing for float32 vectors is approximately 1.1 x (4·d + 8·M) bytes per vector, where d is the dimension and M the graph degree [16]. Its binary-quantized variant replaces the 4·d vector term with roughly d/8 bytes. The exact constants and overhead factors differ by engine; ScyllaDB, for example, publishes its own sizing formula with a different graph term and overhead multiplier [16].

Worked example (d = 1,536, M = 16): 1.1 x (6,144 + 128) ≈ 6.9 KB per vector, so about 6.8-6.9 GB per million vectors in RAM.

Chunks float32 HNSW (approx.) Binary-quantized vectors only (d/8 = 192 B)
1 M ~6.9 GB ~0.2 GB (+ graph links)
100 M ~690 GB ~19 GB (+ graph links)
1 B ~6.9 TB ~190 GB (+ graph links)

The lesson: past roughly 100M chunks, a float32 in-memory HNSW is a multi-node, high-RAM deployment. Propose quantization (binary or product quantization) with float rescoring from disk [12], dimension reduction, or sharding by tenant.

2.4 Traffic and tokens

avg_QPS   = DAU x queries_per_user_per_day / 86,400
peak_QPS  ~ 3-10 x avg_QPS (state assumption)
input_tok = system_prompt + history + k_chunks x chunk_tokens + question
LLM_cost  = (input_tok x p_in + output_tok x p_out) x queries

Example: 50,000 employees x 5 questions/day = 250,000 queries/day, which is about 2.9 QPS on average and perhaps 30 QPS at peak. Each query carries 8 chunks x 500 tokens plus about 1,000 tokens of instructions and history, so about 5,000 input tokens. That totals about 1.25 billion input tokens per day. The point to make in the interview: generation tokens, not vector search, dominate cost and latency. The levers are fewer, better chunks (reranking), prompt caching of static prefixes, smaller models for routing and condensation, and caching frequent answers.

2.5 Latency budget (interactive chat, illustrative)

auth + ACL lookup           10-30 ms
query rewrite (small LLM)   100-300 ms   (skip when query is self-contained)
hybrid retrieval            20-100 ms    (BM25 + ANN in parallel)
rerank top-50..100          50-200 ms    (cross-encoder, GPU)
LLM time-to-first-token     300-1000 ms  (depends on model and prompt size)
guardrail check             50-500 ms    (cheap similarity first, LLM judge if needed)

Dropbox's Dash team describes a latency target on the order of 1-2 seconds for the large majority (about 95%) of queries. They treat retrieval as the layer that shapes both speed and answer quality [17].

3. Design A: Enterprise Q&A assistant

3.1 Problem

"Employees should ask questions in natural language over wiki, drive, tickets, chat, and email, and get cited answers. They must never see content they lack permission to read."

3.2 Requirements that dominate

  • Permissions are the hard constraint. Microsoft 365 Copilot's semantic index inherits Microsoft Graph security trimming, so users only receive content they can already open [18]. Microsoft's own ISE guidance for custom RAG over SharePoint copies document ACLs (Entra ID object IDs) into index fields at ingestion. It then filters on them at query time, and the ingestion app uses least-privilege Graph permissions (Sites.Selected) [19]. A practitioner warning makes the risk concrete: get ACLs wrong and "you've just built a single search index that ignores years of permission work in the source system" [20].
  • Heterogeneous connectors with incremental sync. Glean describes the foundation as a robust, scalable crawler that connects to all enterprise data, together with its permission rules [21].
  • Mixed query types: navigational ("the Q3 OKR doc"), factual ("what is our parental leave policy"), and people/expertise queries. Glean argues that vector search alone is insufficient. It combines a self-learning language model, lexical search, and a knowledge graph, with authority signals inspired by PageRank [21][22].

3.3 Architecture

 +-----------+   webhooks / polling   +-------------------+
 | SaaS apps |----------------------->| connector workers |--+
 | (wiki,    |   (per-source rate     | fetch content +   |  |
 |  drive,   |    limits, backoff)    | ACLs + activity   |  |
 |  tickets) |                        +-------------------+  |
 +-----------+                                               v
                       +----------------------------------------------+
                       | normalize -> chunk -> embed -> index         |
                       | per-chunk fields: tenant, acl_principals[],  |
                       | source, updated_at, author, doc_type         |
                       +---------------------+------------------------+
                                             |
         +---------------+-------------------+--------------+
         v               v                                  v
   inverted index   vector index (tenant-sharded)   knowledge graph
   (BM25)           with ACL filter fields          (people, docs, teams,
                                                     activity edges)
 ONLINE:
 user -> SSO -> expand principals (user + groups, cached) -> query rewrite
      -> parallel BM25 + ANN with filter acl_principals IN user_principals
      -> RRF -> rerank (+authority/recency/graph features) -> top 5-10
      -> LLM answer with inline citations -> post-check: cited doc still visible?

3.4 Key techniques and tradeoffs

  • Pre-filter versus post-filter for ACLs. Pre-filtering (ACL principals as index filter fields) is safe and gives full recall within the user's visible set. It requires ANN engines that handle selective filters well, and an ACL change triggers re-indexing of metadata. Post-filtering (retrieve top-N, drop unauthorized) is simpler but leaks through timing and counts. It can also return empty results when the user sees only a small slice of the corpus. Third-party analyses of Glean describe it as filtering by permission from the start rather than retrieve-then-filter [23]. Treat that as commentary, not official documentation. Always add a final "can this user still read the cited doc?" check at render time, because ACLs change between indexing and query.
  • RAG over fine-tuning. Glean argues fine-tuning is poorly suited to factual recall and permissioning, and recommends a centralized, permission-aware index with RAG [21]. Uber chose RAG for its on-call copilot Genie mainly for time to market, since fine-tuning needs curated examples and ongoing compute [24].
  • Hybrid retrieval plus reranking is table stakes. Use the 35% / 49% / 67% failure-reduction ladder from Contextual Retrieval to justify each added stage [6].
  • Agentic escalation for hard questions. Dropbox Dash pairs RAG for fast single-shot answers with multi-step agents (planning plus a custom interpreter) for complex tasks [17]. Uber later moved its security and privacy domain to an "Enhanced Agentic RAG" (EAg-RAG) design. After traditional RAG fell short on a curated 100+ query test set, it reported about 27% relative more acceptable answers and about 60% relative fewer incorrect-advice answers [25].

3.5 Scale and outcomes (public)

Uber Genie launched in September 2023. Secondary summaries of Uber's reports say it served 154 Slack channels and answered more than 70,000 questions, with a 48.9% helpfulness rate and an estimated ~13,000 engineering hours saved [24][25]. Take two lessons from these numbers. A useful internal assistant need not be "right" on every question. And helpfulness must be measured explicitly, because Genie built a user-feedback pipeline and LLM-as-judge evaluation [24].

3.6 Failure modes to name

  • Permission leakage through stale ACLs, flattened group membership, or a non-delegated service connection. Microsoft's guidance warns that a non-delegated Azure AI Search connection has no security trimming [18].
  • Duplicate and outdated documents (five versions of a policy). Mitigate with recency/authority features and dedupe at ingestion.
  • Missing content, the first of Barnett's seven failure points [13]. The system should say "I couldn't find this" rather than synthesize an answer.
  • Tables and scanned PDFs parsed badly. This is a corpus-scoping question to raise early [2].

4. Design B: Customer support bot

4.1 Problem

"Deflect a large share of inbound support conversations with accurate, policy-compliant answers. Hand off to humans gracefully."

4.2 What is different from enterprise Q&A

  • The corpus is smaller and curated: help-center articles, macros, resolved tickets. Permissions are simpler, usually per-tenant or per-customer-account.
  • Risk is higher. Wrong refund or policy statements create financial and compliance exposure, so pre-delivery guardrails and escalation are core components.
  • Conversations are multi-turn. The retrieval query must be distilled from the whole dialogue, not taken from the last message.
  • Actions matter: order lookup, refunds, account changes. The bot needs tools as well as retrieval.

4.3 Reference architectures

DoorDash Dasher support [26]. There are three parts:

  1. A RAG system that condenses the multi-message conversation into the core issue, then retrieves knowledge-base articles and similar previously resolved cases.
  2. An online guardrail. Every response must pass all checks before the Dasher sees it. Summaries describe this as two tiers: a cheap semantic-similarity check, then an LLM evaluator [26].
  3. An offline LLM judge that scores retrieval correctness, response accuracy, grammar, coherence with context, and relevance to the request.

DoorDash reports that the guardrail reduced hallucinations by about 90% and severe compliance issues by about 99%. When guardrail latency is a problem, the system defaults to human agents rather than trade off quality [26].

LinkedIn customer-service KG-RAG [27]. Instead of chunking historical tickets as flat text, LinkedIn builds a knowledge graph from them. The graph preserves each ticket's internal structure (fields such as summary, description, steps to reproduce) as a tree, and links tickets to each other via explicit references and embedding similarity. At query time, the system parses the customer query into entities and intents and retrieves matching ticket sub-graphs. It then generates the answer from those sub-graphs. The paper (SIGIR 2024) reports a 77.6% MRR improvement over a flat-text baseline. After roughly six months in production it reports a 28.6% reduction in median per-issue resolution time.

Klarna [28]. In its first month, Klarna's assistant handled 2.3 million conversations, about two-thirds of its customer-service chats. Klarna equated that to the workload of 700 full-time agents. It operates in 23 markets and more than 35 languages. Klarna reported customer satisfaction on par with humans and a 25% drop in repeat inquiries, with resolution time down from about 11 to under 2 minutes. These are company-reported launch numbers.

Intercom Fin [29]. Third-party guides describe Fin as a bespoke multi-phase RAG pipeline: query refinement, retrieval, reranking, generation, and validation. They say it uses custom retrieval and reranker models trained on customer-service interactions; the phase counts differ between sources. Anthropic's case study reports a 51% average resolution rate "out of the box" (before customization), and up to 86% of support volume for some customers; it also notes Fin answers in more than 45 languages [29]. Note the metric definition. Guides point out that "assumed" resolutions (the customer leaves after the last answer) count alongside confirmed ones, so headline rates may overstate satisfaction [29]. This makes a strong follow-up talking point about metric hygiene.

4.4 Architecture

 customer msg --> session store (history, account ctx, locale)
       |
       v
 intent + condense (small LLM): "core issue" + entities (order id, product)
       |
       +--> policy router: sensitive intent? (fraud, legal, safety) --> human
       |
       v
 retrieval: help-center (hybrid) + resolved-ticket KG / similar cases
       |                                  + tool calls (order status API)
       v
 rerank --> grounded generation (answer + citations + proposed action)
       |
       v
 guardrail tier 1: similarity(answer, retrieved evidence) >= tau ?
 guardrail tier 2: LLM judge for policy / grounding (only if tier 1 uncertain)
       |pass                                 |fail or timeout
       v                                     v
   send to user                       escalate to agent with summary
       |
       v
 offline: LLM-judge sampling, CSAT, resolution, repeat-contact, reopen rate

4.5 Sizing sketch (illustrative)

At Klarna-like volume (2.3M conversations per month), that is about 77k conversations per day, or about 0.9 conversations per second on average. If each conversation has about 4 bot turns, that is roughly 3.5 LLM turns per second on average, and an order of magnitude more at peak. The knowledge base is typically thousands to tens of thousands of articles plus millions of resolved tickets. The vector index fits on a single node even in float32 (Section 2.3). The cost drivers are LLM turns and guardrail calls, so make the expensive LLM judge conditional on the cheap check.

4.6 Failure modes

  • Retrieval keyed on the last message instead of the condensed issue. DoorDash condenses first for this reason [26].
  • A policy article that is outdated but faithfully cited. Faithfulness metrics such as RAGAS measure consistency with context, not truth [30].
  • Over-deflection: optimizing resolution rate leads to hiding the human-handoff path. Track repeat contacts and CSAT alongside deflection [28][29].
  • Guardrail latency spikes. Use a timeout that falls back to a human, as DoorDash does [26].

5. Design C: Code assistant (autocomplete and chat)

5.1 Problem

"Give completions and chat answers that use the developer's codebase, not just the open file, without leaking code and under tight latency."

5.2 What is different

  • Two products, two latency classes. Inline completion must feel instant and runs on every keystroke pause. Chat can afford seconds.
  • Extreme freshness. The "document" changes as the user types, and per-branch state differs per developer.
  • Code structure (symbols, imports, call graphs) is a stronger signal than semantic similarity of prose.
  • Security. Source code is often the most sensitive asset a company has.

5.3 Reference techniques

  • GitHub Copilot [31]. The prompt is assembled from the current file and "neighboring tabs": other open files are searched for snippets similar to the code around the cursor. A/B tests found a very low inclusion threshold worked best and gave about a 5% relative increase in accepted suggestions. Fill-in-the-middle (sending code both before and after the cursor) gave about a 10% relative boost. Caching let both run without added latency.
  • Sourcegraph Cody [32][33]. Cody frames context retrieval as recommender-style candidate generation followed by ranking. The system must balance recall and precision because only a few items fit. A larger context window does not fully solve this, since it raises inference cost and big codebases still overflow it [33]. Retrievers include keyword search with query rewriting, Sourcegraph code search (with a BM25 variant among its ranking signals), and code-graph context, plus snippets from open IDE files [32]. Sourcegraph also tested a 1M-token Gemini 1.5 Flash context and reported a substantial improvement on its "Essential Recall" benchmark [34]. That result shows long context and retrieval being combined, not one replacing the other.
  • Cursor [35]. Cursor builds a Merkle tree over the workspace: each file is hashed, and each folder's hash derives from its children. Client and server compare trees and sync only the entries that diverge. For a 50,000-file workspace, sending all filenames and SHA-256 hashes would be about 3.2 MB per update, which is what the Merkle comparison avoids. Changed files are split into syntactic chunks and embedded asynchronously, with embeddings cached by chunk content. To reuse a teammate's index safely, the client uploads its own Merkle tree with a similarity hash, and the server filters results against that tree, so users only see code they actually have [35].
  • Augment [36]. Augment claims index updates within seconds of edits (versus "10-minute" delays elsewhere) and custom retrieval models rather than generic embeddings. It keeps per-developer indices to handle branch switching, and shares overlapping index segments between users to control RAM. These are vendor claims.

5.4 Architecture

 IDE plugin                                   server
 +-----------------------------+              +-------------------------------+
 | cursor ctx (prefix/suffix)  |  completion  | low-latency code LLM (FIM)    |
 | open-tab snippet matcher    |------------->| prompt cache                  |
 | local symbol index (LSP)    |  <~ hundreds |                               |
 | Merkle tree of workspace    |  of ms total +-------------------------------+
 +-------------+---------------+
               | diff sync (changed hashes only)
               v
 +---------------------------------------------------------------+
 | chunk by syntax (functions/classes) -> embed (async, cached   |
 | by content hash) -> per-repo/branch vector index + code search |
 | + symbol/code graph                                           |
 +-----------------------------+---------------------------------+
                               |  chat / agent queries
                               v
 retrievers: keyword(+rewrite) | embeddings | graph (defs/refs) | open files
         -> rank (recsys-style) -> pack under token budget -> chat LLM
         -> answer/edit; agent may iterate (grep, read file, run tests)

5.5 Sizing sketch (illustrative)

Take a 100,000-file monorepo averaging 300 lines per file: 30M lines. With function-level chunks of about 40 lines, that is about 750k chunks, roughly 5 GB of float32 HNSW at 1,536 dimensions using the formula in Section 2.3. Per-branch indices multiply this, which is why reusing shared content-addressed chunks and storing only branch deltas matters [35][36]. Re-embedding cost is driven by churn, not repo size, so content-hash caching is the key lever.

5.6 Failure modes

  • Retrieving semantically similar but wrong-version code (other branch, deprecated module).
  • Long-context overconfidence: stuffing the repo and then "losing in the middle" [11].
  • Leakage across repos or users through shared caches. Cursor's server-side filtering against the client's own tree shows the mitigation [35].
  • Evaluating with generic benchmarks instead of product-specific ones. Cody built its own context-recall benchmarks [33][34].

6. Design D: Web answer engine

6.1 Problem

"Answer open-domain questions from the live web with citations, at consumer scale and latency."

6.2 What is different

  • The corpus is the web: billions of documents, adversarial SEO, and continuous change.
  • Freshness is a first-class requirement. FreshLLMs showed all tested LLMs struggle with fast-changing and false-premise questions [37].
  • Scale. Perplexity's research post describes a production search system handling about 200 million daily queries, built on hybrid retrieval, multi-stage ranking, distributed indexing, and a self-improving content-understanding module [38]. That works out to an average of roughly 2,300 QPS (simple arithmetic, not a published figure).
  • Granularity. Perplexity argues that a search API for AI should treat sections and spans of documents as retrievable units, not only whole pages [38].

6.3 Reference architecture: Perplexity on Vespa

Perplexity moved its search in-house onto Vespa (announced by Vespa in 2025). Its stated requirements were: combine keyword and semantic search, filter, rank individual passages, and index new content continuously at consumer latency. It wanted all of this in one platform rather than stitched-together databases, vector stores, and ranking services [39]. Vespa's materials also highlight distributed machine-learned ranking inference that combines many relevance signals [39]. Perplexity published an open evaluation framework (search_evals) and reported a median latency of about 358 ms for its Search API. These are company-run benchmarks [38].

The method lineage is public. FreshPrompt injects search-engine results (answer box, organic results, related questions) into the prompt, ordered by date. With GPT-4 it gave about +49 points of absolute accuracy on FreshQA under strict evaluation. Both the number and the order of evidence snippets mattered, and asking for concise answers reduced hallucination [37]. Trade press has described Perplexity's "online LLMs" as inspired by this work [40].

  crawler fleet --> fetch queue (priority by freshness/authority)
       |                       ^
       v                       | recrawl signals (news, change rate)
  parse + boilerplate removal + spam/quality classifiers
       |
  split into sections/spans --> per-span: text, embedding, signals
       |
       v
  distributed index (sharded by doc id), lexical + vector + attributes
 ----------------------------------------------------------------------
 ONLINE (~hundreds of ms budget for retrieval):
 query --> classify (navigational / fresh / complex) --> rewrite / decompose
       --> fan-out to all shards: hybrid retrieval of spans
       --> stage-1 cheap rank (per shard) --> merge top-N
       --> stage-2 ML ranker (many signals) --> stage-3 cross-encoder (top-K)
       --> LLM synthesize answer with numbered citations (streamed)
       --> complex queries: iterate (search -> read -> search) as agent

6.4 Tradeoffs to discuss

  • Build versus buy search. A third-party search API ships quickly but limits control of ranking, freshness, and cost per query. Perplexity's move in-house shows the trajectory at scale [39].
  • Page versus span indexing. Spans improve precision and context efficiency but multiply index size (10-100 spans per page) [38].
  • Freshness tiers. Use a small, rapidly refreshed news/real-time index next to a large, slowly refreshed index, with the query classifier routing between them.
  • Single shot versus multi-hop. Agentic research modes improve complex answers at several times the latency and cost. Route by query complexity, analogous to Self-Route [10].

6.5 Failure modes

  • Citing low-quality or SEO spam sources. Quality classifiers and authority signals belong before the LLM.
  • False-premise questions answered confidently [37].
  • Citation-answer mismatch, where the claim is not supported by the cited span. Add a post-hoc attribution check.
  • Fan-out tail latency across thousands of shards. Hedge requests and set per-shard timeouts.

7. 2024-2026 developments interviewers now probe

The four designs above are the "classic" pipeline answers. Since 2024 several developments have changed what a strong answer sounds like, and interviewers increasingly ask about them as follow-ups.

7.1 Agentic, just-in-time retrieval (especially for code)

Anthropic's context-engineering guidance (September 2025) contrasts "embedding-based pre-inference time retrieval" with agents that keep lightweight references (file paths, stored queries) and load data at runtime with tools. Claude Code uses grep, glob, and head/tail to explore a repository instead of a pre-built vector index. Anthropic says these primitives avoid "the issues of stale indexing and complex syntax trees". It also recommends a hybrid: put small, stable context (such as CLAUDE.md files) into the prompt up front and fetch everything else just-in-time [42]. The tradeoff it names: runtime exploration is slower than retrieving pre-computed data and needs good tools to avoid wasting context. In a code-assistant interview, contrast this with Cursor's and Augment's continuously synced embedding indices (Section 5.3). Embedding indices win for fuzzy "where is the logic that..." queries over huge monorepos. Agentic search wins on freshness, has no index to secure, and copes better with exact identifiers. Many products now combine the two.

7.2 Multi-agent "deep research" for complex answers

For web answer engines and enterprise research modes, the multi-hop escalation path is now often a multi-agent system. Anthropic's Research feature (June 2025) uses a lead agent that plans and spawns parallel subagents to search, then synthesizes their results with citations. On Anthropic's internal research evaluation, an Opus 4 lead with Sonnet 4 subagents scored 90.2% higher than a single Opus 4 agent. Anthropic also reports that multi-agent runs use about 15x the tokens of a chat interaction, and that token usage alone explained about 80% of performance variance on BrowseComp [43]. Interview point: the deep-research mode is a cost/latency tier of its own. Route only complex, high-value queries there, and say how you would bound spend.

7.3 MCP as the connector layer

Anthropic introduced the Model Context Protocol (MCP) on November 25, 2024 as an open standard for connecting AI assistants to content repositories, business tools, and development environments [44]. In an enterprise Q&A design, MCP servers can stand in for some bespoke connectors, and the assistant can query live systems instead of a copied index. The design questions change accordingly. Does the MCP call run with the end user's delegated credentials, so the source system enforces ACLs, or with a service identity that needs trimming? How do you combine federated live queries, which are fresh and permission-exact but slower, with a central index, which is fast and supports ranking? Tool outputs must be treated as untrusted input, as in the prompt-injection answer in Section 9.

7.4 Built-in citation APIs

Model providers now offer grounding features that return citations natively. Anthropic's Citations feature (2025) splits supplied documents into sentences (or uses caller-provided chunks) and returns the exact passages backing each claim. Anthropic reported that it increased recall accuracy by up to 15% over most custom citation implementations in internal evaluations. One customer, Endex, reported source hallucinations and formatting issues falling from 10% to 0% [45]. This does not replace retrieval, which still selects the documents. It does simplify the "citation-answer mismatch" check in Section 6.5, because the cited span is returned as structured data and can be verified directly.

7.5 GraphRAG for global "sensemaking" questions

Microsoft's GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024) extracts an entity knowledge graph from the corpus with an LLM, detects communities, and pre-generates community summaries. It answers "global" questions ("what are the main themes across all incident reports?") with a map-reduce over those summaries. Chunk-level retrieval handles such questions poorly because no single chunk contains the answer. The paper reports gains in comprehensiveness and diversity over naive RAG on such queries [46]. The cost is a large, LLM-heavy indexing step that must be redone as content changes. Mention it for corpus-level analytics questions, not for the factual lookups that dominate support and enterprise Q&A.

7.6 Vision-based retrieval for visually rich documents

When the corpus is scanned PDFs, slides, and tables (the scoping question from Section 1.2), the parse-then-chunk pipeline is often where quality is lost. ColPali (Faysse et al., 2024; ICLR 2025) embeds page images directly with a vision-language model and scores them with ColBERT-style late interaction. It skips OCR and layout parsing, and the authors report it outperforming text-pipeline baselines on their ViDoRe benchmark [47]. The tradeoff is storage: late interaction keeps many vectors per page, which multiplies index size compared with the single-vector math in Section 2.3. In an interview, offer it as the fallback for document types where OCR quality has been measured to be poor.

Dimension Enterprise Q&A Support bot Code assistant Web answer engine
Corpus size 10^6-10^8 docs 10^3-10^6 articles/tickets 10^4-10^6 files per repo 10^9+ pages
Hardest constraint Per-user ACLs Policy correctness, safety Latency + freshness per keystroke Scale + freshness + spam
Freshness need Minutes-hours Hours-days (policy changes) Seconds Minutes for news
Retrieval core Hybrid + graph/authority [21] Condense + hybrid / ticket KG [26][27] Keyword + embeddings + code graph [32] Hybrid span retrieval, multi-stage ML rank [38][39]
Guardrails Render-time ACL recheck Pre-delivery 2-tier guardrail, human fallback [26] Repo/tenant isolation [35] Source quality, attribution
Public outcome numbers Genie: 70k+ Qs, 48.9% helpful [24] DoorDash -90% hallucinations [26]; LinkedIn -28.6% resolution time [27] Copilot +5% (tabs), +10% (FIM) acceptance [31] ~200M queries/day, ~358 ms median [38]
Primary metric Helpfulness, citation precision Resolution, CSAT, repeat contacts Acceptance rate, context recall Answer accuracy, latency, freshness
Typical escalation Agentic multi-step [17][25] Human agent Agent loop (grep/read/test) Multi-hop research mode

9. Common follow-up questions and strong answers

"How do you know if a bad answer is a retrieval or a generation failure?" Log retrieved chunk IDs for every answer. Build a labeled set of question, gold passages, and gold answer. Measure retrieval recall@k against the gold passages separately from answer correctness given gold context. If the gold passage was not retrieved, the failure is retrieval (failure points 1-2 in [13]). If it was retrieved but the answer was wrong, the failure is consolidation, extraction, or generation (points 3-7). Interviewers report this diagnosis skill is the core of the evaluation discussion [4].

"What metrics would you track?"

  • Offline: recall@k and MRR for retrieval (LinkedIn reported MRR [27]); faithfulness, answer relevance, and context relevance via RAGAS-style reference-free LLM judging [30]; context recall when references exist.
  • Online: product metrics such as acceptance rate [31], resolution and CSAT [28][29], and helpfulness votes [24].
  • Monitoring: LLM-judge sampling over production traffic [26].
  • Caveat: faithfulness does not catch faithfully cited stale content [30].

"Why not just fine-tune the model on our docs?" Fine-tuning is weak at factual recall. It cannot enforce per-user permissions, needs retraining whenever content changes, and gives no citations [21][24]. Fine-tune retrievers, rerankers, or style instead. Intercom reportedly trains its own retrieval and reranker models [29].

"Context windows are 1M tokens now. Do we still need RAG?" Long context can win on accuracy when cost is no object. RAG is far cheaper, and hybrid routing (Self-Route) keeps most of the accuracy [10]. Long prompts also suffer position effects [11], and corpora still exceed windows [33]. Best answer: retrieval narrows the corpus, and long context lets you include whole documents or files rather than tiny chunks.

"How do you handle a document whose permissions change?" Store ACL principals per chunk. Propagate ACL change events through the same incremental pipeline as content changes, updating only metadata with no re-embedding. Cache user-to-group expansion with a short TTL, and re-check access at render time [19][20].

"The corpus grows 10x. What breaks first?" RAM for float32 HNSW (Section 2.3). Mitigate with binary or product quantization plus rescoring [12], tenant sharding, and tiered storage. Re-embedding on a model upgrade becomes a multi-day batch, so version the index and dual-write during migration.

"How do you reduce hallucinations?"

  • Retrieval gating: CRAG-style evaluator [8], or abstain when the top rerank score is low.
  • Explicit instructions to answer only from context and to cite.
  • Concise answers [37].
  • Pre-delivery guardrails [26].
  • Human fallback for high-risk intents.
  • Measure faithfulness continuously.

"How do you make it faster and cheaper?"

  • Skip query rewriting for self-contained queries.
  • Run BM25 and ANN in parallel.
  • Rerank only the top 50-100 results.
  • Send fewer, better chunks.
  • Use prompt caching for static system prompts and document prefixes. Anthropic's contextual chunking cost estimate assumes caching [6].
  • Use a small model for routing and condensation.
  • Cache semantically equivalent frequent questions, keyed by ACL set.
  • Stream tokens.

"How do you handle multi-hop questions?" Decompose the query or iterate as an agent. Dropbox [17] and Uber [25] both moved complex queries to agentic flows. Bound the iterations, and route only complex queries there to protect latency.

"How do you prevent prompt injection from retrieved documents?" Treat retrieved text as data:

  • Delimit it clearly in the prompt.
  • Strip active content at ingestion.
  • Restrict tool permissions to the user's own scope.
  • Require confirmation for side-effecting actions in support bots.
  • Run output guardrails.

See Chapter 16 for detail.

10. Interview anti-patterns

  • Drawing "user -> vector DB -> LLM" and stopping. There is no ingestion path, no ACLs, no reranker, and no evaluation [2][3].
  • Choosing a vector database by brand before stating corpus size, QPS, or filter selectivity.
  • Assuming 50% chunk overlap and float32 vectors at a billion scale without doing the RAM math (Section 2.3).
  • Offering "use a bigger context window" as the answer to retrieval quality [10][11][33].
  • Reporting a single headline metric (deflection, resolution) without its definition [29].
  • Ignoring the "missing content" case. The system must be able to say it does not know [13].

Key takeaways for system designers

  1. Draw two systems. Asynchronous ingestion (connectors, parsing, chunking, enrichment, ACL capture) and the online answer path have different SLOs, failure modes, and scaling axes.
  2. The defining constraint picks the architecture:
    • permissions for enterprise Q&A [18][19];
    • policy safety for support [26];
    • keystroke latency and freshness for code [31][35];
    • scale, freshness, and spam for the web [38][39]. Name it in the first five minutes.
  3. Hybrid retrieval plus reranking is the default. Published ablations show each stage cuts retrieval failures: about 35%, then 49%, then 67% cumulative [6]. RRF is the simple fusion baseline [7].
  4. Do the memory math. Float32 HNSW costs about 6.9 GB per million 1,536-d vectors. Quantization with rescoring keeps about 96% quality at 1/32 the vector memory [12][16].
  5. Generation tokens dominate cost and latency. Fewer, better-ordered chunks beat more chunks [11]. Route easy queries cheaply and hard ones to long context or agents [10].
  6. Guardrails and fallbacks are components, not afterthoughts. DoorDash's two-tier guardrail with human fallback is the canonical pattern [26].
  7. Structure beats flat text when the data has it. LinkedIn's ticket knowledge graph improved MRR by about 78% [27], code graphs help code assistants [32], and authority graphs help enterprise search [22].
  8. Evaluate retrieval and generation separately, offline and online. Expect robustness to come from operation, not upfront design [13]. Uber, DoorDash, and LinkedIn all built judge-based evaluation pipelines [24][26][41].
  9. Read headline metrics critically. Resolution and deflection rates depend on definitions [29]. Company benchmarks are self-reported [38][39].
  10. Know the 2024-2026 alternatives. Be ready to argue when agentic just-in-time search beats a pre-built index [42], when a multi-agent research tier is worth its ~15x token cost [43], how MCP connectors change the permission model [44], and when GraphRAG [46] or vision-based retrieval [47] fits the corpus better than chunk-and-embed.

22. Master Index of RAG Engineering Blogs, Talks and Guides

This chapter is the atlas's bibliography in working form. It lists the engineering blogs, conference talks, vendor guides, practitioner essays and papers that people building retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems actually cite, grouped by company and by topic. Each entry has a one-line summary and a numbered reference that carries the full URL. The second half is a flat annotated index of 240+ entries.

The first half reads the most informative primary sources as one body of evidence. It covers the problem each team set out to solve, the architecture they shipped, the numbers they published, and the failures they admitted. The pattern that emerges is consistent across companies. Production RAG wins came mostly from retrieval and data preparation, not from the generator. Systems moved from single-shot "embed, top-k, stuff" pipelines toward agentic retrieval and structured indexes (graphs, Merkle-synced code indexes, page images). Evaluation and guardrails became first-class components rather than afterthoughts.

Method and caveats. The entries were collected through web searches and direct reads of primary sources in October 2026. Many company blogs could not be fetched directly from the research environment. For those posts the facts below come from search-result extracts of the primary page or from clearly labeled secondary summaries; the ZenML LLMOps database is the most common one. Numbers that come from secondary sources are marked "(secondary)". Numbers that could not be checked against the original are marked approximate. Coverage is broad but not complete. A second research pass (October 2026) added text-to-SQL and data-agent posts (Uber, Swiggy), more DoorDash, LinkedIn, Dropbox, Instacart and Airbnb posts, Cursor's semantic-search study, Google's "sufficient context" work, and more vendor and framework guides (entries 172-235). A third editorial pass (October 2026) checked headline numbers against the Anthropic and Microsoft Research primary posts, corrected several of them, and added entries 236-242 on tool protocols, agent tool design, GraphRAG 1.0, HippoRAG 2 and reasoning-model search agents. Several well-known company posts (for example from Spotify, Netflix, Notion, Slack and Shopify) still did not show up in searches. They are left out rather than cited from memory.

R | Agent | Uber EAg-RAG| Multi-agent | LangChain   | Chip Huyen  |
S | -ic   |             | research,   | decon. RAG  |             |
  |       |             | ctx. eng.   |             |             |

To answer a design question, read across a row. For example, to decide on a chunking strategy, compare Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval [91], Jina's late chunking [117], LlamaIndex's decoupled retrieval and synthesis chunks [123], and Cursor's syntactic chunks [61]. To see how a single company's thinking changed over time, read down a column.

22.2 Deep reads: company engineering case studies

22.2.1 Uber: Genie and Enhanced Agentic RAG

Problem. On-call engineers at Uber asked roughly 45,000 questions a month in Slack help channels. The answers were spread across Engwiki, an internal Stack Overflow and other stores [44]. Uber chose RAG over fine-tuning mainly for time to market: fine-tuning needs curated, diverse examples and recurring compute to stay current [44].

Architecture (v1, 2023-2024). Internal sources go through ETL into chunks, then into embeddings and a vector store. A Slack bot retrieves the top chunks and generates an answer with citations, and users leave helpfulness feedback. According to a secondary summary, Genie reached 154 Slack channels, answered more than 70,000 questions with a 48.9% helpfulness rate, and saved about 13,000 engineering hours (approximate) [164].

Architecture (v2, May 2025: EAg-RAG). Pointed at more than 40 security and privacy policy documents stored as PDFs, the traditional pipeline "revealed significant gaps" [45]. The redesign added richer document processing: custom Google Docs loaders, and LLM-driven content formatting so that tables and structure survive parsing. It also added pre-processing agents (query optimization, source identification) and post-processing agents (context refinement) around a hybrid vector and BM25 retriever [45][165]. The reported result was a 27% relative increase in acceptable answers and a 60% relative reduction in incorrect advice (secondary) [165].

 Slack question
      |
      v
 +-----------------+    +--------------------+    +---------------------+
 | Query optimizer |--->| Source identifier  |--->| Hybrid retrieval    |
 | (agent)         |    | (agent: which docs)|    | vector + BM25 top-k |
 +-----------------+    +--------------------+    +----------+----------+
                                                             |
                     +---------------------------+           v
 answer + cites <----| Generator (LLM)           |<---| Post-processor     |
                     +---------------------------+    | (context refine)   |
                                                      +--------------------+
 Offline: PDF/GDoc loaders -> LLM formatting (tables, headings) -> chunks -> index

Lesson. The jump in quality came from document enrichment plus query-side agents, not from changing the generator. This agrees with the controlled comparison in "Is Agentic RAG worth it?" [37]: agentic retrieval helps on hard, policy-heavy corpora but costs latency and tokens.

22.2.2 DoorDash: RAG with a two-tier guardrail and LLM judge

Problem. DoorDash wanted to automate support for Dashers (delivery drivers) without hallucinated or policy-violating answers [46].

Architecture. The multi-turn chat is first condensed into a single issue statement. That summary drives retrieval over knowledge-base articles and past resolved cases, and an LLM then drafts the reply [46]. DoorDash first tried a more sophisticated guardrail model but found it too slow and too token-expensive. The shipped version has two tiers. The first is a cheap in-house semantic-similarity check between the response and the knowledge-base segments. Only responses that fail it go to an LLM evaluator. A separate LLM Judge monitors quality offline [46][151].

Numbers. Secondary sources cite a 90% reduction in hallucinations and a 99% reduction in compliance issues across thousands of daily requests [153][166]. These were not verified against the original post and should be treated as approximate. A 2025 follow-up extends the knowledge base with user-generated content, because a manually curated knowledge base does not scale [46].

Lesson. Run the expensive grounding check only on the tail. A cheap similarity filter in front of an LLM evaluator keeps guardrail latency close to retrieval latency.

22.2.3 LinkedIn: knowledge-graph RAG for support, and the GenAI product postmortem

LinkedIn's SIGIR 2024 paper argues that treating historical tickets as flat text loses both the structure inside each ticket and the links between tickets [40]. The paper builds a dual-layer knowledge graph. The intra-issue layer is a tree of ticket sections. The inter-issue layer links tickets through explicit metadata and through implicit links inferred from embeddings. Queries are parsed into entities and intents, sub-graphs are retrieved, and the answer is generated from them. Reported results: MRR improved by 77.6%, and median per-issue resolution time fell by 28.6% after deployment on LinkedIn's customer service team [40][171].

The companion "Musings on building a generative AI product" post [47] is one of the most widely quoted postmortems. According to secondhand accounts, the team reached about 80% of the target experience in roughly one month, then spent about four more months pushing past 95%, with each additional 1% "discouragingly" hard because of hallucinations. Earlier LinkedIn posts and a 2025 talk describe the platform that grew out of this work [48][49][150][167].

22.2.4 Pinterest: RAG for table selection in text-to-SQL

Pinterest's text-to-SQL feature lives in Querybook, its open-source SQL tool. The first version assumed users knew which tables to query. The second added RAG for table discovery: an LLM writes a summary of each table from its schema and sample queries, those summaries and historical queries are embedded into a vector index, and only "top-tier" tables are indexed so that low-quality datasets never reach the prompt [50][51][53]. At query time, the question is embedded and matched against the index. An LLM re-selects the best tables from the candidates, the user confirms them, and SQL is generated. Reported impact: 35% faster task completion and a first-shot acceptance rate that rose from about 20% to over 40% [50][52]. A later Pinterest write-up on unified context-intent embeddings for analytics tables (covered in Korean by [54]) and academic follow-ups such as CSR-RAG [38] continue the line.

22.2.5 Ramp and Grab: RAG as a constrained classifier and an analytics engine

Ramp's January 2025 post (by Ryne Carbone) rebuilds industry classification as RAG over the NAICS taxonomy [57]. Retrieval restricts the LLM to valid six-digit codes, which turns open generation into a multiple-choice question. A secondary summary describes two stages: optimized embeddings produce candidate codes, then a dual-prompt LLM makes the final selection. The same summary reports about 60% better recommendation retrieval and 5-15% better final accuracy (secondary) [168]. Ramp's engineering index also lists a separate post on transaction embeddings trained with triplet loss [58].

Grab's Integrity Analytics team paired an internal LLM tool (Spellvault) with a data middleware layer (Data-Arks) that exposes vetted SQL and API outputs as retrievable context. A secondary summary reports savings of 3-4 hours per report and fraud investigations shortened to minutes [55][56].

22.2.6 Harvey: vector-store selection for legal RAG

Harvey's February 2025 post describes three data scales [66][68]:

  • Ad-hoc uploads of about 1-50 documents
  • Project "vaults" of about 100-100,000 documents
  • Third-party corpora of millions of legal documents, which a related talk puts at tens of millions [67]

Harvey runs two vector stores in parallel. Postgres with pgvector uses brute-force KNN, which gives high accuracy at small-to-medium scale. LanceDB uses an IVF-PQ index with tunable recall versus latency, and its decentralized storage can sit in per-customer cloud buckets, which matters for confidentiality and customer isolation [66]. The comparison table quotes LanceDB latency at 15M rows with metadata filtering [66].

Lesson. In regulated domains, tenancy and retention shape the index topology as much as recall does.

22.2.7 Code assistants: GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Sourcegraph

GitHub (2025). A new Copilot embedding model raised the average retrieval score from 0.362 to 0.498 (37.6%) and lifted code-acceptance ratios for C# users in VS Code by 110.7% [59]. InfoQ adds that index throughput doubled and memory dropped eightfold [60]. Training on "hard negatives" (code that looks right but is wrong) is reported by weaker sources [59][60].

Cursor. Cursor hashes every file and builds folder hashes from their children's hashes, forming a Merkle tree. Client and server compare trees and sync only the branches that differ. Changed files are split into syntactic chunks and embedded in the background, with embeddings cached by chunk content [61]. Third-party write-ups add that a new teammate's index can be bootstrapped by copying a similar existing index from the team namespace, and that the vector store is reported to be Turbopuffer [62][63]. These details are unverified.

Cursor, semantic search for agents (November 2025) [192]. In an era of grep-capable agents, Cursor asked whether an embedding index still earns its keep. It trained a custom embedding model using agent sessions as training data, then compared agents that had grep only with agents that had grep plus semantic search. Search-result extracts of the post report:

  • Question-answering accuracy rose by an average of 12.5% (6.5% to 23.5%, depending on the model).
  • Code retention also rose, by a smaller 2.6% on large codebases (1,000+ files).

Lesson: lexical tools and dense retrieval work well together for agents, and the gain grows with repository size [192][193].

Sourcegraph Cody. Sourcegraph chose RAG over fine-tuning because code changes too quickly for a fine-tuned snapshot to stay current [64]. Context comes from three sources: keyword search with automatic query rewriting, the Sourcegraph search backend, and a code graph that follows structural relationships. Users can also pull context in explicitly with @-mentions [65].

      Cursor-style incremental code index
 local repo --hash--> Merkle tree --diff vs server--> changed files only
                                                          |
                                         syntactic (AST) chunking
                                                          |
                         content-hash cache hit? --yes--> reuse vector
                                    | no
                                    v
                           embed -> vector namespace (per repo / team)

22.2.8 Enterprise search: Glean and Dropbox Dash

Glean's posts describe a knowledge graph built from three pillars: content, people and activity. It is assembled per customer from 100+ connectors through continuous crawling rather than federated search [69][70]. The RAG layer runs plan, retrieve, generate. The planner learns to query Glean's own hybrid engine (semantic search, lexical search and the graph) and to rewrite queries with knowledge of the enterprise. Retrieval enforces permissions, so the LLM never has blanket access to company data [69][71]. The "Scholastic" semantic model is fine-tuned on each customer's corpus and click data [71]. Newer posts move to agentic reasoning built on the same retrieval layer [72].

Dropbox's engineering blog lists "How Dash uses context engineering for smarter AI" (November 2025), a December 2025 post on the feature store behind Dash, and a January 2026 post on knowledge graphs, MCP and DSPy in Dash [75]. A podcast with Dropbox's VP of Engineering covers the "context engine" in more depth [74]. The Dropbox posts themselves could not be fetched, so no numbers are reported here. The earlier "Building Dash" post [182] describes Dash as universal search plus knowledge management with content access control. A third-party summary describes its retrieval as a fast lexical candidate search followed by an embedding rerank, with documents sliced at query time rather than pre-chunked (secondary) [182].

22.2.9 Text-to-SQL and data agents: Uber QueryGPT, Swiggy Hermes

Text-to-SQL is RAG in which the "documents" are table schemas and example queries. The hard part is again the retrieval step, here choosing tables. Pinterest (22.2.4) and the two systems below converge on the same fix: scope retrieval to a business domain before searching.

  • Uber QueryGPT [172]. Uber's data platform serves about 1.2 million queries a month, and Operations issues about 36% of them (secondary). QueryGPT groups SQL samples and table schemas into "workspaces" by business domain (Mobility, Ads, Core Services and others). It then retrieves similar samples and schemas from a vector index within the selected workspace. The later Finch post [173] turns the same idea into a conversational financial data agent.
  • Swiggy Hermes [174][175][176]. V1 was a thin GPT-3.5 prompt. V2 moved to a RAG architecture on GPT-4o, partitioned into business-unit "charters", each with its own metadata and knowledge base. It answers several thousand queries for hundreds of users, with turnaround under 2 minutes. A V3 summary reports a conversational multi-turn analyst and query accuracy rising from 54% to 93% (secondary; approximate).
 question --> domain router --> [workspace / charter]
                                    |  table summaries + example SQL (vector index)
                                    v
                         candidate tables (top-N) --> LLM re-select (top-K)
                                    |                       |
                                    +------> user confirms --+--> SQL gen --> run/validate

Lesson. A domain partition does three jobs at once. It shrinks the retrieval search space, raises precision, and gives each team ownership of its metadata quality.

22.3 Deep reads: model-provider and research-lab blogs

22.3.1 Anthropic

Contextual Retrieval (September 2024) [91].

  • Before indexing, Claude 3 Haiku reads the whole document and writes a 50-100 token context for each chunk. That context is prepended to the chunk before both embedding and BM25 indexing.
  • Failure rate is measured as 1 minus recall@20. With the best embedding model tested (Gemini Text 004), the baseline failure rate was 5.7%. Contextual embeddings alone cut failures by 35% (to 3.7%). Adding contextual BM25 brought the cut to 49% (2.9%). Adding a reranker brought it to 67% (1.9%).
  • With reranking, the top 150 chunks are retrieved and reranked down to 20. Twenty chunks beat 5 or 10.
  • Prompt caching brings the one-time indexing cost to about $1.02 per million document tokens. The estimate assumes 8k-token documents, 800-token chunks, 50 tokens of instructions and 100 tokens of context per chunk.
  • Cohere's reranker was used in the tests (Voyage's was mentioned but not tested).
  • Secondary coverage [155][156], and a critique arguing that context is "not all you need" [157], are indexed below.

Citations (2025) [92]. The API splits PDF and text sources into sentences (developers can also pass their own chunks) and returns grounded citations. Anthropic's internal evaluations show up to 15% better recall accuracy than most custom citation implementations; this is a vendor claim, not an independent benchmark. Endex reports that source hallucinations and formatting issues fell from 10% to 0%, with 20% more references per response.

Building effective agents (December 2024) [95]. The post frames the "augmented LLM" (retrieval, tools, memory) as the basic building block of agentic systems. It notes that a single call with retrieval and in-context examples is often enough, so agentic complexity is not always needed.

Multi-agent research system (June 2025) [94]. A lead agent plans and spawns parallel subagents that search and compress what they find. A citation agent then attributes each claim to a source. With Claude Opus 4 as lead and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents, this setup beat single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on an internal research eval. The cost is tokens: single agents use about 4x the tokens of a chat interaction and the multi-agent system about 15x. Token usage alone explained about 80% of the variance on BrowseComp; with tool-call count and model choice it explained about 95%. The lead agent runs 3-5 subagents in parallel, and each subagent runs 3+ tools in parallel, which cut research time by up to 90% on complex queries. Admitted failure modes include:

  • spawning 50 subagents for simple queries
  • duplicated work from vague delegation
  • a bias toward SEO-optimized content farms over authoritative sources such as academic PDFs, fixed by adding source-quality heuristics to the prompts

The post explicitly contrasts its adaptive multi-step search with static top-k RAG.

Effective context engineering (September 2025) [93]. The post argues for "just-in-time" retrieval. The agent holds lightweight references (paths, queries, links) and loads content through tools such as glob and grep when it needs it. A hybrid approach preloads a little context (for example CLAUDE.md files) and explores the rest at runtime, which avoids stale indexes. The trade-off is that runtime exploration is slower than querying a pre-built index.

The arc of this series is instructive. Microsoft first showed that global "sensemaking" questions need structure [17][96]. It then spent a year driving down the cost of that structure [98][100][101], and finally built a benchmark that measures it without hand-written test sets [102]. The BenchmarkQED result is relevant to the long-context debate: even vector RAG with a 1M-token window (on GPT-4.1) lost to LazyGraphRAG across query classes, with only one comparison (answer relevance on local queries) short of statistical significance [102].

22.3.3 Databricks, AWS, Google, Microsoft Azure, OpenAI

  • Databricks [77][24]. More than 2,000 experiments on 13 LLMs (20 in the paper). Llama-3.1-405B performance starts to fall after 32k tokens of retrieved context and GPT-4-0125-preview after 64k. Failure modes vary by model: some answer incorrectly, some fail to follow instructions, and some refuse.
  • AWS Generative AI Innovation Center [78][79]. Part 1 covers text RAG: hybrid search, preprocessing that enriches context, query rewriting, and both quantitative and qualitative evaluation. Part 2 extends to tables, databases and images. AWS prescriptive guidance [80] and the Bedrock Knowledge Bases documentation [81] cover the managed path.
  • Azure [82][83] and Google Cloud [84][85][86] publish reference architectures and design guides. OpenAI's accuracy guide frames RAG, prompting and fine-tuning as separate levers to tune [87], and its file-search documentation describes the managed retrieval tool [88]. The current Responses API documentation describes file search as a hosted tool that combines semantic and keyword search over uploaded files [235].
  • Google Research, "sufficient context" (ICLR 2025) [196][197]. This work separates RAG errors into two kinds: the retrieved context was insufficient, or the model failed despite sufficient context. Large models answer well when the context is sufficient, but they tend to guess rather than abstain when it is not. A selective-generation method that uses sufficiency signals improves the share of correct answers among the responses given by about 2-10% across Gemini, GPT and Gemma.
  • AWS Bedrock GraphRAG GA (March 2025) [198]. Managed GraphRAG on Neptune Analytics. It extracts entities and relationships alongside embeddings, and offers semantic, hierarchical, fixed-size or Lambda-based custom chunking. AWS's worked example costs about $0.48 per hour for Neptune Analytics.
  • Azure AI Search [200][201] runs full-text and vector search in parallel and merges them with Reciprocal Rank Fusion. Microsoft's query-engine whitepaper adds generative query rewriting with a fine-tuned small language model and a new semantic ranker. Vertex AI RAG Engine [199] is Google's managed pipeline covering ingestion, chunking, embedding, indexing, retrieval and generation.

22.3.4 Tools, protocols and memory: 2024-2026 developments

The first two passes of this index concentrated on retrieval pipelines. Several 2024-2026 developments change where retrieval lives in a system, and they are cited often enough to belong in the core reading list.

  • Model Context Protocol (Anthropic, November 2024) [236]. MCP is an open standard for connecting assistants to "the systems where data lives". It launched with prebuilt servers for Google Drive, Slack, GitHub, Git, Postgres and Puppeteer. For RAG it moves connectors out of each application into reusable servers, so a retriever becomes one tool among many that an agent can call. The Dropbox Dash posts on MCP [75] are an example.
  • Writing effective tools for agents (Anthropic, September 2025) [237]. This is the tool-side companion to context engineering [93]. Its retrieval advice: prefer targeted search_* tools to list_* tools that dump everything into context; expose a response_format switch (in the post's Slack example, concise responses used about a third of the tokens of detailed ones); return readable fields instead of opaque IDs, which reduced hallucinations and improved retrieval precision; and paginate or truncate with sensible defaults. Claude Code caps tool responses at 25,000 tokens by default.
  • GraphRAG 1.0 (Microsoft Research, December 2024) [238]. The production release of the library [103]. It adds an incremental update command so a changed corpus does not need full re-indexing, builds a default vector store (LanceDB, with Azure AI Search supported) during indexing, cuts Parquet output by 80% and total disk use by 43%, and drops CLI startup from about 148 s to 2 s. It is not backward compatible with pre-1.0 indexes. It answers the "stale graph" failure mode listed in the technique table below.
  • HippoRAG 2 (OSU, ICML 2025) [239][240]. "From RAG to Memory" recasts graph retrieval as non-parametric continual learning. It extends the Personalized PageRank memory of HippoRAG [18] so that new knowledge can be added without retraining. It is the main research counterpoint to treating graph RAG only as a summarization device.
  • Reasoning models that search (2025) [241][242]. Search-o1 [241] puts an agentic search step and a "reason-in-documents" condensation step inside a large reasoning model's chain of thought. OpenAI's deep research [242] productized the same pattern (multi-step browsing with citations) in February 2025. Together with Search-R1 [33] and Anthropic's research system [94], these mark the 2025 shift from "retrieve then generate" to retrieval as a tool that a reasoning loop calls repeatedly.

Lesson. By 2026 the retriever is increasingly a tool behind a protocol, not a fixed pipeline stage. Tool ergonomics (response size, search granularity, readable identifiers) have become retrieval-quality levers in their own right.

22.4 Deep reads: infrastructure vendors and techniques

  • Late chunking (Jina, August 2024) [117][21]. Run a long-context embedding model (8,192 tokens) over the whole document, then split into chunks after the transformer and just before mean pooling. Each chunk vector is then conditioned on the surrounding document.
  • ColPali on Vespa [112]-[116][20]. Embed page screenshots as multi-vectors, which skips OCR and chunking. Vespa reports better ViDoRe results than BM25 and BGE-M3. For billions of pages, it adds a Hamming-distance MaxSim over binary-quantized vectors inside a phased ranking pipeline [112].
  • Hybrid fusion (Weaviate) [109][110]. Run BM25 and vector search in parallel, normalize, and fuse. Weaviate offers rankedFusion and relativeScoreFusion; the latter has been the default since v1.24. AutoCut (v1.20) trims the tail of the result list.
  • Two-stage retrieval (Pinecone) [105]-[108]. A bi-encoder retrieves candidates and a cross-encoder reranks them. Pinecone hosts rerankers such as bge-reranker-v2-m3 as a separate inference step.
  • Decoupled chunks (LlamaIndex) [123]. Use different chunks for retrieval and for synthesis: embed small units for precision, then expand to a window or the parent section before generation ("small-to-big").
  • Query transformations (LangChain) [125][126]. Multi-query, RAG-Fusion, decomposition, step-back and HyDE [9], plus a multi-vector retriever that indexes summaries but returns the full documents.

22.5 Practitioner canon: essays, courses, talks

  • Eugene Yan [139][140]. Seven patterns for LLM systems, with RAG as the pattern for adding fresh external knowledge. His 2023 AI Engineer keynote covers evals, RAG, guardrails and feedback.
  • Applied LLMs [141][142]. Written by Yan, Bischof, Frye, Husain, Liu and Shankar (May-June 2024). Do not neglect keyword search, prefer RAG over fine-tuning for new knowledge, and long-context models will not make RAG obsolete.
  • Jason Liu [144][145][146]. Treat RAG as a recommender system. Measure retrieval precision, recall and MRR on synthetic evaluation sets, and separate leading from lagging metrics.
  • Hamel Husain [143]. A multi-part "Stop saying RAG is dead" series featuring guest talks.
  • Chip Huyen [147]. Places retrieval inside a full GenAI platform reference architecture.
  • Simon Willison [148]. A running tag archive of RAG experiments and commentary.
  • Jerry Liu, AI Engineer [149]. A production-ready RAG talk: start with table-stakes tuning (chunk size, metadata filters, hybrid search), then move to small-to-big retrieval and agents.

22.7 Cross-cutting lessons from the corpus

The same failure modes come up again and again across the sources:

  1. Parsing loses structure. Uber's policy PDFs [45], the messy-PDF warnings in [160], and the ColPali line of work [20][112] all point at ingestion as the first place quality drops.
  2. Chunks lose their document. Contextual Retrieval [91], late chunking [117] and small-to-big retrieval [123] are three answers to the same problem at different points in the pipeline: before embedding, inside the encoder, and after retrieval.
  3. Lexical signals still matter. Hybrid BM25 plus vector search shows up at Uber [45], Glean [69], Anthropic [91] and AWS [78], and in Applied LLMs' advice [141].
  4. Global questions break top-k. GraphRAG [96][97] and BenchmarkQED [102] show that bigger context windows do not substitute for structure on whole-corpus questions. Databricks [77] shows that quality falls past 32-64k tokens for many models.
  5. The last 20% is most of the work. LinkedIn's 80%-to-95% timeline [47] and Genie's 48.9% helpfulness rate [164] suggest planning for months of evaluation-driven iteration.
  6. Agentic retrieval is a cost decision. Anthropic's 15x token multiplier [94] and the Uber and EAg-RAG trade-offs [45][37] put agentic retrieval in the "high-value queries only" tier.

22.8 Key takeaways for system designers

  • Start from retrieval metrics, not answer vibes. Build a labeled or synthetic retrieval set and track recall@k, MRR and failure rate before tuning prompts [91][124][144]. Anthropic's 5.7% to 1.9% failure progression is a template for this kind of ablation.
  • Default to hybrid retrieval plus a reranker, and over-fetch before reranking (for example 150 candidates down to 20) [91][105][109].
  • Fix context loss at index time when the corpus is stable (Contextual Retrieval at about $1.02 per million tokens) and at query time when it churns (just-in-time agent retrieval) [91][93].
  • Choose index topology by question type. Use vectors for local lookups. Use graph or community structures for global sensemaking, and prefer budgeted, deferred variants (LazyGraphRAG) when indexing cost matters [101][102].
  • Constrain the output space when you can. Ramp's NAICS classification and Pinterest's table selection turn generation into choosing among retrieved candidates, which removes whole classes of hallucination [57][50].
  • Put cheap checks first. Use a similarity guardrail before an LLM evaluator, and a cheap LLM to prune communities before an expensive one [46][100].
  • Tenancy is architecture. Permission-aware retrieval (Glean) and per-customer storage (Harvey with LanceDB) must be designed in from the start [69][66].
  • Code RAG is an indexing problem. Incremental Merkle sync, syntactic chunking, content-hash caches and domain-trained embedders give the largest gains [59][61].
  • Treat agentic RAG as a tier, not a default. Route only complex or high-stakes queries through multi-step agents [94][95][37].
  • Design retrieval tools for agents, not humans. Targeted search tools, bounded and paginated responses, and readable identifiers behind a standard protocol such as MCP [236][237].
  • Partition retrieval by domain before you search. Uber's workspaces, Swiggy's charters and Pinterest's top-tier table index all shrink the candidate set and assign ownership of metadata quality [172][174][50].
  • Let the system say "not enough context". Sufficiency signals and abstention trade a little coverage for accuracy. DoorDash's guardrail does the same at the post-generation layer [196][46].
  • Benchmark continuously and automatically. Synthetic query generation and LLM-judge pairwise evaluation (BenchmarkQED, Ragas, ARES) make regression testing affordable [102][28][29].
