31. Real-Time and Time-Aware RAG: Streaming Ingestion, Temporal Retrieval and Staleness Evaluation

Overview

Most RAG systems quietly assume the corpus is fixed: documents are parsed, chunked, embedded and indexed once, and every query reads the same snapshot. That assumption fails in three common situations.

  1. The source of truth changes continuously. Product catalogs, tickets, CRM rows, wiki pages, prices, on-call rotas. If the index lags the database, the system answers from the past without saying so.
  2. The question is about "now". "Who is the current CEO?", "What did the Fed decide this week?", "Which alerts fired in the last hour?" Here the right document depends on when the question is asked, not only on what it says.
  3. The question is about a time in the past. "Who coached the team in 2014?", "What did the runbook say before the March change?" Here the system has to pick the version of a fact that was valid at a stated time, and ignore newer versions.

This chapter treats these as one design space with three layers:

  • Freshness of the index: change data capture (CDC), Kafka/Flink/Pathway-style streaming pipelines, and in-database "vectorizers" that keep embeddings in step with the source [14][15][16][17][19].
  • Time-awareness of retrieval and ranking: recency decay functions, time-weighted retrievers, valid-time (bi-temporal) fact stores and versioned datasets [20][21][22][13][26].
  • Evaluation of staleness and temporal reasoning: FreshQA, RealTime QA, TimeQA, SituatedQA, StreamingQA, TempLAMA, TempRAGEval, TemporalWiki and LongMemEval [1][4][6][8][9][10][11][30][31].

It closes with two application families where time is the main axis: news- and market-feed RAG [25], and event-stream/log RAG for observability and SIEM copilots [23][24].

A note on sourcing: claims below are tied to repository READMEs, documentation sources or source code read directly. Where a paper's numbers could not be checked against its PDF, the text says so and does not quote them.

          THE THREE LAYERS OF TIME IN A RAG SYSTEM

  +-------------------+     +---------------------+     +-------------------+
  |  SOURCE SYSTEMS   |     |  INDEX / KNOWLEDGE  |     |  QUERY + ANSWER   |
  |  OLTP DB, docs,   | --> |  vectors, BM25,     | --> |  retrieve, rank,  |
  |  feeds, logs      |     |  temporal KG, vers. |     |  generate, cite   |
  +-------------------+     +---------------------+     +-------------------+
        |                           |                          |
   (1) INDEX FRESHNESS        (2) TEMPORAL MODEL         (3) TEMPORAL INTENT
   lag from commit to         valid-time vs              "now" vs "as of T"
   searchable                 transaction-time           recency vs relevance
        \___________________________|__________________________/
                                    |
                      (4) STALENESS EVALUATION
              index lag SLOs, fast-changing QA sets, canaries

1. Why time breaks the default RAG pipeline

1.1 Failure taxonomy

Time-related RAG failures fall into a small number of types. Benchmarks in Section 5 test most of them.

Failure Example Root cause Layer
Index lag Price changed 10 min ago, answer quotes old price Batch re-index, slow embed queue Ingestion
Zombie documents Deleted policy still retrieved Deletes not propagated to vector store Ingestion
Recency blindness Retrieves a 2019 article for "latest guidance" Pure semantic similarity ranks on topic, not date Ranking
Over-recency Retrieves yesterday's tweet over the canonical spec Decay too steep, or applied to time-invariant queries Ranking
Wrong version Answers "as of 2014" with the 2022 holder No valid-time model; latest version overwrote history Data model
Parametric override LLM ignores fresh context and answers from training data Knowledge conflict (see Chapter 29) Generation
False premise "Why did X resign?" when X never resigned Model accepts the premise Generation

FreshQA's design targets the last row on purpose: it includes false-premise questions next to never-changing, slow-changing and fast-changing ones [1][2].

1.2 Two clocks: valid time and transaction time

Database theory separates two timestamps, and temporal RAG needs both:

  • Valid time: when a fact was true in the world ("Alice was VP of Sales from 2021-03 to 2024-07").
  • Transaction (system) time: when the system learned or recorded the fact (the row was written on 2024-07-15; the vector was indexed at 10:02:13).

Recency ranking usually runs on one of these, sometimes on the wrong one. Zep's Graphiti framework keeps both explicitly. Its README describes "explicit bi-temporal tracking with automatic fact invalidation", where "old facts are invalidated, not deleted" so a caller can "query what's true now, or what was true at any point in time" [13]. A news article adds a third clock, publication time, which StreamingQA records as evidence_ts next to the question's own question_ts [9].

2. Streaming ingestion into vector indexes

2.1 The CDC pattern: Debezium + Kafka as the change log

Problem. An application writes to Postgres/MySQL/Mongo. The RAG index must reflect inserts, updates and deletes without the application doing "dual writes" to the database and the vector store.

Architecture. Debezium describes itself as "a low latency data streaming platform for change data capture". It watches a database's replication log and emits one event per committed row-level change. "Only committed changes are visible, so your application doesn't have to worry about transactions or changes that are rolled back" [14]. Each connector runs inside Kafka Connect, watches one upstream server, and writes changes to Kafka topics, "typically one topic per database table". Kafka gives total ordering per table, so consumers that stop and restart "resume exactly where they left off" [14].

The Debezium README names "update search indexes" as a reason to avoid dual writes. If an application crashes after the database commit but before the secondary write, the systems fall out of sync. CDC moves that work into a separate consumer that cannot miss events [14]. A vector index is one more such derived read model, in the CQRS sense the README also describes [14].

   CDC -> STREAM -> EMBED -> VECTOR SINK (canonical streaming RAG ingestion)

  +-----------+  WAL/binlog  +-----------+   topic per table   +----------------+
  | Postgres  | -----------> | Debezium  | ------------------> | Kafka          |
  | (OLTP)    |              | (Connect) |   c/u/d events      | (ordered log)  |
  +-----------+              +-----------+                     +-------+--------+
                                                                       |
                         +---------------------------------------------+
                         v
              +------------------------+     +-------------------+
              | Stream processor       |     | Embedding service |
              | Flink / Pathway /      |<--->| (batched, cached, |
              | Bytewax: parse, chunk, |     |  rate-limited)    |
              | dedupe, key by doc_id  |     +-------------------+
              +-----------+------------+
                          | upsert(doc_id#chunk_i, vec, payload{ts,...})
                          | delete(doc_id#*) on tombstone
                          v
              +------------------------+       +----------------------+
              | Vector / hybrid index  | <---- | Query service (RAG)  |
              | Qdrant/Milvus/Mongo/ES |       | filters on ts fields |
              +------------------------+       +----------------------+

Key techniques.

  • Key everything by a stable document ID. A changed row must replace all of its old chunks. Re-chunking a longer text can produce a different number of chunks, so the sink must delete doc_id#* before upserting, or keep a doc-to-chunk manifest.
  • Propagate tombstones. Deletes are the change most often lost. Sink support varies. Qdrant's sink "supports streaming dense/sparse/multi vectors into Qdrant collections", requires the collection "to be created in advance with the appropriate vector dimensions", and does handle Kafka tombstones: on a record with a null value it deletes the point whose id appears in the record key [18]. Note that this deletes one point, so a document split into many chunks needs one tombstone per chunk ID (or a manifest-driven delete upstream). The Milvus sink requires the Kafka message schema to match the collection schema, "containing one and only one vector field" [18]. Check how each sink handles deletes before relying on it.
  • Carry timestamps as payload. Each point should store at least source_updated_at (transaction time from the CDC event), indexed_at, and, where known, valid-time or publication-time fields. These feed the recency ranking and staleness metrics later.

Failure modes. Schema drift between topic and collection [18]; embedding-API outages that back up the stream; cross-partition reordering of one document's chunks; lost deletes; and re-embedding storms when a field outside the embedded text changes.

2.2 Flink-native RAG: Confluent Cloud streaming agents

Confluent's public quickstart shows a version where the whole RAG flow is a chain of Flink SQL tables over Kafka topics [17]. Lab 2, "Vector Search & RAG", deploys a chain of Flink tables (the walkthrough says six, but lists seven), named so they sort in pipeline order: documents, documents_embed, documents_vectordb_lab2, queries, queries_embed, search_results and search_results_response. It also deploys two registered models (llm_embedding_model, llm_textgen_model) and a MongoDB sink connector that "stream[s] embeddings from documents_embed to Atlas" [17].

The design choice that matters: queries are events too. A question "land[s] in the queries topic, which immediately feeds into queries_embed", and search results and answers appear as rows downstream [17]. Retrieval and generation become durable, replayable, joinable streams, which helps auditing and offline evaluation at the cost of per-hop latency and a less natural synchronous API. Other labs add MCP tool calling and CREATE AGENT definitions [17]. Apache Flink now also has a Flink Agents sub-project [19], and open-source Flink itself has gained native AI operators (Section 2.5) [29].

     QUERIES-AS-STREAMS (Confluent quickstart Lab 2 shape)

  documents --> documents_embed --> [Mongo Atlas sink] --> vector index
                                                               ^
  queries ----> queries_embed ----> search_results ------------+ (vector search)
                                         |
                                         v
                              search_results_response  (LLM answer + snippets)

2.3 Incremental dataflow engines: Pathway

Problem. Keep a vector plus full-text index live over files, SharePoint, Google Drive, Kafka and Postgres, without running a separate vector DB, cache and API layer.

Architecture. Pathway is a Python framework whose code runs on "a scalable Rust engine based on Differential Dataflow" that "performs incremental computation" [16]. Its LLM app templates "connect and sync (all new data additions, deletions, updates)" with sources including "Kafka, PostgreSQL, real-time data APIs". They build vector, hybrid and full-text indexes "in-memory, with cache": usearch for vectors and Tantivy for full text [16]. The live document-indexing template runs connectors that "poll the changes with low latency". Each change is reflected in internal tables, then parsed with unstructured, chunked, embedded and indexed. The service exposes /v1/retrieve, /v1/statistics (indexer health) and /v1/inputs (files currently indexed) [16].

Distinctive technique: answer-change alerting. The Google Drive alert template goes further than a fresh index. After answering a query, Pathway "monitors changes to documents and selectively re-triggers potentially affected queries. If the new answer is significantly different from the previously presented one, a new notification is created" [16]. This is a standing query: the reverse of normal RAG, where a data change triggers the answer. It suits compliance and deal-desk uses ("tell me if the campaign start date changes").

Consistency and scale claims. Pathway "manages late and out-of-order points by updating its results whenever new (or late...) data points come into the system". The free version gives at-least-once consistency; the enterprise version gives exactly-once [16]. The templates are said to scale to "millions of pages of documents" [16]. The README also states Pathway is "made to outperform" Flink, Spark and Kafka Streams. That is a vendor claim this chapter has not verified independently.

2.4 In-database vectorizers: pgai Vectorizer

Problem. Many RAG corpora already live in Postgres. Running Kafka and Flink just to keep embeddings in sync is heavy.

Architecture. Timescale's pgai Vectorizer treats embeddings as "a declarative, DDL-like feature, akin to an index". A single ai.create_vectorizer(...) call names the source table, the column to embed, the destination table and the embedding model. Embeddings then stay "continuously synchronized with source data (asynchronously)" [15]. The system has three parts: the application, the database (which holds a work queue) and "stateless vectorizer workers" that "process the data queue into embeddings and chunked text" and write results back [15].

Key properties.

  • Failure isolation. Application writes only enqueue work; the background worker makes embedding generation "resilient to intermittent LLM endpoint failures" [15], so an embedding outage grows the backlog instead of failing the source transaction.
  • Tunable freshness. Each worker drains the queue until it is empty. It then sleeps for a configurable --poll-interval (default five minutes) and runs with a configurable -c/--concurrency number of async tasks [15]. So the index-lag ceiling is roughly poll interval plus queue drain time.
  • Built-in staleness telemetry. The ai.vectorizer_status view exposes pending_items. It returns max-bigint once the backlog passes 10,000; an exact count needs ai.vectorizer_queue_pending(id, exact_count=>true) [15]. This is the simplest public example of index lag exposed as a first-class metric.

Lesson / caveat. The pgai README states that "as of February 2026, this project is no longer being maintained or supported" [15]. The pattern (queue table, async workers, pending-items metric) is still a sound reference design. Teams adopting it should treat the code as a starting point to fork, not a supported dependency.

Python teams that want custom logic in the "stream processor" box often use Bytewax, "a Python framework and Rust-based distributed processing engine for stateful event and stream processing" with Kafka inputs, windowing and state recovery [19]. Checkpointed state means a restart does not re-embed the whole topic.

2.5 Native AI operators in open-source Flink (2.1 and 2.2, 2025)

The Confluent design in Section 2.2 relied on vendor-specific SQL extensions. Apache Flink has since moved much of this into the open-source engine. The Flink 2.1 release notes describe a Model DDL that lets users "define and manage AI models programmatically through the Table API in both Java and Python", and an expanded ML_PREDICT table-valued function "to perform realtime model inference in SQL queries" [29]. Flink 2.2 adds VECTOR_SEARCH, "provided in Flink 2.2 to enable users to perform streaming vector similarity searches", closing a gap the notes state directly: Flink previously "lacks real-time online querying and similarity analysis capabilities for vector spaces" [29]. Together they make an all-Flink pipeline possible: CDC topic in, ML_PREDICT for embeddings, VECTOR_SEARCH against an external store for each streaming query event, ML_PREDICT again for generation. The queries-as-streams trade-offs of Section 2.2 (durable, replayable, auditable, but higher per-hop latency) apply unchanged.

2.6 Comparison of ingestion designs

Design Change source Freshness knob Deletes Ops weight Best fit
Debezium + Kafka + sink [14][18] DB replication log Consumer lag; sink batch size Tombstones; check sink support High (Kafka, Connect) Many sources, many consumers, audit
Flink SQL pipeline (Confluent; OSS Flink 2.1+/2.2) [17][29] Kafka topics Per-hop streaming latency Modeled in SQL Medium (managed) Queries and answers as replayable streams
Pathway live index [16] Connectors (FS, Drive, SharePoint, Kafka, PG) Connector polling; incremental dataflow Yes ("deletions, updates") Low-medium (single service) Doc-centric live RAG, answer-change alerts
pgai Vectorizer [15] Postgres table changes via queue --poll-interval, --concurrency Synced with source rows Low (Postgres + workers) Postgres-resident corpora; now unmaintained
Bytewax / custom [19] Kafka, files, sockets Window size, checkpoint cadence Developer-implemented Medium Python teams with custom logic
Nightly batch re-index Full scan Cron period (hours to days) Implicit on full rebuild Low Slow-changing corpora only

3. Recency-weighted ranking and time decay

Once timestamps are in the index, the ranker has to decide how much age should count. Public implementations fall into three groups: search-engine decay functions, framework time-weighted retrievers, and hard recency filters or sorts.

3.1 Elasticsearch/OpenSearch decay functions

Elasticsearch's function_score query supports gauss, exp and linear decay over numeric, date or geo fields. Each is set by origin, scale, optional offset and optional decay. For date fields, origin defaults to now and accepts date math such as now-1h [20]. The documented semantics, written in plain text:

  • decay is the score a document gets at distance scale from origin +/- offset (default 0.5). Documents within offset of origin are not penalized [20].
  • gauss: S = exp(-max(0, |t - origin| - offset)^2 / (2 * sigma^2)), with sigma^2 = -scale^2 / (2 * ln(decay)) [20].
  • exp: S = exp(lambda * max(0, |t - origin| - offset)), with lambda = ln(decay) / scale [20].
  • linear: falls to exactly 0 once the distance passes scale / (1 - decay). With the default decay of 0.5 that is twice the scale. "In contrast to the normal and exponential decay, this function actually sets the score to 0" past that point [20].

The docs' own date example uses origin: 2013-09-17, scale: 10d, offset: 5d, decay: 0.5. Documents from 09-12 to 09-22 get weight 1.0, and documents 15 days out get 0.5 [20]. Function scores combine with the text or vector score through score_mode and boost_mode, and per-function weight [20].

Design guidance. exp with scale = half-life and decay = 0.5 gives a true half-life. gauss keeps recent items nearly flat and then drops sharply, which suits "this week's news". linear is the only one that removes old items entirely, which is dangerous for evergreen content. The offset parameter is the main tool against over-recency: it defines a grace window in which age does not count.

3.2 LangChain TimeWeightedVectorStoreRetriever

LangChain's retriever "combines embedding similarity with recency" [21]. From the source:

  • Score = (1 - decay_rate) ** hours_passed + vector_relevance + sum(other_score_keys). The terms are added, not multiplied, and other_score_keys can bring in fields such as importance [21].
  • decay_rate defaults to 0.01, so a document loses half its recency term after about 69 hours (0.99^69 is about 0.5).
  • hours_passed is measured from last_accessed_at, not creation time. Each retrieval resets last_accessed_at for the returned documents "to ensure frequently accessed memories aren't forgotten" [21].
  • The retriever always considers the last k items in its in-memory memory_stream, plus the vector store's top results (default search_kwargs={"k": 100}), and returns k documents (default 4) [21].
  • The last_accessed_at refresh is applied to the in-memory copies only; a TODO in the source notes the vector store entries are not updated [21]. After a restart, recency falls back to whatever timestamp was persisted.

This scoring comes from agent memory, in the style of Generative Agents' combination of recency, importance and relevance [27]. Its semantics are access recency, not content freshness. Pointed at a news or policy corpus without changes, it keeps popular stale documents high because reading them refreshes their timestamp. For content freshness, swap the date field for a publication or update time and turn off the access refresh.

3.3 LlamaIndex recency postprocessors

LlamaIndex provides three node postprocessors [22]:

  • FixedRecencyPostprocessor: sorts candidates by a metadata date field and keeps the newest top_k (default 1). This is a hard "latest wins" rule.
  • EmbeddingRecencyPostprocessor: sorts by date, then walks from newest to oldest. It drops older nodes whose embedding similarity to a newer node passes a cutoff (default 0.7). The query template tells the embedder that the other documents "are older than the current document, meaning that certain details may be changed" [22]. This is version de-duplication: keep the newest version of each near-duplicate, drop its ancestors.
  • TimeWeightedPostprocessor: score = similarity + (1 - time_decay) ** hours_passed, using a __last_accessed__ key and refreshing it on access by default [22].

A parameter trap. In TimeWeightedPostprocessor the default is time_decay=0.99, and the formula is (1 - time_decay) ** hours. So the recency term is 0.01 after one hour and close to 0 after two [22]. LangChain uses the same exponent form with decay_rate=0.01, which gives a 69-hour half-life [21]. Two libraries with the same formula and similar parameter names can therefore produce half-lives that differ by about two orders of magnitude. Always convert decay settings into an explicit half-life and test them. The source also contains a commented-out, unused LLM prompt that classifies whether a question "requires finding the most recent context" [22]. That is the query-intent gate discussed next.

3.4 Temporal-intent gating

Every public implementation above applies decay without regard to the query. That fixes recency blindness but causes over-recency on time-invariant questions. FreshQA's split of questions into never-changing, slow-changing and fast-changing [1][2] shows the problem: decay helps the third group and can hurt the first. SituatedQA's first task, "Context-Dependent Question Identification", is a binary classifier for "whether the answer to a given question does or does not depend on the extra-linguistic contexts" [8]. That is the gate a production system needs. A practical design:

              TEMPORAL-INTENT-GATED RETRIEVAL

  query --> [temporal intent classifier] --+-- "timeless"  --> pure relevance
              (LLM prompt or small model)  |
                                           +-- "current"   --> relevance x decay(now)
                                           |                   + filter valid_to=NULL
                                           |
                                           +-- "as of T"   --> valid_from<=T<valid_to
                                           |                   decay centered on T
                                           +-- "range"     --> filter ts in [T1,T2]
                                                               (logs, events)

The "as of T" branch reuses Elasticsearch's origin parameter. Centering the decay on a past date instead of now [20] turns recency ranking into temporal-proximity ranking, which is what TimeQA- and SituatedQA-style questions need [6][8].

3.5 Research: time-aware retrievers

TempRALM (Gade and Jetcheva, 2024) adds a temporal term to a retriever's score next to semantic relevance. It is a published example of learned or parameterized time-aware scoring inside an Atlas-style RAG model [12]. MRAG (Zhang et al., 2024) proposes a modular framework for time-sensitive QA. It separates the question's main content from its temporal constraint, retrieves and summarizes evidence, and then ranks with a hybrid semantic-plus-temporal score. The same paper introduces TempRAGEval [11]. The PDFs of [11] and [12] could not be fetched in this research session. This chapter therefore describes only their overall approach and does not quote their numbers.

4. Valid-time and versioned document retrieval

4.1 Temporal knowledge graphs: Zep / Graphiti

Problem. Agent memory and enterprise knowledge contain facts that change ("Kendra loves Adidas shoes (as of March 2026)") [13]. Overwriting the old fact loses history. Keeping both without validity windows lets the retriever surface contradictions.

Architecture. Graphiti builds a "temporal context graph" of entities (nodes), facts (edges as entity-relationship-entity triplets "with temporal validity windows"), episodes (the raw ingested data, which carries provenance) and communities [13]. Its key mechanisms:

  • Incremental construction. "New data integrates immediately without batch recomputation" [13].
  • Automatic invalidation. When new information contradicts an edge, the old edge is closed (its validity ends). It is not deleted, so point-in-time queries still work [13].
  • Hybrid retrieval. Semantic embeddings, BM25 and graph traversal, with "typically sub-second latency". The README contrasts this with "seconds to tens of seconds" for batch GraphRAG-style summarization [13].
  • LLM-dependent extraction. Entity/edge extraction and dedupe depend on structured JSON output, and the README routes edge resolution and dedupe to specific models [13].

The design is described in the Zep paper, "Zep: A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory" [13].

        BI-TEMPORAL FACT EDGE (Graphiti-style)

   (Alice) --[ROLE: VP Sales]--> (Acme)
        valid_from = 2021-03     valid_to = 2024-07      <- world time
        created_at = 2021-03-04  invalidated_at = 2024-07-15  <- system time
        episode_ref = slack#88213 (provenance)

   (Alice) --[ROLE: CRO]-------> (Acme)
        valid_from = 2024-07     valid_to = NULL (current)

   "Who runs sales now?"      -> edges with valid_to = NULL
   "Who ran sales in 2022?"   -> edges with valid_from <= 2022 < valid_to
   "What did we believe on 2024-07-10?" -> filter on created/invalidated (system time)

Failure modes. Extraction errors become permanent "facts". Contradiction detection depends on the LLM. Valid-time has to be inferred from text, and text often states dates loosely ("last spring"). The third query type above, "what did the system believe at time T", only works if system time is stored separately from valid time.

4.2 Versioned vector datasets

When the unit is a document, not a fact, versioning the index itself is often simpler. Lance, the format under LanceDB, advertises "zero-copy versioning: automatic versioning with ACID transactions, time travel, tags, and branches" [26]. For RAG this enables reproducible evals pinned to a dataset version, as-of retrieval for audit ("what would the assistant have said on date D"), and safe re-embedding on a branch before promotion. The costs are storage growth and compaction. Version time travel follows transaction time only, not valid time inside a document.

4.3 Document-level valid-time schema

For a plain vector store, the minimal schema that supports both "current" and "as of" queries is metadata on each chunk:

Field Clock Used for
doc_id, version - Replace/delete all chunks of a version; dedupe
valid_from, valid_to (NULL = current) Valid time "Current" filter; "as of T" filter
published_at / source_updated_at Valid/publication Recency decay origin
indexed_at Transaction time Index-lag metrics; audit
superseded_by - Point the generator to the newer version

An update then writes the new version and closes the old one (sets valid_to) instead of deleting it. Queries with "current" intent filter valid_to IS NULL. This is Graphiti's invalidate-not-delete rule applied to documents [13]. Benchmarks such as SituatedQA store gold answers with explicit start and end dates. Their sampled contexts are drawn "between an answer's start and end dates" [8], and that is exactly the data needed to test the as-of filter.

4.4 Contrast: append-only memory with time-aware ranking (Mem0)

Not every memory layer invalidates. Mem0's 2026 README describes the opposite choice: "Single-pass ADD-only extraction -- one LLM call, no UPDATE/DELETE. Memories accumulate; nothing is overwritten." Temporal correctness then moves from the write path to the read path, as "time-aware retrieval that ranks the right dated instance for queries about current state, past events, and upcoming plans" [32]. The README reports large gains on LongMemEval (Section 5.9) and LoCoMo for this version, but labels them as managed-platform results that open-source users should expect to be "directionally similar ... but not identical" [32]. Treat them as vendor claims.

The two designs trade cost differently. Invalidate-on-write (Graphiti) pays an LLM contradiction check per ingest and keeps reads simple (valid_to IS NULL). Append-only (Mem0) keeps ingest cheap but puts every "which version is current?" decision on the ranker at query time, so a ranking error shows up as a stale answer with no record marked superseded.

5. Temporal QA benchmarks

5.1 FreshQA / FreshLLMs (Google, UMass; 2023, continuously updated)

What it tests. Whether an LLM, with or without search augmentation, answers questions whose answers change, including false-premise questions. The paper is "FreshLLMs: Refreshing Large Language Models with Search Engine Augmentation" [1].

Distinctive design: a living benchmark. The dataset is published as dated snapshots. The repository lists versions from February 2024 through April 21, 2026, roughly weekly at first and less often later. It states the maintainers "update our dataset weekly or upon request" [2]. An eval result is therefore only meaningful with its snapshot date.

Method: FreshPrompt. The paper's few-shot prompting method puts search-engine results into the prompt. A public notebook implements it [2]. The README states that FreshQA and FreshPrompt have "inspired or been used for the development of" Google's Gemini, Perplexity's online LLMs, You.com's API and Contextual AI's RAG 2.0 [2].

Evaluation. Two modes. Relaxed judges whether the main answer is correct. Strict also penalizes any hallucinated or outdated claim in the response. The maintainers say human raters are the most reliable judges. They also release FreshEval, "a simple automatic metric that uses few-shot in-context learning to teach an LLM to judge model responses" with "high agreement with human raters", and recommend a specific GPT-4 snapshot (gpt-4-1106-preview) as the judge [2]. You.com reported FreshQA recall as a cheaper overlap metric [2]. The README points to SealQA as a follow-up that builds on FreshQA "with a stronger focus on reasoning", released on Hugging Face (vtllms/sealqa) [3].

Lesson. The strict-versus-relaxed gap measures staleness inside the answer. A RAG system can retrieve the current fact and still repeat an outdated parametric claim elsewhere in its response. Only strict mode catches that.

5.2 RealTime QA (UW, AI2, Tohoku; NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks)

What it tests. "A dynamic question answering (QA) platform that inquires about the present." The organizers announce about 30 questions on a regular schedule (weekly in the released version) and evaluate baseline systems such as GPT-3 and T5 [5]. The submission window "closes when the next set of questions is announced (3 am GMT on every Saturday)" [5].

Baselines. Six real-time baselines run every week. They pair retrieval from Google Custom Search or DPR with readers, in multiple-choice and open-generation settings. The repository publishes the retrieval results of each run [5]. Real-time baselines started on June 17, 2022, and "backnumber" questions cover the earlier period [5]. The paper is Kasai et al. [4].

Lesson. RealTime QA treats freshness as a scheduled, continuously graded property: every week brings questions no training set could contain, a template for internal staleness evaluation (Section 7).

5.3 TimeQA (UCSB; NeurIPS 2021 Datasets and Benchmarks)

What it tests. "Existing reading comprehension models' capability to perform temporal reasoning, and ... whether they are sensitive to the temporal description in the given question" [7]. Crowd workers annotated passages with "time-evolving facts". Template-synthesized train/dev/test splits were then built in easy and hard versions, plus a human-written test set [7]. Baselines are BigBird (extractive) and Fusion-in-Decoder (generative), initialized from NQ or TriviaQA checkpoints. An open-domain setting uses a TF-IDF/BM25 retriever [7]. The paper is Chen, Wang and Wang [6].

Lesson for RAG. TimeQA separates retrieving the right passage from reading the right time slice inside it. One Wikipedia passage can hold several valid-time intervals. Chunking that splits a passage across interval boundaries, or a reader that ignores "in 2009" or "before 2009", fails even with perfect retrieval.

5.4 SituatedQA (UT Austin/UW; EMNLP 2021)

SituatedQA covers questions whose answers depend on temporal or geographical context [8]. Its temporal task pairs each question with a date. Dates are either sampled "between an answer's start and end dates" or set to the answer's start or end. Gold answers come from NaturalQuestions, and an edited_question folds the context into the text [8]. Its context-dependence classification task is a ready-made training set for the temporal intent gate in Section 3.4 [8].

5.5 StreamingQA (DeepMind; 2022)

StreamingQA evaluates "adaptation to new knowledge over time in question answering models". It is built on a deduplicated subset of the English WMT News Crawl, with document files spanning 2007 to 2020 [9]. Each QA item records question_ts (when the question is asked) and evidence_ts (when the evidence article was published). It also records a recent_or_past split and whether the item was written by humans or generated [9]. The authors estimate that about 0.5% of items remain toxic after filtering. They warn that answers "reflect information from the news articles, and ... may not always be factually correct" [9]. Both points matter for news-RAG evaluation sets built the same way.

5.6 TempLAMA (Google; TACL 2022)

TempLAMA probes language models as temporal knowledge bases, using cloze queries built from a November 1, 2020 Wikidata dump [10]. That dump is no longer downloadable, so rebuilding today gives "slightly different" data [10], a small staleness lesson in its own right.

5.7 TempRAGEval (2024)

TempRAGEval was introduced with MRAG [11]. It evaluates time-sensitive QA end to end in a RAG setting, scoring both retrieval and answer accuracy on questions with temporal constraints. The paper's dataset statistics and results could not be fetched in this session, so the chapter only names it as the RAG-specific complement to the reader-focused TimeQA and SituatedQA.

5.8 TemporalWiki (KAIST; EMNLP 2022)

TemporalWiki is "a lifelong benchmark for training and evaluating ever-evolving language models" [30]. It is built from consecutive English Wikipedia snapshots (the released data covers five monthly snapshots, 2021.08 to 2021.12). TWiki_Diffsets hold only what changed between snapshots, and TWiki_Probes test whether updated models know the new and unchanged facts [30]. It frames freshness as a diff problem: how cheaply can a system absorb only the changed knowledge? That is the parametric counterpart of CDC-driven re-indexing in Section 2, and the diffsets are a convenient test corpus for incremental indexing pipelines.

5.9 LongMemEval (ICLR 2025)

LongMemEval benchmarks "chat assistants on long-term interactive memory" with 500 questions over long multi-session chat histories [31]. Two of its five core abilities are temporal: knowledge updates (the user's facts changed across sessions; answer with the latest) and temporal reasoning (questions that depend on when things were said), next to information extraction, multi-session reasoning and abstention [31]. It is the de facto yardstick for agent-memory systems such as Zep/Graphiti and Mem0 (Section 4), and the knowledge-update category is a direct test of invalidate-versus-append designs.

5.10 Benchmark comparison

Benchmark Year Corpus / source Temporal axis tested Live? Eval
FreshQA [1][2] 2023 to 2026 Curated Qs; web search Never/slow/fast-changing, false premise Yes, dated snapshots Human; FreshEval relaxed/strict
SealQA [3] 2025 Builds on FreshQA Reasoning over noisy/conflicting search Not stated See paper
RealTime QA [4][5] 2022 to 2023 News; GCS/DPR retrieval "Now" (this week's events) Yes, weekly MC accuracy; open-gen
TimeQA [6][7] 2021 Wikipedia time-evolving facts Time-scoped reading (easy/hard) No EM/F1 style
SituatedQA [8] 2021 NaturalQuestions Answer as of a date; context-dependence ID No EM style
StreamingQA [9] 2022 WMT News 2007 to 2020 Question time vs evidence time; recent vs past No (time-sliced) Multi-reference
TempLAMA [10] 2022 Wikidata (Nov 2020) Facts with time qualifiers No Cloze accuracy
TempRAGEval [11] 2024 Derived from temporal QA sets RAG retrieval + answer under time constraints No Retrieval + QA
TemporalWiki [30] 2022 Monthly Wikipedia snapshots + diffs Absorbing changed vs unchanged knowledge Time-sliced Probe accuracy
LongMemEval [31] 2024 to 2025 Multi-session chat histories (500 Qs) Knowledge updates; temporal reasoning in memory No QA accuracy (LLM-judged)

6. Application families where time is the main axis

6.1 News- and market-feed RAG

Problem. Finance is "highly dynamic". FinGPT's README makes the economic case for retrieval over retraining. It cites BloombergGPT's training at about 53 days and roughly $3M; its own table estimates about $2.67M on 512 A100s. It contrasts that with "less than $300 per fine-tuning" for lightweight adaptation [25][28]. Even weekly fine-tuning leaves gaps of days, so the newest market information has to arrive through retrieval.

Architecture patterns (FinGPT). FinGPT describes a layered stack. A data-source layer "addressing the temporal sensitivity of financial data through real-time information capture". A data-engineering layer for "real-time NLP data processing" that handles "high temporal sensitivity and low signal-to-noise ratio". Above those sit model and application layers [25]. Two components are relevant here:

  • FinGPT-RAG: "a retrieval-augmented large language model framework specifically designed for financial sentiment analysis", published at ICAIF-23 [25].
  • FinGPT-Forecaster: takes a ticker, a prediction date, "the number of past weeks where market news are retrieved", and an optional flag to add the latest basic financials. It then produces an analysis and a next-week price-movement prediction [25]. The retrieval window here is an explicit, user-set time range anchored to a chosen date, the "range" branch of the intent gate. It also prevents look-ahead leakage in backtests.

Lessons for feed RAG.

  • Point-in-time correctness is a hard constraint in finance. A backtest that retrieves news published after the prediction date is invalid. Filter on publication time no later than the as-of date. StreamingQA's question_ts and evidence_ts fields are the evaluation version of this rule [9].
  • Dedupe syndicated stories. Wire stories get republished many times. Newest-wins near-duplicate collapse (LlamaIndex's EmbeddingRecencyPostprocessor pattern [22]) stops one event from filling the context window.
  • Decay on publication time, not on ingestion or access time. See the pitfalls in Sections 3.2 and 3.3.

6.2 Event-stream and log RAG: observability copilots

Logs, metrics and traces are append-only, high-volume and mostly time-range queried. Embedding every log line is rarely worth it. Public observability copilots instead treat the time-series backends as tools and the LLM as the query planner.

Grafana MCP server. Grafana's MCP server exposes tools that let an agent run PromQL range and instant queries, run LogQL log and metric queries against Loki, read Loki label and stream metadata, and pull log patterns "detected by Loki to identify common log structures and anomalies" [24]. It also covers Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, Quickwit, ClickHouse, CloudWatch and Google Cloud Logging. Cloud Logging results come back "newest-first with severity, body, labels, and trace ID". Other tools cover alert rules, incidents and a hand-off to Grafana Assistant that "may use tools, metrics, logs, and other stack context" [24].

Retrieval here means generating a time-bounded query, so freshness is close to perfect by construction. The hard parts move elsewhere:

  • Choosing the time window. "What broke after the deploy?" needs the deploy time first.
  • Compressing results. Log patterns are a pre-aggregation that turns millions of lines into a few dozen templates the LLM can read [24].
  • Permissions. Each tool maps to fine-grained Grafana RBAC scopes, such as datasources:query on a specific datasource UID [24].
        OBSERVABILITY COPILOT: TOOL-MEDIATED TEMPORAL RETRIEVAL

  user: "why did p99 latency spike after 14:00?"
     |
     v
  +--------------+  1. alert rules / incidents   +---------------------+
  |  LLM agent   | ----------------------------> | Grafana / Alerting  |
  |  (planner)   |  2. PromQL range [13:30,15:00]| Prometheus / Mimir  |
  |              | ----------------------------> |                     |
  |              |  3. Loki patterns, same range | Loki                |
  |              | ----------------------------> |                     |
  |              |  4. runbook / postmortem RAG  | vector KB (static)  |
  +------+-------+ ----------------------------> +---------------------+
         |
         v   answer = live telemetry (exact time range) + static knowledge (semantic)

6.3 SIEM copilots: Elastic AI Assistant for Security

Elastic's AI Assistant for Security is a clear public example of mixing a time-windowed live feed with a semantic knowledge base:

  • Alerts as recency-bounded context. The "Knowledge base for alerts" feature sends open or acknowledged alerts from the last 24 hours. They are "ordered by risk score, then by the most recently generated", and building-block alerts are excluded [23]. A slider sets how many alerts to include. The docs warn that too many alerts "may cause your request to exceed the maximum token length", so the count is a user-tuned context budget [23]. This is a hard recency window followed by a sort on importance then recency, which is the same idea as LangChain's importance-plus-recency score [21], done with filters instead of a decay function.
  • Indices as live knowledge sources. Admins can add whole Elasticsearch indices (asset inventories, on-call matrices, threat intel reports, vulnerability scans). "When you update the index with new information, AI Assistant will gain access to the new information". Each source has a natural-language "Query Instruction" and a list of output fields [23]. Freshness is inherited from the index, with no separate embedding pipeline. Indices must have a semantic_text field, or from 9.1 a plain text field, which "perform[s] better for retrieval based on specific document values or attributes, such as email or username" [23].
  • A dated static corpus. The knowledge base comes pre-loaded with Elastic Security Labs articles "current through September 30, 2024" [23]. Even a vendor's curated corpus has a stated freshness horizon. Stating it, as Elastic does, is good practice.
  • User-asserted memory with time. Entries such as "Remember that I changed my password today, October 24, 2024" carry their date in the text [23], a simple form of valid-time stamping.
  • From 9.1 the agent uses "index names and field metadata" to improve ES|QL generation [23]. Event retrieval is again partly query generation, not only vector search.

7. Evaluating staleness

The benchmarks in Section 5 measure whether a model handles time-dependent questions. A production team also needs to measure whether its own pipeline is stale. The public sources above suggest a layered method. The metric names below are this chapter's synthesis; the components come from the cited systems.

7.1 Pipeline-level metrics (does the index lag the source?)

Metric Definition Public precedent
Index lag (p50/p99) indexed_at - source_updated_at per change event Debezium event timestamps [14]; pgai queue [15]
Backlog Changes captured but not yet embedded pgai pending_items [15]; Kafka consumer lag
Delete propagation lag Time from source delete to absence in top-k Tombstones in CDC [14]
Coverage Source docs present in index / source docs Pathway /v1/inputs, /v1/statistics [16]
Corpus horizon Newest published_at in each static KB Elastic Security Labs "through Sept 30, 2024" [23]

Set freshness SLOs per source, for example "p99 index lag under 60 s for pricing; under 24 h for wiki". Alert on them like any other data-pipeline SLO. With poll-based workers, the poll interval plus the drain time bounds lag from below. A five-minute default poll [15] means sub-minute freshness is impossible without retuning.

7.2 Canary facts (end-to-end freshness probes)

Borrow RealTime QA's continuous schedule [5] for internal use:

  1. On a schedule, write a synthetic, uniquely identifiable fact into each source system ("Canary 7f3a: the test SKU price is 41.17"). Also update or delete a previous canary.
  2. Query the RAG endpoint with the matching question on a schedule.
  3. Record time-to-correct-answer, time-to-forget for deleted canaries, and whether the answer cites the new version.

This catches failures that pipeline metrics miss: caching layers, a reranker that buries fresh chunks, decay misconfiguration (Section 3.3), and the generator preferring parametric knowledge.

7.3 Answer-level temporal evaluation

  • Build a FreshQA-style internal set split into never-, slow- and fast-changing questions [1][2]. Re-label answers for fast-changing items on a schedule and version the set by date, as FreshQA does [2].
  • Score strict and relaxed [2]. The strict-minus-relaxed gap shows outdated claims mixed into otherwise-correct answers.
  • Include false-premise and "as of T" items. For as-of items, store gold answers with validity intervals, following SituatedQA's start and end dates [8]. Test both the "current" and the "as of a past date" query paths.
  • Check for look-ahead leakage in any backtest or historical eval. Assert that every retrieved evidence_ts is no later than question_ts [9].
  • Pin the corpus version for regression tests, using dataset time travel [26]. Otherwise score changes mix retriever changes with corpus drift.
  • LLM judges. FreshEval shows few-shot LLM judges can approximate human ratings on freshness [2]. Its authors still prefer human raters and pin a specific judge model, because judge drift is itself a temporal confound.

7.4 Ranking-level diagnostics

  • Compare the age distribution of retrieved chunks with the corpus's, per intent class: timeless queries should show little skew, "current" queries should skew young.
  • Track the superseded-hit rate, the share of retrieved chunks with a superseded_by pointer. A high rate means valid-time filtering is broken.

8. Reference architecture

            REFERENCE: TIME-AWARE STREAMING RAG

  SOURCES             INGEST                    STORES                QUERY
  -------             ------                    ------                -----
  OLTP DB --CDC--+                        +-> vector/hybrid idx --+
  Docs/Drive ----+--> stream processor ---+   (valid_from/to,      |   +----------+
  News feeds ----+    chunk, dedupe,      |    published_at,       +-->| intent   |
  Kafka topics --+    version, embed      |    indexed_at)         |   | gate     |
                      (batch+retry)       +-> temporal KG ---------+   +----+-----+
                           |              |   (bi-temporal edges)  |        |
                           |              +-> versioned snapshot --+   timeless/now/
                           v                  (time travel, eval)  |   as-of/range
                    lag + backlog metrics                          |        |
                           |                LIVE TELEMETRY ---------+   +---v------+
                           v                (Prom/Loki/SIEM via     |   | retrieve |
                    freshness SLO alerts     tools, time-bounded)   +-->| + decay  |
                           ^                                            | + filter |
                           |                                            +----+-----+
                    canary writer/prober <------------------------------+    |
                                                                       +-----v-----+
                                                                       | generate  |
                                                                       | cite dates|
                                                                       +-----------+

Key takeaways for system designers

  1. Use CDC instead of dual writes. A vector index is a derived read model. Feed it from the database's committed change log (Debezium + Kafka) or an in-database queue (the pgai pattern), never from application-side dual writes [14][15].
  2. Deletes and re-chunking are the hard part. Key chunks by stable doc_id and version, delete all chunks of a superseded version, and test tombstone handling in every sink connector [14][18].
  3. Expose index lag as a first-class metric. pgai's pending_items view [15] and Pathway's /v1/statistics endpoint [16] are the public examples. Set per-source freshness SLOs, and remember that poll intervals set a floor on lag.
  4. Store at least three timestamps per chunk: valid time, publication/update time and indexed time. Most temporal bugs come from decaying or filtering on the wrong clock.
  5. Convert every decay parameter into a half-life. LangChain's default is about 69 hours. LlamaIndex's TimeWeightedPostprocessor default effectively zeroes the recency term after about an hour. Both use the same formula shape [21][22]. Elasticsearch's exp with decay=0.5 makes scale the half-life, and offset gives a grace window [20].
  6. Access recency is not content freshness. Retrievers that refresh last_accessed_at on read are memory heuristics [21][27]. For document corpora, decay on publication or update time.
  7. Gate decay on temporal intent. Classify queries as timeless, current, as-of-T or range (SituatedQA provides training data for this gate [8]). Apply decay only to "current". Re-center on T for as-of. Use hard filters for ranges.
  8. Invalidate, don't delete, when history matters. Bi-temporal edges (Graphiti [13]) or valid_to closure on document versions support both "now" and "as of" queries, plus audit of what the system believed at a given time.
  9. For logs and telemetry, retrieval is query generation. Observability and SIEM copilots get freshness by running time-bounded PromQL/LogQL/ES|QL through tools, then compressing results (log patterns, risk-sorted alerts) to fit the context budget [23][24].
  10. Evaluate freshness continuously, not once. Use dated, re-labeled question sets (FreshQA [2]), scheduled question batches (RealTime QA [5]), strict scoring for outdated claims [2], canary facts for end-to-end lag, and look-ahead-leakage checks on any historical eval [9].
  11. State the corpus horizon to users. If a knowledge base is current only through a date, say so, as Elastic does for its Security Labs corpus [23]. That makes a silent staleness failure a visible, known limit.

32. Personalized and Conversational RAG: User Profiles, Per-User Scopes, Conversational Search, Voice Latency, Clarification and Shopping Assistants

Overview

Chapter 18 covered long-term memory: how an assistant decides what to remember about a user and how it stores and recalls those memories. This chapter covers the retrieval problems around that memory store. They arise when the same question should get different answers for different users, or when the query is not a self-contained string but the latest turn of a conversation. Six design problems recur:

  1. Profile-as-corpus personalization. The user's own history (past reviews, emails, papers, tweets, purchases) is treated as a small private corpus. Retrieval picks the few items that should condition generation. LaMP and LongLaMP are the reference benchmarks [1][5].
  2. Personal-knowledge retrieval inside a conversation. TREC iKAT gives each simulated user a Personal Text Knowledge Base (PTKB) of natural-language statements. Systems must rank those statements and web passages at every turn and produce a grounded, cited answer [7][9].
  3. Context-dependent query understanding. TREC CAsT (2019-2022) made conversational query rewriting and conversational dense retrieval standard components [11][13][14].
  4. Per-user indexes and access scopes. Personal corpora have to be isolated from each other at scale. Vector databases now offer tenant shards, payload-partitioned tenants and partition keys for this [25][26][27].
  5. Retrieval under a voice latency budget. Realtime speech-to-speech assistants (OpenAI Realtime, Gemini Live) must hide retrieval latency behind speech. They use filler preambles, supervisor delegation and non-blocking tool calls [19][20][21][22].
  6. Clarify or answer. Mixed-initiative systems must decide when to ask a clarifying question instead of retrieving. Qulac, ClariQ, CAsT 2022's mixed-initiative subtask and the clarification steps in deep-research agents cover this decision [15][16][17][18].

The chapter ends with retrieval for recommendation and shopping assistants: tool-based conversational recommenders [28], product-search relevance data [30], and the public outlines of Amazon Rufus and Instacart's LLM search features [31][32]. Section 32.9 then surveys 2024-2026 benchmarks for personalized QA, evolving preferences and multi-turn enterprise RAG [34]-[38].

Coverage note. arXiv, vendor documentation sites (platform.openai.com, ai.google.dev), amazon.science, aboutamazon.com, tech.instacart.com and trecikat.com could not be reached from the research environment for this chapter, and web search was unavailable. Facts here therefore come mostly from primary GitHub sources: benchmark repositories, official topic files, baseline code, SDK source and official cookbooks. Paper-level claims are taken from the abstracts the authors reproduce in their repositories. The Rufus and Instacart sections are short and flagged, because their primary posts could not be re-read. Statistics on iKAT topics were computed for this chapter from the official topic JSON files [9] and were re-computed during fact-checking with the same results. Section 32.9 adds 2024-2026 benchmarks (LaMP-QA, PersonaMem, PrefEval, CORAL, MTRAG and MTRAG-UN), again described from their official repositories [34]-[38].

                        | profile retrieval (LaMP)      | (Ch. 18)    | recsys tools
 user turn t --> [context resolver] --> rewritten query + selected profile facts
